weeks.title: FAR U3·W1 — Statement of Cash Flows (CPA Core · from CMA m2/m8)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — profit is not cash

MBG can post net income and still run short of cash — the CMA program's whole liquidity thread (months 2 and 8). The statement of cash flows reconciles the two by sorting every cash movement into three activities and reconciling net income to operating cash. FAR tests its structure, the classification of each item, and the indirect-method reconciliation.

Three sections

  • Operating — cash effects of transactions that enter net income (collections from customers, payments to suppliers and employees). Interest received, interest paid, and dividends received are operating under US GAAP.
  • Investing — buying and selling long-term assets and investments (equipment purchases, proceeds on disposals).
  • Financing — transactions with owners and lenders (issuing/repaying debt, issuing stock, paying dividends).

The classic trap: interest paid is operating, but dividends paid are financing.

Direct versus indirect

Only the operating section differs between methods. The direct method lists actual operating cash receipts and payments. The indirect method (far more common) starts with net income and adjusts for non-cash items and working-capital changes. Investing and financing sections are identical either way, and a reconciliation of net income to operating cash is required even under the direct method.

Indirect-method reconciliation

Starting from net income, add back non-cash expenses (depreciation, amortization), reverse gains/losses on asset sales (they belong in investing), and adjust for changes in operating working capital: an increase in a current asset uses cash (subtract), an increase in a current liability provides cash (add).

Illustrative: net income $988,000; + depreciation $80,000; − increase in accounts receivable $120,000; − increase in contract assets $100,000; + increase in accounts payable $60,000. Operating cash flow = $988,000 + $80,000 − $120,000 − $100,000 + $60,000 = $908,000. The $80,000 add-back is the same depreciation from FAR Unit 1; the contract-asset increase is the underbilling growth from ASC 606.

Non-cash and disclosures

Significant non-cash investing and financing activities — acquiring equipment with a capital lease, converting debt to equity, exchanging assets — are not in the body of the statement but are disclosed separately. Cash paid for interest and for income taxes is also disclosed under the indirect method. The statement reconciles beginning to ending cash and cash equivalents.

The direct method line by line

The direct method restates each accrual figure to its cash counterpart. Cash collected from customers = sales − the increase in accounts receivable (or plus a decrease). Cash paid to suppliers = cost of goods sold + the increase in inventory − the increase in accounts payable. Cash paid to employees = wage expense − the increase in wages payable. Cash paid for taxes = tax expense − the increase in income-taxes payable − the increase in a deferred tax liability + the increase in a deferred tax asset (signs reverse for decreases) — both deferred-tax movements back out the non-cash portion of tax expense. The sum of these cash flows equals the same operating total the indirect method reaches from net income — only the presentation differs. FASB encourages the direct method for clarity, but most filers choose indirect, which is why the indirect reconciliation is the one the exam drills hardest.

Finding investing cash flows from the accounts

Investing figures are usually reconstructed from asset accounts rather than handed to you. Suppose equipment that cost $90,000 with $50,000 of accumulated depreciation is sold at a $10,000 gain: proceeds = book value $40,000 + gain $10,000 = $50,000, reported as an investing inflow, while the $10,000 gain is subtracted in the operating section so it is not counted twice. Equipment purchases are found by rolling the gross asset account: beginning balance + purchases − cost of assets sold = ending balance. The same T-account logic recovers proceeds, purchases, and — with accumulated depreciation — the depreciation add-back, a favorite multi-step exam pattern.

Financing cash flows and non-cash conversions

The financing section captures changes in debt and equity for cash: issuing bonds or stock (inflows), repaying principal, repurchasing treasury shares, and paying dividends (outflows). Two subtleties recur. First, only the cash portion appears — converting bonds to stock or declaring a stock dividend are non-cash and are disclosed, not shown in the body. Second, dividends paid = dividends declared − the increase in dividends payable, because declaration and payment can straddle year-end. Repayment of principal is financing, but the interest on that same debt is operating — the split that catches the unwary.

Cash equivalents and special reconciling items

Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments with an original maturity of three months or less (Treasury bills, money-market funds); the statement reconciles beginning to ending cash and cash equivalents, so buying a T-bill is not an investing flow. Beyond depreciation, several non-cash items adjust the indirect reconciliation: equity-method income is subtracted (and dividends received added) because earnings exceed cash received; deferred tax expense is added back as a non-cash charge; stock-based compensation is added back; and amortization of a bond discount is added (it raised interest expense without cash). Each restates an accrual that moved net income but not cash.

IFRS contrast

IAS 7 permits more classification choice. Interest and dividends paid may be shown as either operating or financing, and interest and dividends received as either operating or investing, provided the choice is applied consistently — versus US GAAP, which fixes interest (paid and received) and dividends received in operating and dividends paid in financing. IFRS also allows bank overdrafts repayable on demand to be included within cash and cash equivalents, whereas US GAAP generally treats them as financing. Both frameworks allow the direct or indirect method and require the three-way operating/investing/financing structure, so the architecture is shared even where the line-item rules diverge.

A worked direct-method operating section

Tie the direct method back to the same facts. With operations producing $988,000 of net income, cash collected from customers is sales minus the $120,000 rise in receivables and the $100,000 growth in contract assets (an unbilled receivable, so it belongs in the collections bridge); cash paid for operating costs is the related expenses adjusted for the $60,000 rise in payables; and depreciation never appears because it is non-cash. When every operating receipt and payment is listed and netted, the direct method arrives at the identical $908,000 of operating cash the indirect reconciliation produced — proof that the two methods present one number, not two different results. Because a filer choosing the direct method must still show the indirect bridge, candidates have to be fluent in both directions: from net income to cash, and from each accrual line to its cash equivalent. A related analyst measure, free cash flow — operating cash flow minus capital expenditures — is not a required GAAP line but is built straight from this statement, underscoring why the cash-flow statement, not the income statement, is where liquidity is ultimately judged.

CMA bridge

CMA month 2 built the 13-week cash forecast and month 8 the cash conversion cycle; FAR formalizes the historical statement of cash flows with its three sections and the indirect reconciliation. The $80,000 depreciation and the contract-asset movement tie straight back to the FAR units before this.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify each cash flow as operating, investing, or financing (interest paid = operating; dividends paid = financing).
  2. Know that only the operating section differs between direct and indirect.
  3. Reconcile net income to operating cash: add non-cash items; increase in current asset subtract, increase in current liability add.
  4. Disclose significant non-cash investing/financing activities.

Recap: the statement sorts cash into operating, investing, and financing; the indirect method reconciles $988,000 of net income to $908,000 of operating cash by adding back $80,000 depreciation and adjusting working-capital changes — and interest paid is operating while dividends paid are financing.

weeks.title: FAR U3·W2 — Governmental Accounting (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — a different rulebook entirely

Governmental accounting is its own FAR world: a different standard-setter (GASB, not FASB), fund accounting, and a measurement basis that does not exist in business accounting. MBG itself is a private company, but state and local governments are major construction clients, so understanding how a municipality accounts for the project it hires MBG to build is genuinely useful — and it is heavily tested.

Fund accounting and the standard-setter

The Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) sets standards for state and local governments. Governments account through funds — self-balancing sets of accounts for specific activities — grouped into three categories:

  • Governmental funds: general, special revenue, capital projects, debt service, and permanent funds.
  • Proprietary funds: enterprise (services to the public for a fee, e.g., a water utility) and internal service funds.
  • Fiduciary funds: custodial and trust funds held for others.

Two measurement focuses and bases

This is the heart of the topic:

  • Governmental funds use the current financial resources measurement focus and the modified accrual basis. They report fund balance, not net position, and record expenditures (not expenses).
  • Proprietary and fiduciary funds, and the government-wide statements, use the economic resources focus and full accrual basis — like a business.

Under modified accrual, revenue is recognized when it is measurable and available (collectible within the period or soon enough after — commonly within 60 days — to pay current liabilities), and expenditures are recognized when the related liability is incurred. So a long-lived asset purchase is an expenditure in full when acquired in a governmental fund, with no depreciation in that fund.

Government-wide versus fund statements

A government presents both government-wide statements (full accrual, economic resources, all activities together except fiduciary) and fund financial statements (governmental funds on modified accrual). A reconciliation bridges the two — for example, adding back capital assets and long-term debt that the fund statements do not carry. Encumbrance accounting reserves budgetary resources when a purchase order is issued, a budgetary control unique to governments.

The five governmental fund types

Within the governmental category each fund has a job. The General Fund accounts for all resources not required to be in another fund — the main operating fund. Special revenue funds account for revenues legally restricted to specific purposes (a gas-tax fund for road maintenance). Capital projects funds account for resources used to acquire or build major capital assets (the school a municipality hires a contractor to construct). Debt service funds accumulate resources to pay principal and interest on general long-term debt. Permanent funds report resources legally restricted so that only earnings, not principal, may be spent (a cemetery-care endowment). The capital assets built through a capital projects fund and the bonds that financed them do not sit in the fund — they appear only in the government-wide statements.

Fund balance classifications

GASB 54 sorts governmental-fund fund balance into a hierarchy reflecting how constrained the resources are: nonspendable (not in spendable form — inventory, prepaids, the principal of a permanent fund), restricted (constrained by external parties or law), committed (constrained by the government’s highest decision-making authority), assigned (intended for a purpose but not formally committed), and unassigned (the residual, found mainly in the General Fund). The classification communicates spending constraints to users and is a reliable exam item — distinguishing committed (formal action) from assigned (mere intent) in particular.

Nonexchange revenue recognition

Governments earn much revenue without an exchange, and GASB sorts these into four classes. Derived tax revenues (sales and income taxes) are recognized when the underlying transaction occurs. Imposed nonexchange revenues (property taxes, fines) are recognized in the period for which they are levied — property tax is recorded when an enforceable legal claim arises and recognized for the budget year it funds. Government-mandated and voluntary nonexchange transactions (grants) are recognized when all eligibility requirements are met. On modified accrual the additional available criterion still applies — revenue measurable but not yet available is deferred as a liability.

Budgetary accounting and encumbrances

Governments record their legally adopted budget in the accounts. The opening budgetary entry debits Estimated revenues, credits Appropriations (the spending authority), and books the difference to budgetary fund balance. During the year, issuing a purchase order records an encumbrance — debit Encumbrances, credit budgetary fund balance reserved for encumbrances — reserving appropriation so the government cannot overspend. When the goods arrive, the encumbrance is reversed and the actual expenditure and liability are recorded. Encumbrances are not expenditures and not GAAP-basis expenses; they are a budgetary control, and any outstanding at year-end are disclosed as commitments.

The government-wide statements and net position

The two government-wide statements use full accrual. The Statement of Net Position reports all assets and deferred outflows less liabilities and deferred inflows, with the residual net position split into net investment in capital assets, restricted, and unrestricted. The Statement of Activities uses a distinctive net-(expense)/revenue format: each function’s direct expenses are reduced by its program revenues (charges for services, operating and capital grants) to show the net cost borne by taxpayers, with general revenues (taxes) reported below. Fiduciary activities are excluded from the government-wide statements because the resources are not the government’s to use.

Reconciliation and the reporting package

Because the fund statements (modified accrual) and government-wide statements (full accrual) differ, a reconciliation bridges them: it adds back the capital assets (net of accumulated depreciation) and the long-term debt that governmental funds do not report, and converts capital-outlay and debt-principal expenditures back to the accrual measures. The full annual report — the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) — wraps the basic statements with Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) and other required supplementary information (RSI) such as the budgetary comparison schedule. Proprietary funds add a statement of cash flows with four categories (operating, noncapital financing, capital and related financing, and investing) — note the two financing categories, unlike the single financing section in business accounting.

Interfund activity and capital project flows

Resources move between funds, and the labels matter. Interfund transfers (the General Fund subsidizing a debt service fund) are reported as other financing sources/uses, not revenues or expenditures. Interfund loans create a due-to/due-from and are not revenue at all. When a city issues bonds in a capital projects fund to build a school, the proceeds are an other financing source — the fund records no long-term liability, since that debt appears only government-wide — and the construction payments to the contractor are expenditures as incurred. The matching debt service fund later records principal and interest as expenditures only when due and payable, not as they accrue — another modified-accrual hallmark. Special items and significant one-time flows, when present, are reported separately below the normal revenues and expenditures so users can see them distinctly.

CMA bridge

CMA taught accrual job-cost accounting for a private builder; governmental accounting flips several assumptions — modified accrual, expenditures instead of expenses, and no depreciation in governmental funds. Recognizing where business GAAP does and does not apply is the exam skill.

Practice and recap

  1. Know GASB sets state/local government standards and the three fund categories.
  2. Governmental funds: current financial resources + modified accrual + expenditures.
  3. Proprietary/fiduciary and government-wide: economic resources + full accrual.
  4. Modified-accrual revenue = measurable and available; reconcile fund to government-wide statements.

Recap: governments use fund accounting under GASB; governmental funds run on modified accrual (revenue when measurable and available, expenditures when incurred, no depreciation) while proprietary funds and the government-wide statements use full accrual.

weeks.title: FAR U3·W3 — Not-for-Profit Accounting (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — two net-asset buckets, not retained earnings

Not-for-profit entities (charities, foundations, private universities, many hospitals) follow FASB but with their own twists: equity is called net assets and split by donor restriction, and contributions are the defining transaction. The construction connection is real — MBG-style builders frequently work for nonprofits and faith-based developers — and FAR tests NFP every form.

Two classes of net assets

Under current standards, an NFP reports just two classes of net assets:

  • Net assets without donor restrictions — available for any purpose at the board's discretion.
  • Net assets with donor restrictions — limited by donors as to purpose or time (including permanently restricted endowments).

When a donor restriction is satisfied (the purpose is fulfilled or the time passes), the amount is reclassified from net assets with donor restrictions to net assets without donor restrictions — shown as a "net assets released from restrictions" line.

Contributions

A contribution is an unconditional, nonreciprocal transfer of assets. It is recognized as revenue at fair value when received or unconditionally promised (a pledge). Classify it by whether the donor imposed a restriction.

A conditional contribution — one with a barrier the NFP must overcome and a right of return if it does not — is not recognized until the condition is substantially met; cash received in advance is a refundable liability. Distinguish a condition (a barrier) from a restriction (a donor limit on use): a conditional gift is not yet revenue, while a restricted gift is revenue now, just in the restricted class.

Exchange versus contribution

An exchange transaction is reciprocal — the NFP provides commensurate value (tuition, a service fee) — and follows ASC 606 revenue recognition. A contribution is nonreciprocal. Many transactions are part-exchange, part-contribution (a $500 gala ticket for a $100 dinner has a $400 contribution element).

Statements and donated items

NFPs present a statement of financial position, a statement of activities, and a statement of cash flows; expenses are reported by function (program services vs supporting — management and general, and fundraising) and by nature. Donated services are recognized only if they create or enhance a nonfinancial asset, or require specialized skills the donor possesses and the NFP would otherwise buy. Donated materials are recognized at fair value.

Endowments and UPMIFA

An endowment is a fund meant to be invested with the principal preserved. A donor-restricted endowment (the donor requires principal be held permanently or for a term) sits in net assets with donor restrictions; a board-designated endowment — a quasi-endowment — is the board’s own earmarking of unrestricted funds and stays in net assets without donor restrictions, because a board can reverse its own designation. Most states’ UPMIFA statute governs spending: absent explicit donor terms, the original gift amount is classified as restricted and appreciation is restricted until appropriated for spending. An underwater endowment — fair value below the original gift — is still reported within net assets with donor restrictions, with the shortfall disclosed.

Promises to give and investment return

Unconditional promises to give collectible in future years are recorded at the present value of expected cash flows, with the discount accreted to contribution revenue over time, and reduced by an allowance for uncollectible pledges. Investment returns — interest, dividends, and realized and unrealized gains on endowment and other investments — are reported net of external and direct internal investment expenses and classified by the presence or absence of donor restrictions on the income. A donor may restrict the income of an endowment even when the principal is permanent, so the return can land in either net-asset class depending on the gift terms.

Required statements and functional expenses

Every NFP must present an analysis of expenses by both function and natural classification — historically a separate statement of functional expenses, now required of all NFPs in some form (statement, schedule, or notes). Functions divide into program services (the mission) and supporting services (management and general, fundraising, and membership development). Costs that benefit more than one function are allocated, and the methods are disclosed; the program-to-supporting ratio is a metric donors and watchdogs scrutinize. The core statements remain the statement of financial position, the statement of activities (showing the change in each net-asset class), and the statement of cash flows.

Liquidity, agency transactions, and contributed assets

ASU 2016-14 added a required liquidity and availability disclosure: qualitative information on how the NFP manages liquidity plus a quantitative measure of financial assets available within one year to meet general expenditures, since donor restrictions can lock up resources. An agency (pass-through) transaction — where the NFP receives assets to transfer to a specified third party — is not contribution revenue; the NFP records a liability to the ultimate beneficiary. A gift of a long-lived asset (or cash restricted to acquire one) may be released from restriction either when placed in service or over the asset’s useful life, depending on the NFP’s accounting policy.

Healthcare NFPs and the bottom line

Not-for-profit healthcare entities add wrinkles: they report a performance indicator (analogous to income from operations) on the statement of operations, present patient service revenue net of contractual adjustments with explicit and implicit price concessions, and recognize charity care as a disclosure only (no revenue) because payment was never expected. Across all NFPs the through-line is the same: equity is net assets viewed through the lens of donor intent, contributions — not retained earnings — drive the change in net assets, and the statements exist to show whether the organization honored the restrictions attached to the resources entrusted to it.

Split-interest gifts and special events

Two recurring NFP transactions round out the picture. A split-interest agreement — a charitable remainder trust or charitable gift annuity — gives the NFP a future interest while another beneficiary receives payments for a time; the NFP recognizes contribution revenue for the present value of its expected residual interest and a liability for amounts owed to the other beneficiary, remeasured as actuarial assumptions update. A special event such as a gala is split into its exchange and contribution elements: the fair value of the direct benefit to the attendee (the meal) is exchange revenue, and the excess paid is a contribution. Worked split: a $500 gala ticket where the dinner’s fair value is $90 yields $90 of exchange revenue and a $410 contribution — and it is the fair value received, not whether the attendee shows up, that fixes the split. The direct costs of the benefit may be netted against special-event revenue or shown as a cost of supporting services, with the policy disclosed. These mechanics reinforce the unit’s core test — separate what the donor gave freely from what they received in return, and recognize each under its own rule.

CMA bridge

The contribution-recognition logic mirrors ASC 606's control and condition concepts from FAR Unit 1, and the functional-expense split parallels the responsibility-center thinking from CMA month 3 — here the categories are program versus supporting services.

Practice and recap

  1. Report two net-asset classes: with and without donor restrictions.
  2. Recognize contributions at fair value when unconditional; reclassify when restrictions are met.
  3. Do not recognize conditional contributions until the barrier is overcome.
  4. Separate exchange transactions (ASC 606) from contributions; report expenses by function.

Recap: NFPs split net assets into with- and without-donor-restriction classes, recognize unconditional contributions at fair value now and reclassify on release, defer conditional gifts until the barrier is met, and report expenses by function.

flashcards.front: Two net-asset classes for an NFP
flashcards.back: Net assets without donor restrictions and net assets with donor restrictions.

flashcards.front: When is an unconditional contribution recognized?
flashcards.back: At fair value when received or unconditionally promised (pledged).
A condition is a barrier (gift not yet revenue); a restriction is a donor limit on use (revenue now, restricted class).

flashcards.front: How is a conditional contribution treated before the condition is met?
flashcards.back: Not recognized as revenue; advance cash is a refundable liability.

flashcards.front: What happens when a donor restriction is satisfied?
flashcards.back: Reclassify from net assets with donor restrictions to without (net assets released from restrictions).
Exchange is reciprocal (ASC 606); contribution is nonreciprocal.
Only if they create/enhance a nonfinancial asset or require specialized skills the NFP would otherwise purchase.
By function (program services vs supporting: management/general and fundraising) and by nature.

questions.q: How many net-asset classes does an NFP report under current standards?
questions.explain: Current standards use two classes: with and without donor restrictions.

questions.q: An unconditional pledge to donate is recognized:
choices: At fair value when the promise is made
questions.explain: Unconditional contributions, including pledges, are recognized at fair value when promised.

questions.q: A gift with a barrier the NFP must overcome and a right of return is:
choices: A conditional contribution — not recognized until the condition is met
questions.explain: A conditional contribution is deferred until the barrier is substantially met.

questions.q: When a purpose restriction is satisfied, the amount is:
choices: Reclassified from with-restriction to without-restriction net assets
questions.explain: Satisfying a restriction reclassifies net assets (net assets released from restrictions).

questions.q: Tuition charged by a private university is primarily:
questions.explain: Tuition is reciprocal value — an exchange transaction recognized under ASC 606.

questions.q: NFP expenses must be reported by:
questions.explain: NFPs report expenses by function and by nature.

questions.q: Donated services are recognized only when they:
choices: Create/enhance a nonfinancial asset or require specialized skills otherwise purchased
questions.explain: Donated services are recognized only under the create/enhance or specialized-skills criteria.

weeks.title: FAR U3·W4 — Accounting Changes, Errors, Interim & Segment Reporting (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — restate, adjust, or just go forward?

When MBG changes how it accounts for something — or discovers a prior mistake — FAR prescribes exactly one of three treatments, and choosing the wrong one is a classic exam miss. The rule turns on whether it is a change in principle, a change in estimate, or an error. This week settles all three and adds interim and segment reporting.

The three treatments (ASC 250)

  • Change in accounting principle — switching from one acceptable GAAP method to another (e.g., FIFO to weighted-average inventory). Apply it retrospectively: restate prior periods presented and adjust the opening balance of retained earnings for the earliest period.
  • Change in accounting estimate — revising a judgment as new information arrives (useful life, salvage, bad-debt rate, warranty rate). Apply it prospectively: current and future periods only; do not touch prior periods.
  • Error correction — a mistake in previously issued statements (math error, misapplied GAAP, overlooked facts). Restate the prior periods (a prior-period adjustment to beginning retained earnings).

The depreciation-method trap

A change in depreciation method (say, double-declining-balance to straight-line) looks like a change in principle but is treated as a change in estimate effected by a change in principle — so it is accounted for prospectively, not retrospectively. This is one of FAR's favorite distractors: it is the prior estimate of how the asset is consumed that is changing.

A change in reporting entity (e.g., changing the entities in consolidated statements) is applied retrospectively, like a principle change.

Counterbalancing errors

Some errors counterbalance — they self-correct over two periods (e.g., an inventory misstatement reverses the next year). If found after two years and the books are closed, no entry is needed for the income effect, though prior-period statements presented still need correcting. Non-counterbalancing errors (e.g., a depreciation error) persist until fixed.

Interim and segment reporting

Interim reporting (ASC 270) generally treats each interim period as an integral part of the annual period: income taxes, for instance, use the estimated annual effective tax rate applied to year-to-date income. Segment reporting (ASC 280) uses the management approach — segments are reported the way management runs the business — and a segment is reportable if it meets any 10% threshold of total revenue, profit or loss, or assets, with reported segments covering at least 75% of external revenue.

Retrospective application and its limits

Applying a principle change retrospectively means restating each prior period presented as if the new method had always been used, and adjusting the opening retained earnings of the earliest period shown for the cumulative effect on still-earlier years. Only the direct effects (and related income-tax effects) are restated; indirect effects — such as a profit-sharing accrual that would have differed — are recognized in the period of change, not restated. When it is impracticable to determine the period-specific or cumulative effect (the data simply do not exist), the change is applied prospectively from the earliest practicable date — an explicit exception the exam tests against students who assume retrospective is always possible.

Disclosures and the justification requirement

A voluntary change in principle is permitted only if the new method is preferable, and management must justify that preferability — you cannot switch methods to smooth earnings at will. The change is disclosed with its nature and reason, the method of applying it, and the effect on income, per-share amounts, and affected line items for each period presented. A material change in estimate is disclosed as to its effect, and an error correction is disclosed as a restatement, including the nature of the error and the effect on each prior period and on opening retained earnings. This audit-trail discipline mirrors the integrity controls emphasized throughout the program.

Interim reporting — integral view and exceptions

Treating an interim period as an integral part of the year drives several rules. The estimated annual effective tax rate is re-estimated each quarter and applied year-to-date, so a later quarter catches up any change. Some costs that benefit the whole year may be allocated across interim periods. But several items are recognized discretely, in the period they occur: a permanent inventory write-down (a temporary market decline expected to reverse by year-end is not recognized), a loss contingency, and a LIFO liquidation expected to be replaced by year-end (interim cost of sales includes the expected replacement cost). Publicly traded companies present condensed interim statements under SEC rules, with minimum disclosures emphasizing seasonality and significant changes.

Segment reporting mechanics

Under the management approach, operating segments are the components whose results the chief operating decision maker reviews to allocate resources. A segment is reportable if it meets any one of three 10% tests: its revenue (including intersegment) is 10% or more of combined revenue; the absolute value of its profit or loss is 10% or more of the greater (in absolute value) of total segment profit or total segment loss; or its assets are 10% or more of combined segment assets. If the reportable segments’ combined external revenue is below 75% of consolidated revenue, add segments until the 75% threshold is met. Segments similar in economics and other factors may be aggregated.

A worked threshold and entity-wide disclosures

Worked test: total combined segment revenue is $10,000,000. A division with $1,300,000 of revenue clears the 10% revenue test ($1,300,000 > $1,000,000) and is reportable even if it runs at a loss, because any single 10% test suffices. Beyond segment detail, ASC 280 requires entity-wide disclosures regardless of segments: revenues from external customers by product or service and by geographic area (domestic versus foreign, with material individual countries), long-lived assets by geography, and the existence of any major customer providing 10% or more of total revenue (with the amount and segment, though the customer need not be named). These reveal the concentration information consolidated totals hide.

A worked counterbalancing error

Suppose ending inventory in Year 1 is understated by $30,000. Understated ending inventory overstates cost of goods sold and understates Year 1 net income by $30,000. Because Year 1 ending inventory is Year 2 beginning inventory, Year 2 cost of goods sold is understated and Year 2 net income is overstated by the same $30,000 — the error counterbalances, leaving retained earnings correct by the end of Year 2. If discovered during Year 2 before closing, correct both years; if discovered after Year 2 closes, retained earnings has already self-corrected and no income adjustment is needed, though any comparative statements still shown must be restated. A non-counterbalancing error — for example, capitalizing an item that should have been expensed — does not self-correct and must be fixed whenever found.

CMA bridge

CMA month 3 covered segment reporting for performance; FAR adds the ASC 280 quantitative thresholds and the management approach. The estimate-versus-principle distinction echoes the relevant-cost discipline — know precisely which rule applies before you compute.

Practice and recap

  1. Change in principle → retrospective; change in estimate → prospective; error → restate.
  2. A depreciation-method change is a change in estimate (prospective).
  3. Recognize counterbalancing errors that self-correct over two periods.
  4. Interim tax uses the estimated annual effective rate; segments use the management approach and 10% thresholds.

Recap: retrospective for principle and reporting-entity changes, prospective for estimates (including depreciation-method changes), and restatement for errors — while interim periods apply the estimated annual effective tax rate and segments follow the management approach with 10% reportability thresholds.

flashcards.back: Retrospective: restate prior periods and adjust opening retained earnings.
Prospective: current and future periods only.
Restate prior periods (prior-period adjustment to beginning retained earnings).
Change in estimate effected by a change in principle → prospective.
Retrospective.
An error that self-corrects over two periods (e.g., an inventory misstatement reversing next year).
Use the estimated annual effective tax rate applied to year-to-date income.
Reportable if a segment meets any 10% test of revenue, profit/loss, or assets (management approach).

units.title: FAR Unit 4 — Revenue Recognition, Inventory, PP&E/Intangibles & Pensions/Stock Comp

weeks.title: FAR U4·W1 — Revenue Recognition (ASC 606) (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — one model for all revenue

ASC 606 replaced dozens of industry rules with a single five-step model for recognizing revenue from contracts with customers. For MBG it is the engine behind construction revenue — the contract assets and liabilities from FAR Unit 1 and the percentage-of-completion the auditor scrutinizes both flow from this model. Master the five steps and the construction application falls out.

Step 1 — identify the contract

A contract exists when it has commercial substance, the parties have approved it and are committed, rights to goods/services and payment terms are identifiable, and collection is probable. If collection is not probable, there is no contract for revenue purposes and any cash received is a deposit (a liability) until the criteria are met. Contracts can be combined when negotiated as a package.

Step 2 — identify the performance obligations

A performance obligation is a promise to transfer a distinct good or service. A good or service is distinct if the customer can benefit from it on its own (or with readily available resources) and it is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract. A construction contract is usually a single performance obligation — the many activities (site work, framing, finishing) are integrated into one combined output, the building — so they are not accounted for separately.

Step 3 — determine the transaction price

The transaction price is the consideration the entity expects to be entitled to. It includes variable consideration (incentives, penalties, change orders, claims) estimated by the expected value or most likely amount, but constrained so revenue is recognized only to the extent a significant reversal is not probable. The price is also adjusted for a significant financing component (the time value of money when payment timing is far from transfer), noncash consideration (at fair value), and consideration payable to the customer (usually a reduction of revenue).

Step 4 — allocate the transaction price

When a contract has multiple performance obligations, the transaction price is allocated to each in proportion to its standalone selling price (SSP) — the price at which the entity would sell that good or service separately. When an SSP is not observable, it is estimated (adjusted market assessment, expected cost plus margin, or, as a residual, only in limited cases). A discount is generally allocated proportionately across all obligations unless evidence shows it relates to specific ones.

Step 5 — recognize revenue as obligations are satisfied

Revenue is recognized when (or as) the entity satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control. Control transfers either at a point in time (most goods — when the customer obtains physical possession, legal title, risks/rewards, and has accepted the asset) or over time. An obligation is satisfied over time if any one of three criteria is met: the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits; the entity creates or enhances an asset the customer controls; or the entity creates an asset with no alternative use and has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date.

Over-time recognition and construction

A typical construction contract meets the over-time criteria (the contractor builds on the customer's land, or the asset has no alternative use plus a right to payment), so MBG recognizes revenue over time using a measure of progress — an input method (cost-to-cost is the most common) or an output method (units or milestones). Worked example: a $5,000,000 contract with $3,000,000 of costs incurred against $4,000,000 of total estimated costs is 75% complete by cost-to-cost, so MBG recognizes $3,750,000 of revenue to date. When total costs are not reliably estimable, revenue is recognized only to the extent of recoverable costs until the estimate becomes reliable; an expected loss on the whole contract is recognized immediately.

Contract costs

Two cost types are capitalized rather than expensed. Incremental costs of obtaining a contract (a sales commission that would not have been incurred otherwise) are capitalized if the entity expects to recover them (with a practical expedient to expense them if the amortization period is one year or less). Costs to fulfill a contract (that are not in another standard) are capitalized when they relate directly to the contract, generate or enhance resources used to satisfy it, and are expected to be recovered. Both are amortized as the related revenue is recognized.

Special issues

Several recurring patterns: in a principal-versus-agent question, a principal controls the good/service before transfer and reports gross revenue, while an agent arranges for another party and reports only its net commission. A warranty that is merely assurance the product works is a cost accrual (not a separate obligation), but a service-type warranty the customer can buy separately is a distinct performance obligation. Licenses of intellectual property are recognized over time (a right to access) or at a point in time (a right to use) depending on whether the IP changes over the license period. Bill-and-hold and consignment arrangements turn on who controls the goods.

Contract modifications

A modification (a change order, common in construction) is treated three ways. If it adds distinct goods/services at their standalone price, it is a separate contract. If it adds distinct goods/services but not at standalone price, it is accounted for prospectively (terminate the old, create a new contract for the remaining work). If the remaining goods/services are not distinct (part of a single performance obligation, like most construction change orders), the modification is folded into the existing contract with a cumulative catch-up adjustment to revenue. Distinguishing these is a frequent exam and practice point for a contractor.

Presentation and disclosure

ASC 606 also reshapes presentation. A contract asset arises when the entity has performed but its right to payment is conditional on something other than the passage of time (MBG's underbillings); a receivable is an unconditional right to payment; and a contract liability arises when the customer pays before the entity performs (overbillings or deposits). Required disclosures include disaggregated revenue, the opening and closing contract balances, the remaining performance obligations (backlog), and the significant judgments made — the transparency that lets a reader of MBG's statements see how much work is sold but not yet earned.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 1 introduced the contract assets (underbillings) and contract liabilities (overbillings) that ASC 606 produces; this unit supplies the full five-step engine behind them. The cost-to-cost measure of progress is the same percentage-of-completion the CMA WIP accounting computes and the auditor re-performs — revenue recognition is where the construction numbers originate.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply the five steps: identify the contract, the performance obligations, the transaction price, allocate by standalone selling price, and recognize as control transfers.
  2. Estimate variable consideration (expected value or most likely amount) subject to the constraint; adjust for significant financing and consideration payable to the customer.
  3. Recognize over time when one of the three criteria is met; use cost-to-cost for construction; book an expected contract loss immediately.
  4. Capitalize incremental costs to obtain and costs to fulfill; classify modifications as separate, prospective, or cumulative catch-up.

Recap: ASC 606's five-step model recognizes revenue as control transfers — a construction contract is usually one performance obligation satisfied over time, so a $5,000,000 job that is 75% complete by cost-to-cost recognizes $3,750,000; variable consideration is constrained, the transaction price is allocated by standalone selling price, expected losses are booked immediately, and change orders are separate, prospective, or a cumulative catch-up depending on whether the added work is distinct.

flashcards.back: 1) Identify the contract; 2) identify performance obligations; 3) determine the transaction price; 4) allocate by standalone selling price; 5) recognize revenue as control transfers.
The customer can benefit from the good/service on its own AND it is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract.
Estimated by expected value or most likely amount, CONSTRAINED so revenue is recognized only to the extent a significant reversal is not probable.
Customer simultaneously receives/consumes benefits; entity creates/enhances an asset the customer controls; OR no alternative use + enforceable right to payment for performance to date.
Costs incurred ÷ total estimated costs = % complete; applied to the transaction price (e.g., 75% of $5,000,000 = $3,750,000).
Recognized immediately and in full when total estimated costs exceed the contract price.
A principal controls the good/service before transfer and reports gross revenue; an agent arranges for another and reports only its net commission.
Separate contract (distinct + standalone price); prospective (distinct, not standalone); cumulative catch-up (not distinct — typical construction change order).

questions.q: The five steps of ASC 606 begin by:
choices: Identifying the contract with a customer
questions.explain: Step 1 is identifying the contract; recognition is the final step.

questions.q: Variable consideration is included in the transaction price:
choices: Only to the extent a significant reversal is not probable (the constraint)
questions.explain: Variable consideration is estimated but constrained to avoid a probable significant reversal.

questions.q: A construction contract is typically recognized:
choices: Over time, using a measure of progress
At a point in time at completion
Only when the building is sold
questions.explain: Construction usually meets an over-time criterion (no alternative use + right to payment, or customer-controlled asset).

questions.q: A $5,000,000 contract has incurred $3,000,000 of $4,000,000 total estimated costs. Revenue recognized to date (cost-to-cost) is:
An expected loss on a contract is:
questions.explain: A provision for the entire expected loss is recognized as soon as it is probable.

questions.q: The transaction price is allocated to multiple performance obligations based on:
questions.explain: Allocation is in proportion to each obligation's standalone selling price.

questions.q: An entity that controls a good before transferring it to the customer is a(n):
questions.explain: A principal controls the good before transfer and reports gross revenue; an agent reports net.

weeks.title: FAR U4·W2 — Inventory & Cost of Goods Sold (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — which cost leaves and which stays

Inventory accounting answers one question: when identical units cost different amounts, which cost flows to cost of goods sold and which stays in ending inventory? The choice of cost-flow assumption swings reported profit and the balance sheet, especially when prices change. MBG carries construction materials, but the principles apply to any inventory the exam throws at you.

Cost-flow assumptions

Four methods assign cost. Specific identification tracks each actual unit (used for unique, high-value items). FIFO (first-in, first-out) sends the oldest costs to COGS, leaving the newest in ending inventory. LIFO (last-in, first-out) sends the newest costs to COGS, leaving the oldest in inventory. Weighted average uses an average unit cost. In a period of rising prices, FIFO produces the highest ending inventory and net income (and the highest taxes), while LIFO produces the lowest — the recurring exam contrast.

Periodic versus perpetual systems

A perpetual system updates inventory and COGS continuously with each sale; a periodic system updates only at period end via a physical count (beginning inventory + purchases − ending inventory = COGS). The system can change the answer under LIFO and weighted average (moving average under perpetual versus a single period-end average under periodic), so the exam specifies which system applies.

LIFO specifics

LIFO carries unique mechanics. The LIFO reserve is the difference between inventory valued at FIFO (or current cost) and at LIFO, disclosed so users can compare companies. A LIFO liquidation occurs when a company sells more than it buys and dips into old, low-cost layers, which inflates profit (and is a quality-of-earnings red flag). Dollar-value LIFO pools inventory and measures layers in base-year dollars using a price index, reducing the recordkeeping of unit LIFO and limiting liquidations. Note that IFRS prohibits LIFO entirely.

Lower of cost or net realizable value

Inventory is written down when its value falls below cost, but the measure depends on the method. For FIFO, weighted average, and specific identification, the rule is lower of cost or net realizable value (NRV) — NRV being the estimated selling price less costs to complete and sell. For LIFO and the retail method, the older lower of cost or market rule applies, where market is replacement cost bounded by a ceiling (NRV) and a floor (NRV minus a normal profit margin). Write-downs hit cost of goods sold (or a loss); write-ups above original cost are not permitted under US GAAP.

Estimating inventory — the gross profit method

When a physical count is impractical (an interim period, or inventory destroyed in a fire), inventory is estimated. The gross profit method applies the historical gross margin to sales: COGS = sales × (1 − gross margin), and ending inventory = goods available for sale − estimated COGS. Worked example: goods available for sale of $500,000, sales of $600,000, and a 30% gross margin give estimated COGS of $420,000 ($600,000 × 70%) and estimated ending inventory of $80,000. It is an estimate, not acceptable for annual financial statements, but invaluable for interim reporting and insurance claims.

The retail inventory method

Retailers use the retail inventory method, tracking goods at both cost and retail, computing a cost-to-retail ratio, and applying it to ending inventory at retail to estimate cost. The conventional (lower-of-cost-or-market) retail variation excludes markdowns from the ratio to approximate LCM, producing a conservative inventory value. The method handles markups, markdowns, and their cancellations, and is efficient for high-volume retail operations where unit costing is impractical.

Inventory errors and ownership

Inventory errors counterbalance over two years (an overstated ending inventory overstates this year's income and understates next year's), so the analyst traces the effect through both periods. Ownership determines what to include: goods in transit belong to the buyer under FOB shipping point (title passes at shipment) and to the seller under FOB destination; consigned goods stay in the consignor's inventory even though they sit on the consignee's floor. Getting cutoff and ownership right is essential to a correct count — the same discipline the auditor tests.

A worked FIFO/LIFO comparison

The numbers make the contrast concrete. Suppose a company buys 100 units at $10, then 100 at $14, and sells 120 units. Under FIFO, COGS is the first 100 at $10 plus 20 at $14 = $1,000 + $280 = $1,280, leaving 80 units at $14 = $1,120 in ending inventory. Under LIFO, COGS is the last 100 at $14 plus 20 at $10 = $1,400 + $200 = $1,600, leaving 80 units at $10 = $800. So in this rising-price example LIFO reports $320 more COGS, $320 less gross profit, and $320 less ending inventory than FIFO. The weighted-average method lands between them, using a $12 average ($2,400 ÷ 200 units) for a COGS of $1,440 — the systematic effect that drives the method choice and its tax consequences.

Purchase terms and capitalizable costs

What goes into inventory cost also matters. The cost of inventory includes the purchase price, freight-in, and other costs to bring the goods to a salable condition; purchase discounts are usually recorded net (or with an allowance), and abnormal spoilage and idle-capacity costs are expensed rather than capitalized. For a manufacturer or contractor, inventoriable cost includes direct materials, direct labor, and applied overhead — the same product-costing discipline from the CMA cost-management work — while period costs like selling and administration never enter inventory. Getting the capitalizable-cost boundary right is what makes both the inventory balance and cost of goods sold faithful.

Conversion, disclosure, and the LIFO conformity rule

Because LIFO and FIFO produce such different numbers, analysts convert between them using the LIFO reserve: FIFO inventory = LIFO inventory + LIFO reserve, and FIFO cost of goods sold = LIFO COGS − the increase in the LIFO reserve. This adjustment lets a reader compare a LIFO company with a FIFO competitor on a common basis. US GAAP also imposes the LIFO conformity rule — a company using LIFO for taxes must also use it for financial reporting — which is the practical reason a firm accepts lower book income to capture the LIFO tax savings in a period of rising prices. Disclosures of the method, the reserve, and any liquidation give users what they need to undo the distortion.

CMA bridge

CMA cost management tracked MBG's materials and WIP; FAR adds the cost-flow assumptions and the lower-of-cost-or-NRV write-down rules that value that inventory on the balance sheet. The LIFO-liquidation quality-of-earnings flag connects to the BAR analysis unit, where unusual inventory movements signal managed earnings.

Practice and recap

  1. Assign cost by specific ID, FIFO, LIFO, or weighted average; in rising prices FIFO gives the highest income and inventory, LIFO the lowest.
  2. Know LIFO mechanics: reserve, liquidation, dollar-value LIFO; IFRS prohibits LIFO.
  3. Apply lower of cost or NRV (FIFO/average/specific) versus lower of cost or market (LIFO/retail); no write-ups above cost.
  4. Estimate with the gross profit or retail method; correct counterbalancing errors and apply FOB/consignment ownership rules.

Recap: the cost-flow assumption decides which costs go to COGS — FIFO leaves the newest costs in inventory (highest income in rising prices), LIFO the oldest (lowest); inventory is written down to NRV (or market for LIFO/retail) but never written up; and the gross-profit and retail methods estimate inventory when a count is impractical, as when $500,000 of goods available and $600,000 of sales at a 30% margin imply $80,000 of ending inventory.

flashcards.front: FIFO vs LIFO in rising prices
flashcards.back: FIFO → highest ending inventory and net income (oldest costs in COGS); LIFO → lowest (newest costs in COGS). IFRS prohibits LIFO.
The difference between inventory at FIFO/current cost and at LIFO; disclosed for comparability.
Selling into old low-cost layers when purchases fall short of sales; inflates profit — an earnings-quality red flag.
Pools inventory and measures layers in base-year dollars using a price index; reduces recordkeeping and limits liquidations.
FIFO/weighted-average/specific → lower of cost or NRV; LIFO/retail → lower of cost or market (replacement cost bounded by NRV ceiling and NRV-minus-normal-profit floor).
COGS = sales × (1 − gross margin); ending inventory = goods available − estimated COGS. For interim/estimates, not annual statements.
Tracks cost and retail; cost-to-retail ratio EXCLUDES markdowns to approximate lower of cost or market.
Buyer owns under FOB shipping point (title at shipment); seller owns under FOB destination. Consigned goods stay with the consignor.

questions.explain: FIFO/weighted-average/specific use lower of cost or NRV; LIFO/retail use lower of cost or market.

choices: Inflates profit by dipping into old low-cost layers
questions.explain: Selling old low-cost layers pushes low costs into COGS, inflating profit — an earnings-quality flag.

questions.explain: Consigned goods remain the consignor's inventory until sold, even though held by the consignee.

weeks.title: FAR U4·W3 — PP&E, Intangibles & Impairment (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — capitalize, depreciate, impair, dispose

Long-lived assets follow a life cycle: capitalize the cost, depreciate or amortize it over its useful life, test it for impairment when conditions change, and recognize a gain or loss on disposal. MBG's heavy-equipment fleet and the goodwill from any acquisition both run this cycle, and the impairment rules differ sharply between tangible assets, finite-life intangibles, and goodwill.

Capitalizing property, plant, and equipment

PP&E is recorded at historical cost — the purchase price plus all costs to get the asset ready for use (freight, installation, testing). A self-constructed asset includes direct materials, labor, and overhead, plus capitalized interest on debt during the construction period (limited to actual interest incurred). A basket (lump-sum) purchase of several assets is allocated by relative fair value. Costs that merely maintain an asset are expensed; costs that extend its life or capacity are capitalized.

Depreciation methods

Depreciation spreads cost (less salvage) over the useful life. Straight-line is equal annual amounts; units-of-production ties expense to usage; and the accelerated methods front-load expense — double-declining-balance applies twice the straight-line rate to the declining book value (ignoring salvage until the end), and sum-of-the-years'-digits applies a declining fraction. A change in useful life or salvage is a change in estimate, applied prospectively (from FAR Unit 3). For tax, MACRS accelerates depreciation, creating the book-tax difference and deferred taxes from FAR Unit 2.

Impairment of long-lived assets held for use

Tangible assets and finite-life intangibles held for use follow a two-step impairment test. Step 1 (recoverability): compare the asset's carrying amount to the undiscounted future cash flows it will generate; if carrying amount is less than or equal to those undiscounted flows, there is no impairment. Step 2 (measurement): if step 1 fails, write the asset down to its fair value, and the loss is carrying amount minus fair value. Worked example: equipment with a $1,000,000 carrying amount has $900,000 of undiscounted future cash flows (step 1 fails) and a $700,000 fair value, so the impairment loss is $300,000. Under US GAAP, impairment losses on assets held for use are not reversed.

Assets held for sale

An asset (or disposal group) classified as held for sale is measured at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell, and depreciation stops once it is so classified. Unlike held-for-use assets, a subsequent recovery in fair value can be recognized as a gain, but only up to the cumulative loss previously recognized. Classification requires that the sale be probable within one year and the asset be available for immediate sale in its present condition.

Intangible assets

Intangibles split by life. A finite-life intangible (a patent, a customer list) is amortized over its useful life and tested for impairment like a tangible asset. An indefinite-life intangible (a trademark that can be renewed indefinitely) is not amortized but is tested for impairment annually, writing it down when carrying amount exceeds fair value. Critically, most internally developed intangibles (and internally generated goodwill) are expensed as incurred — only purchased intangibles are capitalized — though specific software-development and website-development rules capitalize certain costs after technological feasibility.

Goodwill impairment

Goodwill (from a business combination, per BAR) is not amortized by public companies and is tested for impairment at the reporting-unit level at least annually. Under the simplified one-step test, the entity compares the reporting unit's carrying amount to its fair value; if carrying amount exceeds fair value, the impairment loss equals that excess, capped at the total goodwill of the unit. An optional qualitative assessment can avoid the quantitative test when it is more likely than not that fair value exceeds carrying amount. A private company may elect to amortize goodwill (up to ten years) and test only on a triggering event.

Disposals and natural resources

On disposal, the entity removes the asset and its accumulated depreciation and recognizes a gain or loss equal to proceeds minus net book value. A nonmonetary exchange is generally recorded at fair value (recognizing gain/loss) unless it lacks commercial substance, in which case the new asset is recorded at book value and gain is deferred (except to the extent of boot received). Natural resources (a quarry MBG might own) are capitalized and expensed through depletion on a units-of-production basis as the resource is extracted. Each of these is the end of the long-lived-asset life cycle that began with capitalization.

Component depreciation, partial years, and IFRS revaluation

Several refinements appear on the exam. A partial-year acquisition prorates the first year's depreciation (by months or a convention). Component depreciation — depreciating significant parts of an asset (a building's roof versus its structure) separately — is permitted under US GAAP and required under IFRS. The biggest US-IFRS divergence is the revaluation model: IFRS permits carrying PP&E and intangibles at fair value with revaluation surplus in OCI, while US GAAP holds strictly to historical cost. IFRS also tests impairment in one step (carrying versus the recoverable amount — the higher of fair value less costs to sell or value in use) and permits reversal of impairments, both contrasts with the US two-step, no-reversal rule.

Software and research-and-development costs

Cost-capitalization rules turn on a threshold. Research and development costs are expensed as incurred under US GAAP — a conservative rule that keeps speculative spending off the balance sheet. Software developed to sell is expensed until technological feasibility, then capitalized until release; software for internal use is expensed in the preliminary stage, capitalized during application development, and expensed again post-implementation. These thresholds decide when spending becomes an asset, and they are a frequent source of exam adjustments against a naive capitalize-everything or expense-everything answer.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 2's deferred taxes arose from the book-tax depreciation difference introduced here; BAR's business combinations created the goodwill this unit tests for impairment. The capitalized-interest and self-construction rules apply directly to MBG building its own facilities, and the equipment-impairment test is the accounting behind the salvage-value assumptions CMA capital budgeting uses.

Practice and recap

  1. Capitalize PP&E at cost including readying costs and (for self-construction) capitalized interest; allocate basket purchases by relative fair value.
  2. Depreciate by straight-line, units-of-production, or an accelerated method; a life/salvage change is prospective.
  3. Test held-for-use assets in two steps (undiscounted cash flows, then write down to fair value; no reversal); measure held-for-sale at lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell (stop depreciating).
  4. Amortize finite-life intangibles; test indefinite-life intangibles and goodwill (carrying vs fair value) without amortizing (public companies).

Recap: long-lived assets are capitalized at cost, depreciated over their lives, and tested for impairment — held-for-use assets use the undiscounted-cash-flow recoverability test then a write-down to fair value (so a $1,000,000 asset with $900,000 of undiscounted flows and $700,000 fair value takes a $300,000 loss, never reversed); finite-life intangibles are amortized while indefinite-life intangibles and goodwill are impairment-tested at carrying-versus-fair-value; and disposals recognize gain or loss on proceeds versus net book value. IFRS diverges by allowing a revaluation model and impairment reversals, while US GAAP expenses research and development and capitalizes only certain software costs after technological feasibility — so the capitalize-versus-expense boundary is itself a frequent exam adjustment.

flashcards.back: Interest on debt during construction of a self-constructed asset is capitalized, limited to actual interest incurred.
Twice the straight-line rate applied to declining book value, ignoring salvage until the asset reaches salvage value.
Recoverability: carrying amount vs UNDISCOUNTED future cash flows. If carrying ≤ undiscounted flows, no impairment.
If step 1 fails, write down to FAIR VALUE; loss = carrying amount − fair value. Not reversed under US GAAP.
Measured at lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell; depreciation stops; recovery up to prior loss may be recognized.
Finite-life: amortize + impairment test. Indefinite-life (and goodwill): no amortization (public), impairment test (carrying vs fair value).
Generally expensed as incurred (only purchased intangibles capitalized); internally generated goodwill is never recorded.
One-step: if a reporting unit's carrying amount exceeds its fair value, the loss equals the excess (capped at the unit's goodwill); not amortized.

questions.q: Interest incurred while a company constructs an asset for its own use is:
choices: Capitalized as part of the asset (limited to actual interest)
questions.explain: Capitalized interest during construction is added to the asset's cost, capped at actual interest incurred.

questions.q: The first step of the impairment test for a long-lived asset held for use compares carrying amount to:
questions.explain: Step 1 (recoverability) uses undiscounted cash flows; step 2 writes down to fair value.

questions.explain: Step 1 fails ($900k < $1,000k); loss = carrying $1,000,000 − fair value $700,000 = $300,000.

questions.q: An indefinite-life intangible asset is:
choices: Not amortized but tested for impairment
questions.explain: Indefinite-life intangibles (and goodwill) are not amortized; they are impairment-tested.

questions.q: An asset classified as held for sale is measured at:
choices: Lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell
questions.explain: Held-for-sale assets are at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell, and depreciation stops.

questions.explain: Internally developed intangibles are generally expensed; only purchased intangibles are capitalized.

choices: Not reversed if value later recovers
questions.explain: US GAAP prohibits reversing impairment losses on assets held for use.

weeks.title: FAR U4·W4 — Pensions & Stock-Based Compensation (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — promising to pay employees later

Two forms of deferred employee pay get their own accounting: pensions (and other postretirement benefits) and stock-based compensation. Both recognize expense now for value delivered later, and both are heavy on estimates and on the income-versus-OCI distinction from earlier FAR units. If MBG offers a pension or grants equity to key staff, these standards govern the cost.

Defined contribution versus defined benefit

A defined-contribution plan (a 401(k)) promises only a contribution; the employer's expense each period equals the contribution, and the employee bears the investment risk — simple accounting. A defined-benefit plan promises a future benefit (often based on salary and years of service); the employer bears the investment and actuarial risk, and the accounting is complex because the obligation must be estimated and measured today.

The pension obligation and funded status

The key measure of a defined-benefit obligation is the projected benefit obligation (PBO) — the actuarial present value of benefits earned to date, using future salary levels. The plan's assets (held in a separate trust) are measured at fair value. The funded status = plan assets − PBO, and the net amount is reported on the balance sheet as a pension asset (overfunded) or liability (underfunded). The accumulated benefit obligation (ABO) uses current salaries and is a secondary measure.

Net periodic pension cost

The income-statement expense, net periodic pension cost, has several components — remembered as SIRAGE: Service cost (the PV of benefits earned this year, the only component in operating income), plus Interest cost on the PBO, minus the expected Return on plan assets, plus or minus Amortization of prior service cost, plus or minus amortization of Gains and losses, and amortization of any Existing net obligation. Worked example: service cost $200,000 + interest cost $90,000 − expected return $70,000 + prior-service-cost amortization $20,000 = $240,000 of net periodic pension cost.

Gains, losses, and OCI

Two items bypass net income and sit in other comprehensive income until amortized: prior service cost (from a plan amendment that grants credit for past service) and actuarial gains and losses (from changes in assumptions or differences between expected and actual asset returns). They accumulate in OCI and are amortized into pension cost over time — gains and losses only when they exceed a corridor (10% of the greater of the PBO or plan assets), spread over the average remaining service period. This OCI treatment smooths the volatile actuarial swings out of reported earnings.

Other postretirement benefits

Other postretirement benefit (OPEB) plans — chiefly retiree health care — follow a parallel model, but the obligation is the accumulated postretirement benefit obligation (APBO) and benefits are not salary-based. The cost is recognized over the period from hire to the date the employee is fully eligible for benefits, and like pensions the actuarial gains/losses and prior service cost flow through OCI. The common thread is accruing the cost of a promise over the service period that earns it.

Stock-based compensation

ASC 718 measures equity awards at their grant-date fair value and recognizes the cost as compensation expense over the service (vesting) period. For stock options, fair value comes from an option-pricing model (such as Black-Scholes) using the exercise price, stock price, expected term, volatility, risk-free rate, and dividends; the total is the fair value per option times the number expected to vest. Worked example: 10,000 options with a $9 grant-date fair value vesting over three years produce $90,000 of total compensation, expensed at $30,000 per year. Restricted stock units (RSUs) are measured at the grant-date share price. The offsetting credit is to additional paid-in capital (equity), so equity-classified awards do not create a liability.

Vesting, forfeitures, and modifications

Compensation cost is recognized only for awards that vest. An entity either estimates forfeitures up front or accounts for them as they occur (a policy election), truing up so that cumulative expense reflects awards that actually vest. Service conditions and performance conditions affect whether and how much expense is recognized, while market conditions (a target stock price) are built into the grant-date fair value and not reversed even if unmet. A modification (repricing underwater options) recognizes any incremental fair value. The principle throughout: recognize the grant-date value of awards expected to vest over the period employees earn them.

Pension obligation and asset rollforwards

The two pension accounts each roll forward. The PBO increases with service cost and interest cost and with actuarial losses, and decreases with benefits paid and actuarial gains; a plan amendment adds prior service cost. Plan assets increase with the actual return and employer contributions and decrease with benefits paid. The difference between the expected and actual return on plan assets is itself an actuarial gain or loss deferred in OCI — which is why net periodic cost uses the smoother expected return while the balance sheet reflects the actual asset value. Tracking these rollforwards is how the exam tests whether a plan is over- or underfunded and what the year's expense should be.

Liability awards and the tax angle

Not every stock award is equity-classified. An award that will be settled in cash (a cash-settled stock appreciation right) is a liability, remeasured to fair value each reporting period until settlement, so its expense fluctuates with the share price — unlike an equity award fixed at grant-date value. Stock compensation also creates a book-tax difference: the book expense (grant-date fair value over vesting) rarely equals the tax deduction (often the intrinsic value at exercise), producing deferred taxes and, on settlement, excess tax benefits or deficiencies that flow through the income-tax provision. The unifying idea across pensions and stock comp is that the accounting accrues the economic cost of deferred pay over the period it is earned, routing the volatile pieces through OCI or remeasurement rather than distorting operating income.

CMA bridge

Pension and stock-comp accounting reinforces the income-versus-OCI map from FAR Units 1 and 2: service and interest cost hit income while actuarial gains/losses wait in OCI, mirroring the AFS and hedge treatments. For a closely held contractor like MBG these may be modest, but the exam tests the mechanics — and the deferred-tax consequences tie back to ASC 740.

Practice and recap

  1. Expense a defined-contribution plan at the contribution; measure a defined-benefit obligation at the PBO and report funded status (assets − PBO) on the balance sheet.
  2. Compute net periodic pension cost (SIRAGE): service + interest − expected return ± amortizations.
  3. Route prior service cost and actuarial gains/losses through OCI, amortizing gains/losses outside the 10% corridor.
  4. Measure stock compensation at grant-date fair value and expense it over vesting; recognize cost only for awards that vest.

Recap: defined-benefit pensions report funded status (plan assets minus PBO) on the balance sheet and expense net periodic cost of service + interest − expected return ± amortizations (here $240,000), with prior service cost and actuarial gains/losses deferred in OCI; and stock-based compensation expenses grant-date fair value over the vesting period — 10,000 options worth $9 each over three years give $30,000 of expense per year — recognized only for awards expected to vest — and a cash-settled award is instead a liability remeasured to fair value each reporting period until settlement.

flashcards.back: DC: expense = the contribution (employee bears risk). DB: promises a future benefit; employer bears actuarial/investment risk; complex accounting.
Actuarial present value of benefits earned to date using FUTURE salary levels (ABO uses current salaries).

flashcards.front: Funded status on the balance sheet
flashcards.back: Plan assets (fair value) − PBO; reported as a net pension asset (overfunded) or liability (underfunded).
Service cost + Interest cost − expected Return on plan assets ± Amortization of prior service cost ± amortization of Gains/losses ± amortization of Existing net obligation.
Prior service cost and actuarial gains/losses bypass net income into OCI, then amortize (gains/losses only outside the 10% corridor).
Equity awards at GRANT-DATE fair value, expensed over the service (vesting) period; offset to additional paid-in capital.
10,000 options × $9 grant-date fair value = $90,000 over 3-year vesting = $30,000/year.
Market conditions are built into grant-date fair value (not reversed if unmet); service/performance conditions affect whether/how much expense is recognized.

questions.explain: Defined-contribution expense is simply the contribution; the employee bears investment risk.

questions.q: The funded status reported on the balance sheet equals:
choices: Plan assets at fair value − PBO
questions.explain: Funded status = fair value of plan assets minus the PBO.

questions.q: Service cost $200,000, interest cost $90,000, expected return $70,000, prior-service-cost amortization $20,000. Net periodic pension cost is:
Actuarial gains and losses on a defined-benefit plan are initially recognized in:
questions.explain: They flow through OCI and are amortized to pension cost (outside the 10% corridor).
