choices: Grant-date fair value, expensed over the vesting period
questions.explain: Equity awards use grant-date fair value recognized over the service/vesting period.

questions.q: 10,000 options with a $9 grant-date fair value vest over 3 years. Annual compensation expense is:
Compensation cost for stock awards is recognized:
choices: Only for awards that ultimately vest
For all granted awards regardless of vesting
questions.explain: Expense is recognized only for awards that vest, with forfeitures estimated or recognized as they occur.

units.title: AUD Unit 1 — Engagements & Ethics, the Audit Risk Model & Internal Control

weeks.title: AUD U1·W1 — Engagements, Ethics & Independence (CPA Core · from CMA m5/m12)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — who can audit MBG, and how independent must they be?

Auditing begins before any testing: the right engagement type, the auditor's ethics, and — above all — independence. CMA month 12 covered the IMA ethics standards from the preparer's side; AUD covers the AICPA Code from the auditor's side. The recurring exam theme is that an auditor's value comes entirely from being, and appearing, independent.

Levels of assurance and engagement types

  • Audit — the highest level, reasonable assurance, expressed as a positive opinion that the statements are fairly presented in accordance with the framework.
  • Review — limited (negative) assurance: "we are not aware of any material modifications needed." Based mainly on inquiry and analytical procedures.
  • Compilation — no assurance; the accountant assembles statements from management's data.
  • Examination / agreed-upon procedures — attestation engagements at varying assurance.

Reasonable assurance is high but not absolute — an audit is designed to detect material misstatement, not every error, because of sampling, judgment, and the nature of evidence.

The AICPA Code of Professional Conduct

Core principles: integrity, objectivity, independence, due care, and professional skepticism. The conceptual framework approach asks the CPA to identify threats to compliance (self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, undue influence) and apply safeguards that reduce them to an acceptable level. Professional skepticism — a questioning mind and critical assessment of evidence — runs through the entire audit.

Independence in fact and in appearance

Independence has two dimensions: in fact (an actual unbiased mindset) and in appearance (a reasonable, informed third party would conclude the auditor is unbiased). Both are required. A covered member generally may not have a direct financial interest, or a material indirect interest, in an attest client; may not have certain loans or business relationships; and may not perform management functions for the client. Performing the client's bookkeeping and then auditing it is a self-review threat that typically impairs independence for an issuer.

For MBG's auditor, independence would be impaired by owning an interest in MBG, by a partner's spouse working in MBG's finance function, or by the firm having set up MBG's books and now opining on them. Note independence is required for attest engagements (audit, review, examination) but not for a pure compilation or for non-attest tax/consulting work — though objectivity and integrity always apply.

Engagement acceptance and the preconditions for an audit

Before accepting, the auditor confirms the preconditions: management uses an acceptable financial-reporting framework and acknowledges its responsibility for the statements, for internal control, and for giving the auditor access to evidence. The terms are set in an engagement letter — the contract documenting the objective and scope, each party’s responsibilities, the inherent limitations, and the framework. For a first-year engagement the successor auditor must, with client permission, communicate with the predecessor auditor about disagreements, fraud or illegal acts, and the reason for the change; the client’s refusal to permit that contact is itself a red flag weighing against acceptance.

Independence frameworks beyond the AICPA

Three rule sets can apply at once. The AICPA Code governs private-company attest work through the threats-and-safeguards framework. For issuers, the stricter SEC and PCAOB rules add: a prohibition on most non-audit services (bookkeeping, financial-system design, internal-audit outsourcing, valuation, and management functions for the same audit client), mandatory audit-partner rotation (lead and concurring partners rotate off after five years), audit-committee pre-approval of all services, and a one-year cooling-off period before an audit-team member can take a key financial-reporting role at the client. Government audits add the GAO’s Yellow Book, whose conceptual framework parallels the AICPA but treats preparing the financial statements as a significant self-review threat requiring safeguards.

Financial interests, family, and employment

The detail of who and what impairs independence is heavily tested. A direct financial interest in an attest client impairs independence regardless of amount; an indirect interest (through a mutual fund, say) impairs only if material. Immediate family (spouse, dependents) are generally subject to the same restrictions as the covered member, so a spouse’s direct investment in the client impairs independence, and a spouse’s employment with the client impairs it if the spouse holds a key position. Close relatives (parents, siblings, nondependent children) impair independence in narrower circumstances — a key-position role or a material financial interest the covered member knows of. Most loans to or from a client impair independence, with narrow exceptions (a car loan or a fully collateralized mortgage from a financial-institution client on normal terms).

Fees, confidentiality, and acts discreditable

Several rules protect objectivity beyond independence. Contingent fees and commissions are prohibited for attest clients, because tying the fee to a result corrupts judgment; they are permitted for some non-attest clients with disclosure. The confidential client information rule bars disclosing client data without consent, subject to exceptions (a valid subpoena, a peer review, an authorized regulatory body). Acts discreditable — retaining client records to coerce payment, discrimination, or signing a materially false return — violate the Code regardless of independence. A CPA must also exercise due professional care, working with the competence and diligence of a reasonably prudent practitioner.

Quality management at the firm level

Independence is reinforced by firm-wide quality management. Under the AICPA’s quality-management standards (and PCAOB standards for issuers), a firm designs a system addressing leadership and the tone at the top, relevant ethical requirements including independence, acceptance and continuance of clients, engagement performance, resources, and monitoring and remediation. An engagement quality review — an objective partner not on the engagement reviewing significant judgments and the report before issuance — is required for issuer audits and certain others. The thread tying the week together: the auditor’s opinion is worth nothing unless the firm and the individual are competent, objective, and independent in both fact and appearance — everything in the rest of the audit assumes it.

The period of independence and network firms

Independence must be maintained throughout both the period of the professional engagement and the period covered by the financial statements, so a financial interest held even before the engagement letter is signed can impair independence for the year under audit. The rules also reach beyond the individual firm: in an alliance or network of firms, other network firms must be independent of an audit client where it is reasonable to expect the network is associated with the engagement. When an independence problem is discovered, the firm evaluates its significance, applies safeguards or removes the affected individuals, and documents the resolution. Independence is ultimately judged from the perspective of a reasonable and informed third party weighing all the facts — not from the auditor’s own belief that they remain objective.

CMA bridge

CMA month 12's IMA standards (integrity, credibility) parallel the AICPA principles; the difference is the auditor's independence requirement, which has no exact CMA counterpart because the management accountant is internal. Both, though, demand objectivity and a refusal to misrepresent.

Practice and recap

  1. Match engagement type to assurance level: audit (reasonable/positive), review (limited/negative), compilation (none).
  2. Apply the AICPA principles and the threats-and-safeguards framework; maintain professional skepticism.
  3. Require independence in fact and in appearance for attest engagements.
  4. Identify relationships that impair independence (financial interest, self-review, management functions).

Recap: an audit gives reasonable (not absolute) assurance via a positive opinion; the AICPA Code centers on integrity, objectivity, due care, skepticism, and — uniquely — independence in fact and appearance, which bookkeeping-then-auditing or a financial interest in the client would impair.

flashcards.back: Reasonable assurance, expressed as a positive opinion.
Limited (negative) assurance, based on inquiry and analytical procedures.
None — the accountant assembles statements without assurance.
No — reasonable but not absolute, due to sampling, judgment, and the nature of evidence.

weeks.title: AUD U1·W2 — The Audit Risk Model & Materiality (CPA Core · from CMA m10)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — how much testing is enough?

The audit risk model is the engine that answers "how much evidence do we need?" It links the risk of material misstatement to the amount of substantive testing the auditor must perform. CMA month 10 assessed business risk; AUD turns risk assessment into a testing plan through this model and the materiality thresholds that frame it.

The audit risk model

Audit risk = Inherent risk × Control risk × Detection risk.

  • Audit risk (AR) — the risk the auditor gives an unmodified opinion on materially misstated statements. The auditor sets it low (commonly ~5%).
  • Inherent risk (IR) — susceptibility to misstatement before controls (estimates, complex transactions). The auditor assesses but cannot change it.
  • Control risk (CR) — risk that internal control fails to prevent/detect a misstatement. Assessed, not controlled by the auditor.
  • Detection risk (DR) — risk the auditor's procedures fail to catch a misstatement. This is the only component the auditor controls, by changing the nature, timing, and extent of substantive procedures.

Solving for detection risk

Rearranging: DR = AR ÷ (IR × CR). The product IR × CR is the risk of material misstatement (RMM). Illustrative: target AR 5%, IR 80%, CR 50%. RMM = 0.80 × 0.50 = 40%. DR = 0.05 ÷ 0.40 = 0.125 (12.5%).

The key relationship is inverse: the higher the RMM, the lower the acceptable detection risk, which means the auditor must do more and better substantive testing — larger samples, more reliable evidence, and procedures performed at year-end rather than interim. When controls are strong (low CR), the auditor can accept higher DR and test less substantively (after testing those controls).

Materiality

Misstatements matter only if they could influence users' decisions. The auditor sets:

  • Overall (planning) materiality — usually a percentage of a benchmark (pre-tax income, revenue, or total assets) appropriate to the entity.
  • Performance materiality — set below overall materiality to reduce the chance that the aggregate of undetected and uncorrected misstatements exceeds overall materiality.
  • Clearly trivial threshold — amounts below which misstatements need not be accumulated.

Materiality has a quantitative and a qualitative side: a small misstatement can be material if it changes a loss to a profit, hides a trend, or affects debt covenants — exactly the kind of bank-covenant sensitivity MBG's surety and lenders watch.

Risk assessment procedures

The auditor does not guess at inherent and control risk — they are grounded in required risk assessment procedures: obtaining an understanding of the entity and its environment (industry, regulation, business model), its internal control, and the applicable framework. The procedures are inquiry of management and others, analytical procedures, observation, and inspection of documents. Risk assessment procedures alone do not provide sufficient audit evidence for an opinion — they direct where the substantive work goes. A required part of this phase is the engagement team discussion (the brainstorming session) about where the statements are susceptible to material misstatement, including from fraud.

Assertions — the unit of audit risk

Risk and materiality ultimately attach to management assertions embedded in the statements, and procedures are designed assertion by assertion. For account balances: existence, completeness, rights and obligations, and valuation/allocation. For transactions: occurrence, completeness, accuracy, cutoff, and classification. For presentation and disclosure: occurrence and rights, completeness, accuracy/valuation, and understandability. The auditor maps each significant risk to the specific assertion at stake — for a contractor, the existence of recorded receivables and the cutoff and accuracy of percentage-of-completion revenue are typically the assertions most at risk.

Significant risks and the revenue presumption

Some risks demand special audit consideration. A significant risk — one with higher inherent risk due to complexity, subjectivity, or fraud potential — requires substantive procedures specifically responsive to it and prohibits relying on prior-period control testing without re-testing the controls. Auditing standards presume revenue recognition is a fraud risk unless that presumption is rebutted, because revenue is the account most often manipulated; for a contractor that means heightened scrutiny of estimated costs to complete and the timing of recognized revenue. Significant risks frequently involve accounting estimates with measurement uncertainty, where the auditor evaluates the data, assumptions, and method management used.

From risk to response — nature, timing, extent

The assessed risk drives the further audit procedures along three dimensions. Nature: more reliable evidence for higher risk — external confirmations and inspection over inquiry, and tests of detail over analytics. Timing: testing at year-end rather than interim when risk is high, since interim testing leaves a roll-forward gap. Extent: larger sample sizes as the desired detection risk falls. Procedures are either tests of controls (do the controls operate?) or substantive procedures (tests of detail and substantive analytics); a dual-purpose test does both at once. The auditor responds to financial-statement-level risk with overall responses (more experienced staff, heightened skepticism) and to assertion-level risk with specific procedures.

Analytical procedures and revisiting materiality

Analytical procedures — evaluating financial data through plausible relationships — are required in the risk-assessment (planning) phase and again in the final review near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion; they are optional as a substantive procedure during fieldwork. Materiality is not static: if the auditor learns the benchmark was wrong (actual income differs sharply from the estimate used), materiality is revised and the planned procedures reconsidered. At the end, the auditor accumulates identified misstatements, compares them to materiality, and asks management to correct them — uncorrected misstatements above the clearly-trivial threshold are evaluated, individually and in aggregate, against overall materiality to decide whether the opinion must be modified. Risk and materiality thus bracket the entire audit: they size the work at the start and judge the result at the finish.

Sufficient appropriate evidence and sampling

The output of the risk model is a plan to gather sufficient appropriate audit evidence — sufficiency is the quantity (more is needed as risk rises) and appropriateness is the quality, comprising relevance (does it address the assertion?) and reliability (higher when from independent external sources, under effective controls, in documentary form, or obtained directly by the auditor). Evidence from a knowledgeable source outside the entity, such as a bank confirmation, outweighs the same fact asserted only by management. Because testing every item is rarely economical, the auditor often uses audit sampling, accepting a measured sampling risk that the sample is not representative; lowering the tolerable detection risk drives larger samples. The model, the assertions, materiality, and the evidence standard thus form one chain: risk sets how much and how good the evidence must be, and sampling delivers it efficiently.

CMA bridge

CMA month 10 quantified business risk (likelihood × impact, VaR); AUD's risk model is the audit analogue — assess inherent and control risk, then set detection risk to hold audit risk low. The mindset is identical: more risk demands more rigor.

Practice and recap

  1. Know AR = IR × CR × DR and that DR is the only component the auditor controls.
  2. Compute DR = AR ÷ (IR × CR); RMM = IR × CR.
  3. Apply the inverse relationship: higher RMM → lower DR → more substantive testing.
  4. Set overall and (lower) performance materiality; weigh qualitative materiality.

Recap: with AR 5%, IR 80%, and CR 50%, the risk of material misstatement is 40% and detection risk must be 12.5% — a low DR that forces extensive substantive testing. Performance materiality sits below overall materiality, and small misstatements can still be qualitatively material.

flashcards.back: Audit risk = Inherent risk × Control risk × Detection risk.

Inherent risk × control risk (IR × CR).
Inverse: higher RMM → lower acceptable DR → more substantive testing.
Performance materiality is set below overall materiality to buffer aggregation risk.
A small misstatement that turns a loss into a profit or breaches a covenant is material.

weeks.title: AUD U1·W3 — Internal Control & Fraud in the Audit (CPA Core · from CMA m5/m12)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — MBG's transaction registry, seen by the auditor

CMA months 5 and 12 built MBG's controls — segregation of duties and the VERIFIED/POSTED/FLAGGED transaction registry. AUD looks at those same controls from outside: the auditor must understand internal control, decide whether to rely on it, and stay alert to fraud, including management's ability to override the very controls that look strong on paper.

Understanding and testing internal control

On every audit, the auditor must obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit — all five COSO components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring. Understanding is required even if the auditor does not plan to rely on controls.

To rely on controls (assess control risk below maximum and reduce substantive testing), the auditor must test their operating effectiveness with tests of controls. Tests of controls ask "did the control operate?"; substantive procedures ask "is the balance correct?" If controls are ineffective or the auditor chooses not to rely on them, control risk is high and substantive testing increases (the model from last week).

The integrated audit (SOX)

For issuers, Sarbanes-Oxley §404 and PCAOB standards can require an integrated audit in which the auditor opines on both the financial statements and the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The auditor’s ICFR attestation under §404(b) applies only to issuers that are accelerated or large accelerated filers; nonaccelerated filers and eligible smaller reporting companies are exempt from the auditor attestation, though management still performs its own §404(a) assessment. A material weakness (a reasonable possibility of a material misstatement not being prevented or detected) yields an adverse ICFR opinion. A private company like MBG is not subject to §404, but the same control concepts drive the financial-statement audit.

Fraud and professional skepticism (AU-C 240)

Two fraud types: fraudulent financial reporting (intentional misstatement to deceive users) and misappropriation of assets (theft). The fraud triangle from CMA month 12 — pressure, opportunity, rationalization — drives the auditor's risk assessment. Required procedures include an engagement-team brainstorming about how fraud could occur, inquiries of management and others, and a rebuttable presumption that improper revenue recognition is a fraud risk (the auditor may overcome it only with documented reasons).

Critically, the auditor must always address the risk of management override of controls — even strong controls can be overridden by those who design them. Required responses include testing journal entries (especially nonstandard, period-end, and round-dollar entries), reviewing accounting estimates for bias, and evaluating significant unusual transactions. Professional skepticism means not accepting evidence at face value just because management seems honest.

The five components and control activities

Each COSO component does specific work. The control environment is the tone at the top — integrity, board oversight, competence. Risk assessment is management’s own identification of risks to reporting. Control activities are the policies that address those risks: authorization, segregation of duties (separating authorization, recording, and custody), physical controls over assets and records, reconciliations, and performance reviews. Information and communication captures and shares the data that make controls run, and monitoring evaluates whether controls keep working over time. MBG’s segregation of duties is a control activity; its transaction registry is part of information and communication and supports monitoring.

Design, implementation, and walkthroughs

Understanding control is not one question but three. The auditor evaluates whether a control is designed effectively (would it prevent or detect a misstatement?) and whether it has been implemented (does it actually exist and operate?) — assessed through inquiry combined with observation, inspection, or a walkthrough that traces one transaction from origination through the records. Only when the auditor intends to rely on a control does it additionally test operating effectiveness over the period. Design-and-implementation work is required on every audit; operating-effectiveness testing is required only for reliance (and, for issuers, for the ICFR opinion).

Deficiencies and required communications

Control problems are graded by severity. A control deficiency exists when a control does not let management or employees prevent or detect misstatements on a timely basis. A significant deficiency is important enough to merit the attention of those charged with governance. A material weakness is the most severe — a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or detected — and, for an issuer, forces an adverse ICFR opinion. The auditor must communicate significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in writing to those charged with governance, and that communication is required even if the deficiencies were remediated during the year.

The inherent limitations of any control system

No system of internal control gives absolute assurance, and the exam tests why. Management override lets those who design the controls bypass them; collusion between two or more people defeats segregation of duties; human error and faulty judgment cause breakdowns; and cost-benefit constraints mean management will not control immaterial risks. These limitations are precisely why an auditor cannot rely on controls alone and must always perform some substantive procedures, and why even a clean ICFR opinion is reasonable, not absolute, assurance. They also explain the standing requirement to address management override regardless of how strong the controls appear.

IT controls, service organizations, and illegal acts

Most controls today are embedded in systems. IT general controls (ITGCs) — over access and security, program change management, and computer operations — underpin the application controls (edit checks, validations, automated reconciliations) the auditor may rely on; weak ITGCs can undermine otherwise sound application controls. When a client outsources a process (payroll, hosting) to a service organization, the auditor obtains a SOC 1 report from the service auditor: a type 1 covers design at a point in time, a type 2 covers operating effectiveness over a period, and only a type 2 supports reliance on those controls. Finally, the auditor considers laws and regulations: noncompliance with a direct effect on the statements is audited like any other misstatement, and the auditor responds to identified or suspected noncompliance by evaluating the effect and communicating to the appropriate level — escalating to those charged with governance when senior management is involved.

Communicating and documenting fraud findings

When the auditor identifies fraud or a suspicion of it, the communication path depends on who is involved and how material it is. Any fraud involving senior management, or fraud that causes a material misstatement, is communicated to those charged with governance; even immaterial fraud by an employee is reported to the appropriate level of management. The auditor’s normal duty of confidentiality may yield to a duty to disclose outside the entity in limited circumstances (a successor auditor with client consent, a subpoena, a regulator). Throughout, the auditor maintains professional skepticism and documents the fraud risk assessment, the brainstorming, the responses, and the basis for conclusions — the work that lets a later reviewer confirm the override and revenue-recognition risks were genuinely addressed rather than assumed away. If the risk is so severe that the auditor can no longer rely on management’s representations, withdrawal from the engagement may be the only appropriate response.

CMA bridge

CMA framed segregation of duties and the transaction registry as fraud prevention (denying opportunity); AUD adds the auditor's detection responsibility — test the controls, and never assume they cannot be overridden from the top.

Practice and recap

  1. Obtain an understanding of all five COSO components on every audit.
  2. To rely on controls, test their operating effectiveness; otherwise increase substantive testing.
  3. For issuers, perform an integrated audit of ICFR; a material weakness → adverse ICFR opinion.
  4. Assess fraud risk (triangle), presume revenue-recognition fraud, and always address management override by testing journal entries.

Recap: the auditor understands internal control on every engagement and tests it only to rely on it; issuers get an integrated ICFR audit; and fraud work — brainstorming, the revenue-recognition presumption, and journal-entry testing for management override — runs on professional skepticism.

units.title: AUD Unit 2 — Audit Evidence, Sampling, Substantive Procedures & Reports

weeks.title: AUD U2·W1 — Audit Evidence & Procedures (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the audit runs on evidence

AUD Unit 1 set risk, materiality, and internal control. Now the auditor must gather evidence to support an opinion on MBG's statements. The standard is sufficient appropriate audit evidence, gathered with a defined set of procedures, and documented well enough that an experienced auditor with no prior connection could follow it. This week is the evidence engine of the audit.

Sufficient appropriate evidence

Two dimensions govern evidence. Sufficiency is the quantity — more is needed as the risk of material misstatement rises and as the quality of each item falls. Appropriateness is the quality, made of relevance (does it address the specific assertion?) and reliability (can it be trusted?). The two interact: highly reliable evidence reduces how much is needed, but no amount of low-quality evidence substitutes for relevance. The auditor seeks reasonable, not absolute, assurance, so evidence is usually persuasive rather than conclusive.

The reliability hierarchy

Reliability rises with independence and directness. Evidence is more reliable when it is obtained from independent sources outside the entity, generated under effective internal control, in documentary (especially original) form, and obtained directly by the auditor rather than through the client. So an external bank confirmation outranks a client-prepared schedule, the auditor's own physical count outranks management's representation, and an original invoice outranks a photocopy. Knowing this ranking lets the auditor choose the most convincing procedure for a high-risk assertion.

The audit procedures

The toolbox of procedures, each suited to particular assertions: inspection of records or assets; observation of a process (watching the inventory count); inquiry of personnel (rarely sufficient alone); external confirmation from third parties; recalculation of mathematical accuracy; reperformance of a control or procedure independently; and analytical procedures. The auditor matches the procedure to the assertion — physical inspection tests existence, while tracing source documents into the records tests completeness; vouching from the records back to source documents tests occurrence/existence. Direction of testing is itself an exam point.

External confirmations

Confirmations are powerful because the evidence comes directly from an independent third party. A positive confirmation asks the recipient to respond whether or not they agree, and is used for larger or riskier balances; a negative confirmation asks for a response only if they disagree, and is appropriate only when risk is low, the population is many small homogeneous balances, and a low exception rate is expected. The auditor controls the confirmation process end to end — preparing, sending, and receiving replies directly — and investigates non-responses with alternative procedures (subsequent cash receipts, shipping documents for receivables).

Substantive analytical procedures

Analytical procedures evaluate financial data through plausible relationships and can serve as substantive evidence. The auditor develops an independent expectation (precise enough to detect a material misstatement), defines a tolerable difference, compares the expectation to the recorded amount, and investigates significant differences with corroboration — not by simply accepting management's explanation. They work best for accounts with predictable relationships (a construction company's payroll-tax expense should track wages; interest expense should track average debt and rates). Recall that analytics are required in planning and again in the final review, and optional as a substantive procedure.

Auditing accounting estimates and fair value

Estimates — the allowance for doubtful accounts, warranty reserves, the percentage-of-completion cost-to-complete, and fair values — carry measurement uncertainty and management bias risk, so the auditor responds with specific approaches: test how management made the estimate (its data, assumptions, and method), develop an independent estimate to compare, or review subsequent events that confirm the estimate. The auditor also evaluates whether estimates show a pattern of bias in one direction across the statements — a possible indicator of fraud. For a contractor, the cost-to-complete estimate is the single most judgmental number on the statements and gets the most attention.

Audit documentation

The work is only as good as its documentation. Working papers must let an experienced auditor with no prior connection understand the nature, timing, and extent of procedures, the results and evidence obtained, and the conclusions reached — including who performed and reviewed the work and when. Documentation is the auditor's defense and the basis for the engagement quality review. Standards set a retention period (generally five years for nonissuers, seven for issuers under PCAOB rules) and a documentation completion window after the report date, after which changes must be tracked.

Using the work of others

The auditor may rely on others but remains solely responsible for the opinion. When using a management's specialist (an appraiser the client hired), the auditor evaluates the specialist's competence, objectivity, and the appropriateness of their work as audit evidence. An auditor's specialist assists the audit team directly. The internal audit function may be used to obtain evidence or provide direct assistance if it is competent and objective, but the external auditor cannot delegate judgments about significant risks. These rules let the audit reach specialized areas — like valuing MBG's real estate — without the auditor personally being an expert in everything.

Audit data analytics and the evolving evidence mix

Modern audits increasingly use audit data analytics (ADA) — analyzing entire populations rather than samples to identify outliers, unusual journal entries, and relationships. A 100% test of journal entries for management-override risk, a three-way match across the full purchase population, or a regression linking revenue to operational drivers can be both more effective and more efficient than traditional sampling. ADA does not change the evidence standards — the results still must be relevant and reliable, and exceptions must be investigated — but it shifts the auditor's work from selecting items to evaluating anomalies. The auditor must still assess the reliability of the data used, because analytics on flawed data produce confident but wrong conclusions.

Evaluating evidence and the iterative audit

Evidence gathering is not linear. As procedures surface results, the auditor reassesses risk: an unexpected analytic result or a confirmation exception may reveal a risk not identified in planning, requiring additional procedures. The auditor accumulates identified misstatements, distinguishing factual (clearly wrong), judgmental (a difference in an estimate), and projected (extrapolated from a sample) misstatements, and aggregates them against materiality. Evidence that contradicts earlier conclusions cannot be ignored — professional skepticism requires the auditor to resolve inconsistencies rather than rationalize them away.

CMA bridge

AUD Unit 1 set the risk and control framework; this week is where the auditor responds to that risk with evidence. The estimate-auditing rules apply directly to the percentage-of-completion cost-to-complete that CMA's WIP accounting produces — the auditor tests the very estimate the management accountant prepares.

Practice and recap

  1. Gather sufficient (quantity) appropriate (relevance + reliability) evidence for reasonable, not absolute, assurance.
  2. Rank reliability: external > internal, auditor-obtained > client-provided, original > copy, under good controls > weak.
  3. Match procedures to assertions (inspect existence, trace completeness, vouch occurrence); use positive vs negative confirmations appropriately.
  4. Audit estimates by testing data/assumptions/method or building an independent estimate; document so an experienced auditor could re-perform; use specialists/internal audit without delegating responsibility.

Recap: the opinion rests on sufficient appropriate evidence, weighted by a reliability hierarchy that favors external, auditor-obtained, original documents; procedures are matched to assertions and confirmations come straight from third parties; substantive analytics test predictable relationships; estimates and fair values demand special skepticism; and everything is documented so an experienced auditor with no prior connection could follow it.

flashcards.back: Sufficiency = quantity (rises with risk, falls with quality); appropriateness = quality = relevance + reliability.
More reliable when external > internal, auditor-obtained > client-provided, original > photocopy, and produced under effective controls.
Vouch from records back to source documents = existence/occurrence; trace from source documents into records = completeness.
Positive: respond whether or not you agree (riskier balances). Negative: respond only if you disagree (low risk, many small homogeneous balances, low expected exceptions).
Develop a precise independent expectation, set a tolerable difference, compare to recorded amount, and corroborate significant differences.
Test management's data/assumptions/method, develop an independent estimate, or review subsequent events; watch for one-directional bias.
Sufficient for an experienced auditor with no prior connection to understand procedures, evidence, and conclusions; retained 5 years (nonissuer) / 7 (issuer).

flashcards.back: The auditor may use them but remains solely responsible for the opinion and cannot delegate judgments on significant risks.

weeks.title: AUD U2·W2 — Audit Sampling (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — testing a slice of the whole

The auditor cannot examine every one of MBG's thousands of transactions, so it tests a sample and projects the result to the population. Audit sampling is applying a procedure to less than 100% of a population such that every item could be selected, to draw a conclusion about the whole. The discipline is managing the risk that the sample misleads — the subject of this heavily tested week.

Sampling risk versus nonsampling risk

Two risks attend a sample. Sampling risk is the risk that the sample is not representative, so a conclusion drawn from it differs from the conclusion the auditor would reach by testing the whole population — it is inherent to sampling and is controlled by sample size. Nonsampling risk is the risk of a wrong conclusion for any other reason — using an inappropriate procedure, misinterpreting evidence, or failing to recognize a misstatement — and is controlled by training, supervision, and review, not sample size.

Attribute sampling for tests of controls

Attribute sampling tests a rate of occurrence — how often a control fails (a deviation) — to decide whether to rely on the control. Sample size grows with the expected deviation rate and the desired confidence, and shrinks as the tolerable deviation rate (the maximum failure rate the auditor will accept and still rely) rises. Note that population size has little effect on sample size for a large population — a counterintuitive but tested point.

Evaluating a controls sample

After testing, the auditor computes the sample deviation rate (deviations ÷ sample size) and adds an allowance for sampling risk to get the upper deviation rate. If the upper deviation rate is at or below the tolerable rate, the auditor may rely on the control as planned; if it exceeds tolerable, the auditor cannot rely and must increase substantive testing. Worked example: with a tolerable deviation rate of 7%, a sample of 60 yields 2 deviations — a 3.3% sample rate; if the resulting upper deviation rate (say 6.5%) stays at or below 7%, reliance is supported.

Sampling risks in tests of controls

Two sampling risks have opposite consequences. The risk of assessing control risk too low (overreliance) is the danger that the sample suggests a control works when it does not — this relates to effectiveness and is the more serious risk, because it leads the auditor to do too little substantive work. The risk of assessing control risk too high (underreliance) suggests a good control is bad — a problem of efficiency, leading to unnecessary testing. Auditors guard most carefully against the effectiveness risk.

Substantive sampling and monetary-unit sampling

For substantive tests the auditor samples dollar amounts, not occurrence rates. Monetary-unit sampling (MUS), also called probability-proportional-to-size, treats each dollar as a sampling unit, so larger balances are automatically more likely to be selected — efficient when the auditor expects few misstatements and is testing for overstatement (it is the standard tool for receivables). MUS projects a most likely misstatement plus an allowance to an upper misstatement limit, compared against tolerable misstatement. A weakness: MUS handles understatement and zero/negative balances poorly.

Classical variables sampling

Classical variables sampling uses statistical estimation of an amount rather than a rate, with methods like mean-per-unit, ratio, and difference estimation. It is better suited than MUS when the auditor expects a larger number of misstatements or is concerned with understatement (testing completeness, such as searching for unrecorded liabilities). The trade-off is that it requires an estimate of the population's standard deviation and is more complex, but it gives a two-sided estimate MUS cannot.

Sampling risks in substantive tests

Substantive sampling has its own paired risks. The risk of incorrect acceptance is concluding a materially misstated balance is fairly stated — an effectiveness risk that, like overreliance, undermines the audit and is guarded against most. The risk of incorrect rejection is concluding a fairly stated balance is misstated — an efficiency problem that causes wasted work (extended testing that eventually clears the balance). Sample size rises as the auditor seeks to lower incorrect acceptance, as tolerable misstatement falls, and as expected misstatement rises.

Selecting the sample

How items are chosen affects whether a sample is representative. Random selection gives every item an equal chance; systematic selection takes every nth item after a random start (efficient, but risky if the population follows a pattern); monetary-unit selection picks dollars (favoring large balances); and haphazard selection is a non-statistical attempt at randomness without conscious bias. Block selection — choosing contiguous items — is generally inappropriate, because a block is unlikely to represent the population. Statistical sampling lets the auditor measure sampling risk; nonstatistical sampling relies on judgment; both are permitted if properly designed.

Factors that drive sample size

The exam rewards knowing how each factor moves sample size. For tests of controls, sample size increases with higher desired confidence and a higher expected deviation rate, and decreases as the tolerable deviation rate rises. For substantive tests, sample size increases as the assessed risk of material misstatement rises, as the desired assurance grows (a lower acceptable risk of incorrect acceptance), and as expected misstatement increases, and it decreases as tolerable misstatement rises. A dual-purpose test uses one sample to both test a control and substantiate the related transactions, sized as the larger of the two requirements. Population size, again, has a negligible effect once the population is large.

Projecting and concluding

Whatever the method, the auditor projects the sample result to the population and compares it to the relevant limit. In attribute sampling the projected (upper) deviation rate is compared to the tolerable deviation rate; in substantive sampling the projected misstatement plus an allowance for sampling risk is compared to tolerable misstatement. If the projection exceeds the limit, the auditor responds — expanding the sample, performing alternative procedures, or proposing an adjustment — and never simply accepts a result that breaches tolerance. The discipline is the same across methods: estimate, add a margin for sampling risk, and conclude against a pre-set threshold.

CMA bridge

Sampling is the statistical backbone behind the substantive procedures and tests of controls from AUD Unit 1. The risk-of-incorrect-acceptance and overreliance risks are the sampling expression of the audit-risk model — both are about wrongly concluding things are fine when they are not, the core danger the whole audit is built to avoid.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish sampling risk (controlled by sample size) from nonsampling risk (controlled by supervision and review).
  2. Use attribute sampling for controls: compare the upper deviation rate to the tolerable deviation rate; population size barely affects sample size.
  3. Use MUS for overstatement with few expected misstatements; use classical variables when more misstatements or understatement is the concern.
  4. Guard most against the effectiveness risks — assessing control risk too low (overreliance) and incorrect acceptance — over the efficiency risks.

Recap: sampling risk is the chance an unrepresentative sample misleads, managed by sample size, while nonsampling risk is managed by review; attribute sampling relies on a control only when the upper deviation rate stays at or below tolerable; MUS targets overstatement of larger balances while classical variables sampling handles understatement and more misstatements; and the auditor most fears the effectiveness errors — overreliance and incorrect acceptance — that make a flawed balance look fine.

flashcards.back: Sampling risk = the sample is unrepresentative (controlled by sample size); nonsampling risk = wrong conclusion for any other reason (controlled by training/supervision/review).
Tests a rate of occurrence (control deviation rate) to decide whether to rely on a control.

flashcards.front: Tolerable deviation rate effect on sample size
flashcards.back: A higher tolerable deviation rate lowers required sample size; population size has little effect for large populations.

flashcards.front: Relying on a control from a sample
flashcards.back: Rely if the upper deviation rate (sample rate + allowance for sampling risk) is at or below the tolerable deviation rate.

flashcards.front: Risk of assessing control risk too LOW
flashcards.back: Overreliance — concluding a control works when it doesn't; an EFFECTIVENESS risk (most serious), leading to too little substantive testing.
Each dollar is a sampling unit (PPS); efficient for overstatement with few expected misstatements (e.g., receivables); weak for understatement and zero/negative balances.
Estimates an amount (mean-per-unit/ratio/difference); better when more misstatements or understatement (completeness) is the concern.

flashcards.front: Risk of incorrect acceptance vs rejection
flashcards.back: Incorrect acceptance = a misstated balance looks fair (effectiveness, most serious); incorrect rejection = a fair balance looks misstated (efficiency, wasted work).

questions.q: Sampling risk is controlled primarily by:
questions.explain: Sampling risk (an unrepresentative sample) is managed by sample size; nonsampling risk is managed by supervision/review.

choices: The rate of deviation in a control
The dollar amount of a balance

choices: Upper deviation rate is at or below the tolerable deviation rate
Sample deviation rate is zero only
questions.explain: Reliance is supported when the upper deviation rate does not exceed the tolerable rate.

questions.explain: Overreliance leads to too little substantive testing — an effectiveness (and the more serious) risk.

questions.q: Monetary-unit sampling is MOST efficient when the auditor:
choices: Expects few misstatements and tests for overstatement
questions.explain: MUS suits few-expected-misstatement, overstatement testing (e.g., receivables); it is weak for understatement and zero balances.

choices: A larger number of misstatements or understatement is expected
questions.explain: Classical variables sampling handles more misstatements and understatement (completeness) better than MUS.

choices: A materially misstated balance is concluded to be fairly stated
A fairly stated balance is rejected
questions.explain: Incorrect acceptance — a misstated balance looks fair — is the effectiveness risk the auditor guards against most.

weeks.title: AUD U2·W3 — Substantive Procedures for Specific Accounts (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the right procedure for the right assertion

With evidence and sampling settled, the auditor designs substantive procedures account by account, each aimed at the assertion most at risk. For assets the dominant worry is usually existence and valuation (overstatement); for liabilities it is completeness (understatement). This week walks MBG's major accounts and the signature procedures the exam tests for each.

Cash

Cash is small in balance but high in risk because it is liquid. The auditor sends a standard bank confirmation directly to the bank, obtains the year-end bank reconciliation and tests its reconciling items, and reviews the cutoff bank statement to verify reconciling items cleared. To detect kiting — overstating cash by exploiting the float on interbank transfers around year-end — the auditor prepares an interbank transfer schedule to confirm each transfer was recorded in the same period in both the disbursing and receiving accounts.

Accounts receivable

The signature procedure for receivables is confirmation with customers (existence and rights). Positive confirmations are used for large or risky accounts; non-responses are followed with alternative procedures — examining subsequent cash receipts and the underlying shipping documents and invoices. The auditor separately evaluates the allowance for doubtful accounts (valuation) by reviewing aging, collection history, and subsequent collections, and tests sales cutoff to ensure revenue and receivables fall in the correct period.

Inventory

For inventory the auditor must observe the physical count (a required procedure when inventory is material) to test existence, performing independent test counts and noting the condition of goods. Valuation is tested with price testing (vendor invoices for cost) and the lower-of-cost-or-net-realizable-value rule for obsolete or slow-moving stock. Cutoff is tested by examining receiving and shipping documents around year-end, and consigned or off-site inventory is confirmed. For a contractor, materials inventory is smaller than work in progress, which is audited as part of the construction-revenue work below.

Property, plant, and equipment

PP&E favors vouching additions to invoices and authorizations (existence and rights), examining title documents, and recomputing depreciation. Because PP&E accumulates over years, the auditor focuses on the current-period activity — additions, disposals, and the gain/loss on disposal — rather than re-auditing the whole balance each year, and watches for repairs improperly capitalized or capital items expensed. For MBG, the heavy-equipment fleet and the depreciation that drives the tax shield are the focus.

Accounts payable and the search for unrecorded liabilities

Liabilities flip the risk: the worry is understatement, so the key assertion is completeness and the signature procedure is the search for unrecorded liabilities. The auditor examines cash disbursements after year-end, unmatched receiving reports and vendor invoices, and unpaid bills, looking for obligations that belong in the period but were not recorded. Payables may be confirmed (especially with major vendors and any with small or zero balances, where understatement hides), and accrued liabilities — payroll, warranty, interest — are recomputed.

Revenue

Auditing standards presume revenue recognition is a fraud risk, so revenue gets heightened attention. The core procedures test occurrence (vouching recorded sales to shipping documents and customer orders) and cutoff (examining transactions around year-end to ensure sales are recorded in the right period), supported by substantive analytics comparing margins and trends. For a construction company, revenue is recognized over time under percentage-of-completion, so the auditor focuses on the measure of progress and the cost-to-complete estimate rather than shipping documents.

Long-term debt, equity, investments, and the construction WIP

For long-term debt the auditor confirms balances and terms with lenders and tests interest expense and covenant compliance; for equity, it confirms shares with the transfer agent (or examines the stock ledger) and reviews board minutes for dividends and issuances; for investments, it confirms or inspects securities and tests fair value. The contractor's defining audit area is work in progress: the auditor tests accumulated job costs, re-estimates cost to complete, recomputes percentage complete, and verifies the resulting over- and under-billings — the construction-specific application of the revenue and estimate rules.

The transaction cycles and directional testing

Auditors organize work by transaction cycle — revenue/receipts, purchases/disbursements, payroll, inventory/production, and financing/investing — because controls and risks cluster there. Within a cycle, direction of testing targets the assertion: to test existence/occurrence the auditor vouches from the recorded entry back to source documents (is this recorded sale real?); to test completeness the auditor traces from source documents forward into the records (was every shipment billed?). For an overstatement concern, vouch; for an understatement concern, trace. Misapplying the direction is a classic error — confirming receivables tests existence, not completeness, so it would never catch unrecorded sales.

Litigation, contingencies, and related parties

Three judgment areas demand specific procedures. For litigation, claims, and assessments, the auditor obtains a legal letter (attorney's letter of inquiry) from the client's lawyers — the primary evidence about pending or threatened litigation and the related loss contingencies under ASC 450; a lawyer's refusal to respond is a scope limitation. Related-party transactions are tested for proper authorization and disclosure — they are not eliminated like intercompany transactions, but their existence and terms must be transparent, because related parties are a common vehicle for fraud. And the fair-value and estimate procedures from last week reappear in every cycle: the auditor evaluates the method, the assumptions, and management's potential bias, corroborating with market data or an independent estimate where possible.

Cutoff and analytical review at the close

A theme across every account is cutoff — recording transactions in the correct period. The auditor examines sales, purchases, and cash transactions in the days around year-end against shipping and receiving documents, because a misstated cutoff shifts revenue, expense, and the related asset or liability between periods. Construction cutoff is especially sensitive, because a job's costs and the revenue recognized on them must land in the same period for percentage-of-completion to be faithful. Near the end of fieldwork the auditor performs a final analytical review, standing back to ask whether the statements as a whole make sense — do the ratios from the BAR analysis move as the year's events would predict, and is any unexpected relationship explained? This overall review, with the accumulation of misstatements against materiality, is the last check before the team concludes on each account and on the statements taken as a whole.

CMA bridge

Every procedure here targets a balance MBG's accounting produces. The search for unrecorded liabilities tests the completeness of the payables the CMA cost system records, and the WIP procedures audit the percentage-of-completion estimate at the heart of construction accounting — the auditor independently re-performing the cost-to-complete judgment the controller makes.

Practice and recap

  1. Audit assets mainly for existence/valuation (overstatement); audit liabilities mainly for completeness (understatement).
  2. Cash: bank confirmation, reconciliation, cutoff statement, interbank transfer schedule for kiting.
  3. Receivables: confirm and use subsequent receipts for non-responses; evaluate the allowance and test cutoff. Inventory: observe the count, price-test, apply lower of cost or NRV.
  4. Payables: search for unrecorded liabilities (subsequent disbursements). Revenue: presumed fraud risk — test occurrence and cutoff; for a contractor, audit WIP and cost-to-complete.

Recap: procedures follow the at-risk assertion — existence/valuation for assets, completeness for liabilities; cash uses confirmations and an interbank transfer schedule, receivables use confirmation plus subsequent receipts, inventory requires observing the count, payables require the search for unrecorded liabilities, and revenue (a presumed fraud risk) is tested for occurrence and cutoff — with the construction WIP and cost-to-complete estimate getting the closest scrutiny.

flashcards.back: Assets — existence/valuation (overstatement risk); liabilities — completeness (understatement risk).
Prepare an interbank transfer schedule to confirm each transfer is recorded in the same period in both accounts (no float overstatement).
Alternative procedures: examine subsequent cash receipts and underlying shipping documents/invoices.
Observe the physical count (required when material) and perform independent test counts; price-test for valuation; apply lower of cost or NRV.
The key completeness test for payables: examine post-year-end cash disbursements, unmatched receiving reports, and unpaid invoices.
Presumed fraud risk — test occurrence (vouch to shipping/orders) and cutoff; use analytics on margins.
Emphasize major vendors and small/zero-balance accounts, where understatement is most likely to hide.
Test accumulated job costs, re-estimate cost to complete, recompute percentage complete, and verify over/under-billings.

questions.explain: Liabilities are most at risk of understatement, so completeness is the key assertion.

questions.q: To detect kiting, the auditor prepares a(n):
questions.explain: An interbank transfer schedule verifies transfers are recorded in the same period in both accounts.

questions.q: For receivable confirmations that receive no response, the auditor performs:
choices: Alternative procedures such as examining subsequent cash receipts
questions.explain: Non-responses to positive confirmations are followed with alternative procedures like subsequent receipts and shipping documents.

questions.q: Observing the client's physical inventory count primarily tests:
questions.explain: Observing the count tests inventory existence (with test counts); price testing addresses valuation.

questions.q: The search for unrecorded liabilities primarily addresses which assertion?
questions.explain: It targets completeness — finding obligations that belong in the period but were not recorded.

questions.q: Auditing standards presume which account carries a fraud risk?
questions.explain: Improper revenue recognition is a presumed fraud risk, so revenue gets heightened occurrence and cutoff testing.

questions.q: For a construction contractor, the most judgment-intensive audit area is:
choices: Work in progress and the cost-to-complete estimate
questions.explain: WIP and the percentage-of-completion cost-to-complete estimate are the contractor's most judgmental, closely audited numbers.

weeks.title: AUD U2·W4 — Audit Reports & Communications (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the report is the product

Every procedure exists to support one deliverable: the auditor's report. The opinion expressed there is what users rely on, so the rules for which opinion to issue, and what to add to or change in the report, are the payoff of the whole audit. This week covers the standard report, the modified opinions, the extra paragraphs, and the communications that surround the report.

The unmodified opinion and report structure

When the statements are fairly presented in accordance with the framework, the auditor issues an unmodified (nonissuer) or unqualified (issuer) opinion. The report has a defined structure: a title referencing independence, the addressee, an Opinion section (now placed first), a Basis for Opinion section (stating independence and that sufficient appropriate evidence was obtained), the responsibilities of management (including going-concern evaluation), the auditor's responsibilities (reasonable assurance, materiality, professional skepticism), and the firm's signature, city, and date. The report date is no earlier than the date the auditor obtained sufficient appropriate evidence.

When to modify the opinion

Two problems force a modification, and their severity sets the type. A GAAP departure (a misstatement) or a scope limitation (unable to obtain sufficient evidence) leads to a qualified opinion when the matter is material but not pervasive. When the matter is material AND pervasive, a GAAP departure yields an adverse opinion (the statements are not fairly presented) and a scope limitation yields a disclaimer (the auditor expresses no opinion). The two-by-two — issue type by pervasiveness — is the single most tested reporting concept.

Emphasis-of-matter and other-matter paragraphs

Sometimes the opinion is unmodified but the auditor adds a paragraph. An emphasis-of-matter (EOM) paragraph highlights something properly presented in the statements that is fundamental to users' understanding — a major catastrophe, a significant related-party transaction, or a justified change in accounting principle. An other-matter (OM) paragraph addresses something not in the statements but relevant to the audit or report — for example, prior-period statements audited by a predecessor. Neither changes the opinion; they direct the reader's attention.

Going concern

Management must evaluate whether there is substantial doubt about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern for a reasonable period (generally one year). If substantial doubt exists but is adequately disclosed, the auditor typically issues an unmodified opinion with a separate going-concern section (an emphasis-of-matter). If the disclosure is inadequate, it becomes a GAAP departure (qualified or adverse). A severe, multiple-uncertainty situation can support a disclaimer. The auditor evaluates management's plans to mitigate the doubt before concluding.

Critical and key audit matters

For a PCAOB issuer audit, the report communicates critical audit matters (CAMs) — the matters arising from the audit that involved especially challenging, subjective, or complex auditor judgment and that relate to material accounts or disclosures. The AU-C/IAASB analogue, key audit matters (KAMs), applies to nonissuer and international reporting and is communicated when the auditor is engaged or required to do so. Neither CAMs nor KAMs modify the opinion; both simply give users insight into where the audit focused, increasing the report's informational value without changing the bottom-line conclusion.

Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts

Events after the balance-sheet date but before the report is issued get two treatments (from FAR): a Type I (recognized) event provides evidence about conditions existing at the balance-sheet date and adjusts the statements; a Type II (nonrecognized) event reflects new conditions and is disclosed. If the auditor learns of facts after the report is issued that, had they been known, would have changed the report, the auditor investigates and, if the statements are affected and people are relying on them, ensures the issue is addressed (revised statements or notification). The management representation letter, dated as of the report date, documents management's assertions and is required audit evidence.

Other engagements and communications

Not every engagement is an audit. A review (SSARS for nonissuers) gives limited assurance via inquiry and analytics; a compilation gives no assurance. Statements may be prepared under a special-purpose framework (cash, tax, or regulatory basis), which the report describes and which uses an emphasis-of-matter paragraph. In a group audit, the group auditor decides whether to reference a component auditor (dividing responsibility) or to take full responsibility. Throughout, the auditor must communicate with those charged with governance — significant findings, significant deficiencies and material weaknesses (in writing), disagreements with management, and the auditor's responsibilities — closing the loop the audit opened.

Comparative statements, consistency, and other information

Reports rarely cover a single year. With comparative statements, the auditor's opinion covers all periods presented; if a predecessor audited a prior year, either the predecessor reissues its report or the successor adds an other-matter paragraph describing the prior audit. A change in accounting principle that is properly applied and disclosed warrants an emphasis-of-matter paragraph on consistency — the opinion stays unmodified. The auditor also reads the other information in an annual report (management's discussion, the chair's letter) for material inconsistencies with the audited statements; a refusal by management to correct a material inconsistency can require the auditor to describe it or take further action.

Reporting on internal control and the integrated audit

For an issuer, the auditor of an accelerated or large accelerated filer also reports on the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting in an integrated audit (the §404(b) attestation from AUD Unit 1), and a material weakness there produces an adverse opinion on ICFR even when the financial-statement opinion is unmodified. For nonissuers, an examination of internal control is a separate attestation engagement. The thread tying the unit together is that the report is a calibrated statement: the opinion, the added paragraphs, the ICFR conclusion, and the communications each carry a precise meaning, and the auditor's craft is choosing exactly the right combination for what the evidence showed.

CMA bridge

AUD Unit 1's control deficiencies and Unit 2's evidence all converge here, in the opinion. The going-concern and subsequent-event rules tie back to FAR; the report is where the auditor translates everything learned about MBG's statements into the single conclusion users act on — fairly presented, qualified, adverse, or no opinion at all.

Practice and recap

  1. Know the unmodified report structure (Opinion first, then Basis, responsibilities, signature/date).
  2. Choose the modification by issue and pervasiveness: qualified (material, not pervasive); adverse (GAAP departure, pervasive); disclaimer (scope limitation, pervasive).
  3. Add an EOM (something properly in the statements) or OM (something outside them); report going concern as an EOM when disclosure is adequate; communicate CAMs in PCAOB issuer reports (KAMs only when engaged/required under nonissuer/international standards).
  4. Apply Type I (adjust) vs Type II (disclose) subsequent events; obtain the management representation letter; communicate with those charged with governance.

Recap: the unmodified report leads with the opinion; a material-but-not-pervasive problem yields a qualified opinion, a pervasive GAAP departure an adverse opinion, and a pervasive scope limitation a disclaimer; emphasis-of-matter and going-concern paragraphs flag matters without changing the opinion; critical audit matters (CAMs) inform PCAOB issuer readers (KAMs under nonissuer/international standards when required); and subsequent-event, representation-letter, and governance-communication rules surround the report the audit produces. Comparative statements carry the opinion across all periods presented, a properly disclosed change in principle draws a consistency emphasis-of-matter, and for an issuer the integrated audit adds an ICFR opinion that turns adverse on a material weakness — each element a precisely calibrated signal to the user.

flashcards.back: Title (independence), addressee, Opinion section FIRST, Basis for Opinion, management's responsibilities, auditor's responsibilities, signature/city/date.
A GAAP departure or scope limitation that is material but NOT pervasive.
Adverse = pervasive GAAP departure (statements not fairly presented); disclaimer = pervasive scope limitation (no opinion expressed).
EOM = something properly presented IN the statements that is fundamental; OM = something relevant but NOT in the statements. Neither changes the opinion.
Unmodified opinion with a separate going-concern section (emphasis-of-matter); inadequate disclosure → GAAP departure (qualified/adverse).

PCAOB issuer reports communicate CRITICAL audit matters (CAMs); KEY audit matters (KAMs) are the AU-C/IAASB nonissuer/international concept, communicated when engaged/required. Neither modifies the opinion.

flashcards.front: Type I vs Type II subsequent events
flashcards.back: Type I (conditions existing at year-end) → adjust; Type II (new conditions after year-end) → disclose.
Audit = reasonable assurance (opinion); review = limited (negative) assurance; compilation = no assurance.

questions.explain: Material-but-not-pervasive issues (departure or scope limitation) yield a qualified opinion.

questions.q: A scope limitation that is material AND pervasive results in a(n):
questions.explain: A pervasive scope limitation → disclaimer; a pervasive GAAP departure → adverse.

questions.q: A pervasive GAAP departure (statements not fairly presented) results in a(n):
questions.explain: A material and pervasive GAAP departure yields an adverse opinion.

questions.q: An emphasis-of-matter paragraph is used to highlight:
choices: A matter properly presented in the statements that is fundamental to users
questions.explain: EOM highlights something correctly presented in the statements; it does not change the opinion.

questions.q: When substantial going-concern doubt exists but is adequately disclosed, the auditor usually issues:
choices: An unmodified opinion with a going-concern (emphasis-of-matter) section
questions.explain: Adequate disclosure → unmodified opinion with a separate going-concern section; inadequate disclosure → qualified/adverse.

choices: A Type I event — adjust the statements
A Type II event — disclose only
questions.explain: Type I (recognized) events adjust the statements; Type II (nonrecognized) events are disclosed.

questions.explain: A review gives limited assurance via inquiry and analytics; an audit gives reasonable assurance; a compilation none.

units.title: REG Unit 1 — Ethics & Tax Procedures, Individual Taxation & Property Transactions

weeks.title: REG U1·W1 — Ethics, Professional Responsibilities & Federal Tax Procedures (CPA Core · from CMA m12)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the tax preparer's own rulebook

REG is the CPA section where you become the tax adviser, and before any number reaches a return there is a body of rules governing how a preparer must behave. When Jordan Reed's construction company MBG files its returns, the CPA who signs them is bound by Treasury Circular 230, the Internal Revenue Code's preparer-penalty regime, and the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services. CMA month 12 covered ethics from the management accountant's seat; REG adds the tax practitioner's distinct duties and the real penalties for breaching them.

Circular 230 — practice before the IRS

Circular 230 is issued by the Treasury Department and governs who may practice before the IRS and how. Those with unlimited practice rights are attorneys, CPAs, and enrolled agents (EAs); enrolled actuaries and enrolled retirement plan agents have limited rights. A practitioner's core duties include exercising due diligence as to the accuracy of returns and representations; promptly submitting records the IRS lawfully requests; not charging an unconscionable fee and not charging a contingent fee except in narrow situations (such as an examination or a claim for refund); avoiding conflicts of interest unless each affected client gives informed written consent; and not unreasonably delaying a matter before the IRS. A practitioner must also advise a client of any noncompliance, error, or omission and its consequences — but Circular 230 does not require the practitioner to notify the IRS of the client's error.

Circular 230 sanctions

The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) enforces Circular 230. For incompetence or disreputable conduct, willful violations, or recklessly giving false opinions, the Treasury may censure (a public reprimand), suspend, or disbar a practitioner from practice before the IRS, and may impose a monetary penalty up to the gross income derived from the offending conduct. Disbarment requires willful, reckless, or grossly incompetent conduct — not a mere good-faith mistake.

Preparer penalties under the Code

The Internal Revenue Code imposes its own penalties on paid preparers. §6694 targets understatements from unreasonable positions: a position lacking substantial authority (or, if disclosed, lacking a reasonable basis; for a tax shelter or reportable transaction the bar rises to more likely than not) triggers a penalty of the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income the preparer derived from the return. If the understatement is willful or reckless, the penalty rises to the greater of $5,000 or 75% of that income. §6695 imposes smaller fixed penalties for procedural failures — failing to sign the return, failing to furnish the taxpayer a copy, failing to keep records, failing to provide a preparer tax identification number (PTIN), or negotiating a client's refund check. §6713 and §7216 penalize the unauthorized disclosure or use of taxpayer information, with §7216 carrying criminal exposure.

The reporting-standards ladder

Several confidence thresholds recur, and the exam tests their order. From lowest to highest: frivolous (not arguable); reasonable basis (roughly a 20%-or-greater chance of success — the minimum for a disclosed position); substantial authority (roughly 40%, the standard for an undisclosed position); more likely than not (greater than 50%, required for tax shelters and to avoid certain penalties); and, highest in practice, a should/will opinion. Adequate disclosure of a position is made on Form 8275 (or 8275-R for a position contrary to a regulation), which can reduce both preparer and taxpayer penalties when the position has a reasonable basis.

AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services

The SSTS are enforceable standards for AICPA members in tax practice. Their core rules: a member should not recommend a position unless it meets the applicable reporting standard, and should advise the client of potential penalties; a member may rely in good faith on client-provided information but should make reasonable inquiries when information appears incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistent; a member may use the taxpayer's estimates if reasonable under the circumstances and not presented as exact; on learning of an error in a previously filed return, the member should advise the client to correct it but may not notify the IRS without the client's consent (except where the law requires it); and advice should reflect professional competence and serve the client's needs. The SSTS parallel Circular 230 but are AICPA-enforced and apply specifically to members.

Taxpayer penalties

Separate from the preparer, the taxpayer faces penalties. The accuracy-related penalty (§6662) is 20% of the underpayment attributable to negligence, disregard of rules, or a substantial understatement (for an individual, generally more than the greater of 10% of the correct tax or $5,000). The civil fraud penalty (§6663) is 75% of the portion of the underpayment due to fraud. Failure to file (§6651) runs at 5% per month (up to 25%), while failure to pay runs at 0.5% per month; in a month when both apply, the failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay amount. A reasonable-cause defense, shown by good-faith effort, can abate many of these — but never fraud.

Statutes of limitations and the audit path

The IRS generally must assess additional tax within three years of the later of the due date or the filing date. That extends to six years if the taxpayer omits more than 25% of gross income, and is unlimited for a false or fraudulent return or a failure to file. A taxpayer's refund claim must be filed within the later of three years from filing or two years from payment. A disputed examination goes first to IRS Appeals, an independent function that weighs the hazards of litigation; unresolved cases proceed to the U.S. Tax Court (no prepayment of the tax required), or to a U.S. District Court or the Court of Federal Claims after the taxpayer pays the tax and sues for a refund. These procedures, the penalty regime, and the practitioner standards together define the compliance environment in which every later REG topic is applied.

Bringing it to the construction client

For MBG these rules are concrete. If the CPA takes an aggressive position on the deductibility of a large equipment expenditure, the position needs substantial authority to go undisclosed, or a reasonable basis plus a Form 8275 disclosure, or the preparer risks the §6694 penalty. If Jordan Reed supplies an estimate of materials consumed on an in-progress job, the SSTS permit a reasonable estimate that is not held out as precise. And if the prior-year return overstated a deduction, the CPA must advise correction but cannot go behind the client to the IRS. The professional-responsibility layer is, in short, the frame around the tax computations the rest of REG teaches — get the duty and the standard right before you get the number right.

CMA bridge

CMA month 12 taught the IMA ethics standards for the internal management accountant; REG covers the tax practitioner's parallel but distinct duties under Circular 230 and the SSTS, plus the statutory penalties the IMA framework never reaches. Both demand integrity and a refusal to misrepresent — REG adds the federal enforcement teeth.

Practice and recap

  1. Know who has unlimited practice rights (attorneys, CPAs, EAs) and the core Circular 230 duties.
  2. Apply the §6694 preparer penalty (greater of $1,000/50%; willful or reckless, $5,000/75%).
  3. Order the standards: reasonable basis (disclosed) < substantial authority (undisclosed) < more likely than not (shelters).
  4. Distinguish the §6662 20% accuracy penalty from the §6663 75% fraud penalty, and know the 3/6/unlimited-year assessment statutes.

Recap: Circular 230 and the SSTS govern how a preparer must act; an undisclosed position needs substantial authority while a disclosed one needs reasonable basis (Form 8275); the §6694 preparer penalty is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the fee; taxpayers face a 20% accuracy or 75% fraud penalty; and assessment is generally 3 years, 6 if more than 25% of gross income is omitted, and unlimited for fraud.
