weeks.title: REG U1·W2 — Individual Taxation I: Gross Income, Exclusions & AGI (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — building the individual return from the top down

The individual return is a waterfall: gross income minus adjustments gives adjusted gross income (AGI); AGI minus deductions gives taxable income; tax minus credits gives the liability. This week builds the top of that waterfall — what counts as income, what is excluded, and the above-the-line adjustments that produce AGI. Jordan Reed, the owner of MBG, reports the construction profit on a personal return, so these rules are not abstract for our case.

Filing status

Five statuses set the rate brackets and standard deduction: single; married filing jointly (MFJ); married filing separately (MFS); head of household (HOH) — an unmarried (or considered-unmarried) taxpayer who pays more than half the cost of maintaining a home for a qualifying person for more than half the year; and qualifying surviving spouse — available for two years after a spouse's death if the taxpayer maintains a home for a dependent child. Marital status is generally determined on the last day of the year. HOH is heavily tested because it offers better brackets and a larger standard deduction than single.

Gross income — the broad rule

§61 defines gross income as all income from whatever source derived unless a specific provision excludes it. Common inclusions: wages, interest, dividends, business income (Schedule C), capital gains, rents and royalties, unemployment compensation, gambling winnings, taxable state refunds (only if the tax was deducted and gave a benefit — the tax-benefit rule), and a portion of Social Security benefits for higher-income recipients. Qualified dividends and long-term capital gains are included in gross income but taxed at preferential rates (0/15/20%).

Timing and a TCJA trap

Most individuals are cash-basis: income is recognized when actually or constructively received (available without substantial restriction), and expenses when paid. A classic trap is alimony: for divorce or separation instruments executed after 2018, alimony is neither deductible by the payer nor income to the recipient (the TCJA reversed the old rule, which still governs pre-2019 agreements). Child support is never income to the recipient and never deductible. Prizes and awards are generally taxable at fair value.

Exclusions from gross income

Specific provisions remove items from income. Frequently tested exclusions: gifts and inheritances (excluded to the recipient — the donor may owe transfer tax); life insurance proceeds paid by reason of death; municipal bond interest (state/local government interest); qualified scholarships for tuition and required fees (but amounts for room and board are taxable); the §121 gain exclusion on a principal residence — up to $250,000 (single) / $500,000 (MFJ) if owned and used as the principal residence for two of the last five years; qualified employer fringe benefits (employer-paid health coverage, §132 no-additional-cost and de-minimis fringes); and damages for physical injury or sickness (but not punitive damages or most emotional-distress awards).

Business income and self-employment tax

An owner-operated trade or business reports on Schedule C: gross receipts minus ordinary and necessary business expenses equals net profit, which flows to the Form 1040 and into AGI. Net Schedule C profit also bears self-employment (SE) tax: 92.35% of net SE earnings is multiplied by 15.3% (12.4% Social Security up to the annual wage base, plus 2.9% Medicare with no cap, and an extra 0.9% Medicare surtax on high earners). The employer-equivalent half of the SE tax is an adjustment to income. For MBG's owner this is the bridge between the construction P&L and the personal return.

Adjustments to income (above the line)

Adjustments are subtracted from gross income to reach AGI and are available whether or not the taxpayer itemizes — hence valuable. The tested list includes: one-half of self-employment tax; the self-employed health insurance deduction; self-employed retirement contributions (SEP/SIMPLE); health savings account (HSA) contributions; traditional IRA contributions (subject to active-participant phaseouts); student loan interest (up to $2,500, phased out); and educator expenses. AGI matters because it is the reference point for many phaseouts, the medical-expense and charitable thresholds, and the taxability of Social Security.

Worked AGI on the construction owner

Illustrative: Jordan Reed's personal return shows Schedule C net profit of $120,000, taxable interest of $2,000, and qualified dividends of $3,000 — gross income of $125,000. Adjustments: net SE earnings = $120,000 × 0.9235 = $110,820; SE tax = $110,820 × 15.3% ≈ $16,955, so the one-half deduction is about $8,478; plus a self-employed health insurance deduction of $9,000. AGI = $125,000 − $8,478 − $9,000 = $107,522. The qualified dividends remain in that total but will be taxed at the preferential rate when the liability is computed next week.

Retirement distributions, Social Security, and debt forgiveness

Several income items carry their own rules. Traditional IRA and qualified-plan distributions are ordinary income, and a 10% penalty applies to withdrawals before age 59½ absent an exception, while qualified Roth distributions are entirely tax-free. Social Security benefits are taxed in tiers — as provisional income rises, up to 85% of benefits becomes taxable, and none is taxable for low-income recipients. Cancellation of indebtedness is generally income under §61, but it is excluded in bankruptcy and to the extent the taxpayer is insolvent; the separate qualified-principal-residence-debt exclusion applied only to discharges completed by the end of 2025 (or under a written agreement entered into by then) per IRS Publication 4681, and is not available for later discharges. A state tax refund is income only under the tax-benefit rule — taxable just to the extent the prior deduction produced a benefit, which the SALT cap can reduce.

Dependents and the kiddie tax

A dependent is a qualifying child or qualifying relative meeting the relationship, age, residency, support, and gross-income tests; dependents drive credits and filing thresholds even though the personal exemption is permanently set at zero (Public Law 119-21 §70103 made the post-2017 suspension permanent). A dependent's own standard deduction is limited — broadly the greater of a small floor or earned income plus a set amount, capped at the regular standard deduction. The kiddie tax then taxes a child's net unearned income above an annual threshold at the parents' marginal rate, preventing families from shifting investment income to a low-bracket child. Wages a child genuinely earns working for the construction business are earned income to the child and escape the kiddie tax — a legitimate, often-tested family planning point.

CMA bridge

CMA taught how MBG's construction profit is measured for the financial statements; REG shows how that same profit is taxed on the owner's personal return — Schedule C net profit, self-employment tax, and the adjustments that convert business income into the individual's AGI. The book-to-tax mindset from FAR's ASC 740 unit reappears here from the taxpayer's side.

Practice and recap

  1. Order the waterfall: gross income − adjustments = AGI; identify the five filing statuses (HOH is high-yield).
  2. Apply §61: income from all sources unless excluded; watch the post-2018 alimony reversal.
  3. Know the common exclusions — gifts/inheritances, life insurance, municipal interest, §121 home gain, qualified scholarships.
  4. Compute SE tax (92.35% × 15.3%) and deduct one-half; list the above-the-line adjustments.

Recap: gross income is everything not specifically excluded; key exclusions include gifts, life insurance, municipal interest, and the $250k/$500k §121 home-sale gain; one-half of self-employment tax and self-employed health insurance are above-the-line adjustments; and for MBG's owner a $125,000 gross income nets to an AGI of $107,522 after those adjustments — the figure that drives the deductions, the QBI deduction, and the credits computed next week.

flashcards.back: All income from whatever source derived, unless a specific provision excludes it.
Single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household, and qualifying surviving spouse.
Gifts/inheritances, life insurance death proceeds, municipal interest, qualified scholarships (tuition/fees), §121 home-sale gain, child support.
Up to $250,000 single / $500,000 MFJ if owned and used as the principal residence 2 of the last 5 years.
Neither deductible by the payer nor income to the recipient (pre-2019 instruments keep the old deductible/taxable rule).
½ SE tax, self-employed health insurance, SE retirement (SEP/SIMPLE), HSA, IRA, student loan interest, educator expenses.
92.35% of net SE earnings × 15.3% (12.4% Social Security to the wage base + 2.9% Medicare; +0.9% surtax on high earners).
It is the reference for many phaseouts and for the medical/charitable thresholds; gross income minus above-the-line adjustments.

questions.explain: §121 excludes up to $250,000 (single) or $500,000 (MFJ) of gain if the ownership/use test is met.

weeks.title: REG U1·W3 — Individual Taxation II: Deductions, QBI, Credits & Computation (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — from AGI to the check

Last week ended at AGI. This week finishes the individual return: subtract the greater of the standard or itemized deduction and the qualified business income (QBI) deduction to reach taxable income, apply the rate schedule (with preferential rates on qualified dividends and long-term gains), and subtract credits to reach the liability — then compare to payments. The QBI deduction in particular matters to MBG's owner, because a construction contractor is not a specified service business.

Standard versus itemized deductions

A taxpayer deducts the greater of the standard deduction (a fixed amount by filing status, larger for the age-65-or-blind) or itemized deductions on Schedule A. After the TCJA nearly doubled the standard deduction, most taxpayers take it, so the exam tests when itemizing wins.

Itemized deductions (Schedule A)

The main itemized categories: medical expenses to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI; state and local taxes (SALT) — income (or sales) plus property taxes — capped for 2026 at $40,400 ($40,000 for 2025), subject to a MAGI phasedown to a $10,000 floor for high earners and halved for MFS — Public Law 119-21 §70120; home mortgage interest on acquisition debt up to $750,000 (made permanent by Public Law 119-21; pre-2018 loans grandfathered at $1,000,000); investment interest limited to net investment income; charitable contributions — cash up to 60% of AGI, and appreciated long-term capital-gain property at fair market value up to 30% of AGI; and casualty and theft losses only if attributable to a federally declared disaster (and, for tax years after 2025, a qualifying state-declared disaster). Miscellaneous 2%-of-AGI itemized deductions are permanently terminated (Public Law 119-21 Section 70110), while the above-the-line educator-expense deduction remains.

The qualified business income deduction (§199A)

Owners of passthrough businesses (sole proprietorships, partnerships, S corporations) may deduct up to 20% of qualified business income — a deduction taken after AGI that does not reduce SE tax. The deduction is the lesser of (a) 20% of QBI or (b) 20% of taxable income minus net capital gain (net capital gain includes qualified dividends). Above taxable-income thresholds, two further limits apply: a W-2 wages / UBIA-of-property cap, and a phaseout for a specified service trade or business (SSTB) — law, accounting, health, consulting, and similar. Construction is not an SSTB, so MBG's owner keeps the deduction even above the threshold (subject only to the wage/property cap). Worked limit: if QBI is $100,000 and taxable income less net capital gain is $90,000, the deduction is the lesser of $20,000 (20% × QBI) or $18,000 (20% × $90,000) = $18,000 — the taxable-income limit binds.

Computing the tax

Ordinary taxable income runs through the progressive rate brackets for the filing status. But qualified dividends and net long-term capital gains are pulled out and taxed at the preferential 0% / 15% / 20% rates, stacked on top of ordinary income to determine which preferential rate applies. High earners also owe the 3.8% net investment income tax on the lesser of net investment income or the excess of modified AGI over a threshold. The result is the gross tax before credits.

Credits — nonrefundable and refundable

Credits reduce tax dollar-for-dollar and are more valuable than deductions. Nonrefundable credits can reduce the tax to zero but not below: the base child tax credit, the child and dependent care credit, the lifetime learning education credit, the foreign tax credit, and the retirement savings credit. Refundable credits can generate a refund beyond the tax owed: the earned income credit (EIC), the additional child tax credit, and the partly refundable American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC). Knowing which credits are refundable is a recurring exam point.

The alternative minimum tax

The AMT is a parallel system that limits the benefit of certain preferences. Start from regular taxable income, add back preference and adjustment items (the SALT deduction, certain depreciation, private-activity-bond interest, incentive-stock-option bargain elements), subtract the AMT exemption (phased out at higher income), and apply the 26%/28% AMT rates to alternative minimum taxable income. The taxpayer pays the greater of regular tax or the tentative minimum tax. Because the TCJA raised the exemption, far fewer individuals owe AMT now, but it remains testable.

Payments and the construction owner

The liability is settled by withholding (from wages) and quarterly estimated payments. A self-employed contractor like MBG's owner has no withholding, so estimates matter: to avoid an underpayment penalty the taxpayer generally must pay the lesser of 90% of the current-year tax or 100% of the prior-year tax (110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000). Putting it together — deductions, the QBI deduction, the rate schedule, credits, and payments — converts the AGI from last week into the final number on the return, and completes the individual-tax arc of REG Unit 1.

Education and family credits in detail

The exam tests the contours of the common credits. The American Opportunity Tax Credit is up to $2,500 per student (100% of the first $2,000 of qualified expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000) for the first four years of postsecondary education, and is 40% refundable. The Lifetime Learning Credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses (a $2,000 maximum) per return, nonrefundable, with no year limit. The child tax credit is a per-qualifying-child amount that phases out at higher AGI, with a refundable additional child tax credit portion. The child and dependent care credit is a percentage of up to $3,000 of care expenses for one dependent ($6,000 for two or more) incurred to enable the taxpayer to work. Each credit has its own AGI phaseout, which is why they are sequenced carefully on the return.

Additional taxes and the underpayment mechanics

Beyond the income tax and AMT, high earners face the 0.9% additional Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above a threshold and the 3.8% net investment income tax on the lesser of net investment income or modified AGI over the threshold. The return reconciles the total tax to payments — withholding (treated as paid evenly through the year) plus quarterly estimates. If payments fall short of the safe harbor, the §6654 underpayment penalty accrues like interest on the shortfall for each quarter it persists. Because a contractor's income is lumpy, the annualized-income installment method can lower the required payment in slow quarters, matching estimates to when the construction cash actually arrives rather than assuming even income.

CMA bridge

CMA month 9 weighed decisions on a marginal, after-tax basis; REG supplies the actual individual-tax machinery behind that after-tax rate — the brackets, the preferential rates on capital gains, the QBI deduction, and the credits that determine an owner's true marginal cost of a dollar of construction profit.

Practice and recap

  1. Take the greater of the standard or itemized deduction; know the 2026 SALT cap ($40,400, phased down for high MAGI to a $10,000 floor), the 7.5%-of-AGI medical floor, and the $750,000 mortgage-acquisition limit.
  2. Apply §199A: 20% of QBI, limited to 20% of taxable income less net capital gain; construction is not an SSTB.
  3. Tax ordinary income at the brackets; tax qualified dividends and LTCG at 0/15/20%.
  4. Separate refundable credits (EIC, additional CTC, AOTC) from nonrefundable; pay estimates at 90%/100%/110% safe harbors.

Recap: taxable income is AGI minus the greater of standard or itemized deductions and minus the §199A QBI deduction (lesser of 20% of QBI or 20% of taxable income less net capital gain); ordinary income runs the brackets while qualified dividends and long-term gains get 0/15/20%; refundable credits like the EIC can exceed the tax; and a self-employed owner avoids penalty by meeting the 90%/100%/110% estimated-tax safe harbor.

flashcards.back: Deduct the greater of the two; itemized deductions go on Schedule A.
$40,400 for 2026 ($40,000 for 2025); phased down for high MAGI to a $10,000 floor; MFS uses half (Public Law 119-21 §70120).
Interest on acquisition debt up to $750,000 (older loans grandfathered at $1,000,000).
Deductible only to the extent total medical expenses exceed 7.5% of AGI.
Cash up to 60% of AGI; appreciated long-term capital-gain property at FMV up to 30% of AGI.
Lesser of 20% of QBI or 20% of (taxable income − net capital gain); W-2/UBIA cap + SSTB phaseout above thresholds. Construction is not an SSTB.
Refundable (EIC, additional CTC, partial AOTC) can produce a refund; nonrefundable (base CTC, child-care, LLC, foreign tax) only reduce tax to zero.
Qualified dividends and net long-term capital gains are taxed at 0%/15%/20%.

weeks.title: REG U1·W4 — Property Transactions: Basis, Capital vs Ordinary, §1231/1245/1250 & §1031 (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — every disposition is one subtraction

When MBG sells a backhoe or a parcel of land, the tax answer starts with one formula: gain or loss = amount realized − adjusted basis. The hard part is then characterizing the result — capital or ordinary, and at what rate — because depreciation recapture and the §1231 rules can split a single sale into pieces. This week covers basis, the capital/ordinary divide, recapture, and the like-kind deferral that lets a contractor roll real estate forward.

Basis — cost, adjusted, gift, and inheritance

Cost basis is what you paid, including acquisition costs. Adjusted basis = cost + capital improvements − depreciation/cost recovery taken. Two special rules recur. Gifted property: the donee takes the donor's carryover basis for computing a gain; for a loss, basis is the lesser of carryover basis or fair market value at the gift date (the dual-basis rule, which can produce no gain and no loss in the middle range); the donor's holding period tacks on only when the carryover (gain) basis is used — if the FMV loss basis applies, the holding period instead begins on the gift date. Inherited property takes a stepped-up (or down) basis equal to FMV at the date of death, and is automatically long-term regardless of how long the heir holds it.

Capital assets, netting, and the loss limit

A capital asset is defined by exclusion: §1221 says everything is capital except inventory, accounts receivable, depreciable business property, and real property used in a trade or business. Long-term means held more than one year. Individuals net short-term and long-term gains and losses; a net capital loss is deductible against ordinary income only up to $3,000 per year, with the excess carried forward indefinitely. Net long-term gains enjoy the preferential 0/15/20% rates from last week.

§1231 — the best of both worlds

Depreciable property and real property used in a business and held more than one year are §1231 assets. Their magic: a net §1231 gain for the year is treated as long-term capital gain (preferential rates), while a net §1231 loss is ordinary (fully deductible against other income). A five-year lookback prevents abuse — current-year §1231 gain is recharacterized as ordinary to the extent of net §1231 losses deducted in the prior five years.

Depreciation recapture — §1245 and §1250

Before §1231 applies, recapture converts part of the gain to ordinary income. §1245 (depreciable personal property — equipment, vehicles): gain is ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken; only the excess is §1231 gain. Worked example: MBG sells a loader that cost $100,000 with $60,000 accumulated depreciation (adjusted basis $40,000). Sold for $70,000, the $30,000 gain is entirely ordinary recapture (it is within the $60,000 of depreciation). Sold instead for $110,000, the $70,000 gain is $60,000 ordinary recapture plus $10,000 §1231 gain (long-term). §1250 (depreciable real property): with straight-line depreciation there is generally no ordinary recapture, but the straight-line depreciation is unrecaptured §1250 gain — the lesser of the depreciation taken or the recognized §1231 gain — taxed at a maximum 25% rate.

§1031 like-kind exchanges

A like-kind exchange defers gain when business or investment property is swapped for like-kind property. Post-TCJA, §1031 applies only to real property (equipment no longer qualifies). No gain is recognized except to the extent of boot (cash or non-like-kind property received); recognized gain = the lesser of realized gain or boot. The deferred gain is preserved in a substituted basis. Worked example: MBG exchanges land with a $200,000 adjusted basis for like-kind land worth $260,000 and receives no boot — no gain is recognized, the new land takes a $200,000 carryover basis, and the $60,000 gain is deferred until a future taxable sale. Receiving $20,000 of cash boot would force recognition of $20,000 of the gain.

Cost recovery — MACRS, §179, and bonus

The depreciation that drives recapture comes from MACRS: personal property uses the 200%-declining-balance method over 5- or 7-year lives with a half-year (or mid-quarter) convention; real property uses straight-line over 27.5 years (residential) or 39 years (nonresidential). Two accelerators matter for a contractor: §179 expensing lets a business immediately deduct the cost of qualifying property up to an annual limit, phased out as purchases get large and capped at business taxable income; and bonus depreciation allows an additional first-year percentage on qualifying new or used property. Both increase current deductions — and the depreciation that §1245 will later recapture.

Loss limitations — wash sales and related parties

Two anti-abuse rules disallow losses. The wash-sale rule disallows a loss on a security sold and repurchased within 30 days before or after; the disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement. §267 disallows a loss on a sale to a related party (family members, a more-than-50%-owned entity); the related buyer may later use the disallowed loss to offset a gain on resale. These rules, with recapture and §1231, complete the property-transaction toolkit — and round out REG Unit 1.

Installment sales and involuntary conversions

Two more deferral rules round out dispositions. The installment method spreads gain on a sale with payments received over more than one year: each payment recognizes gain equal to the payment times the gross-profit percentage (gross profit ÷ contract price). It is not available for inventory or for the depreciation-recapture portion, which is fully taxed in the year of sale even if no cash is yet received. An involuntary conversion (§1033) — property destroyed, stolen, or condemned — lets the taxpayer defer gain by reinvesting the proceeds in qualified replacement property within the statutory window (generally two years, three for condemned business real property); gain is recognized only to the extent the proceeds are not reinvested. Both rules, like §1031, defer rather than erase gain and carry the basis and deferred gain forward.

Holding period and the netting order

Character also turns on the holding period: more than one year is long-term, one year or less is short-term, and the period generally starts the day after acquisition. For gifted property the period tacks the donor's, and inherited property is automatically long-term. In capital netting, short-term gains and losses net together and long-term gains and losses net together; a net short-term gain is taxed at ordinary rates while a net long-term gain gets the preferential rate. A net loss in one class then offsets net gain in the other before the $3,000 ordinary-offset limit applies. Getting the holding period and this netting order right is exactly what fixes the rate on MBG's equipment and land sales.

CMA bridge

CMA capital budgeting (month 11) used the depreciation tax shield and after-tax salvage value as cash flows; REG supplies the rules behind them — MACRS and §179 create the shield, and §1245/§1250 recapture determines how the salvage proceeds are taxed when the asset is finally sold. The book gain/loss from FAR becomes a characterized tax gain here.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute gain/loss as amount realized minus adjusted basis; know gift carryover/dual basis and the inherited FMV step-up (auto-long-term).
  2. Net capital gains/losses; cap an individual's net capital loss at $3,000 against ordinary income.
  3. Apply §1231 (net gain = LTCG, net loss = ordinary) after §1245/§1250 recapture.
  4. Defer gain under §1031 (real property only) except to the extent of boot; carry over basis.

Recap: characterization is everything — §1231 net gains become long-term capital gain while net losses are ordinary, §1245 recaptures depreciation as ordinary up to the gain (so MBG's $30,000 loader gain is all ordinary but a $70,000 gain splits $60k ordinary / $10k §1231), real-property straight-line depreciation is unrecaptured §1250 gain (the lesser of depreciation taken or recognized gain) at a 25% max, and §1031 defers real-property gain except to the extent of boot with a carryover basis.

units.title: REG Unit 2 — Entity Taxation (C corp, S corp, Partnerships) & Business Law

weeks.title: REG U2·W1 — C Corporation Taxation (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — a separate taxpayer, taxed twice

Unit 1 taxed the individual owner directly. A C corporation is different: it is its own taxpayer, so its profits are taxed once at the entity level and again when distributed as dividends — the classic double taxation. If Jordan Reed incorporated MBG as a C corporation, the construction profit would face the 21% corporate tax and then a second tax on any dividend to Reed. This week covers formation, the corporate income computation, distributions, and liquidation.

Formation under §351

§351 makes incorporation tax-free when property is transferred solely in exchange for stock and the transferors, as a group, control the corporation — owning at least 80% of the voting power and shares — immediately after the exchange. Services do not count as property (stock for services is compensation income). If the transferor also receives boot (cash or other property), gain is recognized up to the lesser of the boot or the realized gain. Worked example: Reed contributes equipment with a $40,000 basis and $100,000 FMV solely for 100% of the new corporation's stock — no gain is recognized, Reed's stock basis is $40,000 (carryover), and the corporation takes the equipment at a $40,000 transferred basis. With $10,000 of cash boot, Reed would recognize $10,000 of gain (lesser of $10,000 boot or $60,000 realized).

Computing corporate taxable income

A C corporation's taxable income is gross income minus deductions, taxed at a flat 21% rate. Most ordinary and necessary business expenses are deductible, but several items follow special corporate rules. Unlike an individual, a corporation has no standard deduction, no QBI deduction, and no preferential capital-gains rate — net capital gains are taxed at the ordinary 21%.

Special corporate deductions

Three recur on the exam. The charitable contribution deduction is, under Public Law 119-21 §70426 (effective 2026), allowed only for contributions exceeding a 1%-of-taxable-income floor and is capped at 10% of taxable income (computed before the charitable, DRD, and a few other deductions); amounts above the 10% ceiling carry forward five years, while the portion below the 1% floor is disallowed under the new floor rule and is accounted for separately from the 10%-ceiling carryforward. Organizational and start-up expenditures may be partially expensed with the remainder amortized over 180 months. The dividends-received deduction (DRD) mitigates triple taxation of inter-corporate dividends: a corporation deducts 50% of dividends from a payer it owns less than 20% of, 65% if it owns 20% to 80%, and 100% if it owns 80% or more — subject to a taxable-income limitation that does not apply when the full DRD creates or increases an NOL.

Capital losses and net operating losses

Corporate loss rules differ sharply from the individual rules. A corporation's net capital loss offsets only capital gains — never ordinary income — and is carried back 3 years and forward 5 as a short-term loss. A corporate net operating loss arising after 2017 has no carryback, is carried forward indefinitely, and offsets only 80% of taxable income in a future year. These rules, with the special deductions above, drive the M-1 reconciliation below.

Book-tax differences (Schedules M-1 and M-3)

Because financial (book) income and taxable income diverge, a corporation reconciles them on Schedule M-1 (or the detailed M-3 for larger entities). Permanent differences (tax-exempt municipal interest, the 50% meals limit, federal income tax expense, fines) never reverse; temporary differences (depreciation, warranty accruals, deferred compensation) reverse over time and create the deferred taxes from FAR Unit 2. The M-1 starts with book net income and adds back nondeductible items and subtracts nontaxable income to arrive at taxable income.

Distributions and earnings and profits

A distribution to shareholders is a taxable dividend to the extent of the corporation's earnings and profits (E&P) — a tax concept similar to but distinct from retained earnings. Beyond E&P, the distribution is a return of capital that reduces the shareholder's stock basis, and any excess is capital gain. A corporation that distributes appreciated property recognizes gain as if it sold the property at FMV (but not loss). This ordering — dividend, then basis recovery, then gain — is a reliable exam pattern.

Liquidations, penalty taxes, and the corporate AMT

In a complete liquidation under §331, the shareholder treats the distribution as a sale of the stock, recognizing capital gain or loss, and the corporation generally recognizes gain or loss on the distributed property. A §332 liquidation of an 80%-owned subsidiary into its parent is tax-free to both. Two penalty taxes discourage hoarding earnings to defer the shareholder-level tax: the accumulated earnings tax (on earnings retained beyond reasonable business needs) and the personal holding company tax (on closely held corporations with mostly passive income). Finally, a 15% corporate alternative minimum tax applies to the financial-statement income of very large corporations (those averaging over $1 billion of book income) — not to a contractor the size of MBG, but testable.

Consolidated returns, reorganizations, and small-business stock

Related corporations get special regimes. An affiliated group connected through 80% ownership may elect to file a consolidated return, combining members' incomes and deferring gains on intercompany transactions until the asset leaves the group. Tax-free reorganizations let corporations combine without immediate tax when the deal has a business purpose and continuity of interest: a Type A statutory merger, a Type B stock-for-stock acquisition (solely for voting stock, ending in 80% control), and a Type C stock-for-substantially-all-assets acquisition are the most tested; boot triggers gain and the acquirer takes a carryover basis. Worked DRD: if MBG Corp owns 30% of a supplier and receives a $100,000 dividend, the 65% DRD is $65,000, leaving $35,000 taxed at 21% (absent the taxable-income limitation).

Two shareholder-favorable provisions round out the basics. §1244 stock lets an individual treat a loss on qualifying small-business-corporation stock as an ordinary loss (up to $50,000, or $100,000 MFJ) instead of capital — a rare conversion in the taxpayer's favor. §1202 excludes gain on qualified small business stock; for stock acquired after the July 4, 2025 enactment of Public Law 119-21 §70431 the exclusion is tiered — 50% after a 3-year hold, 75% after 4 years, and 100% after 5 years — with an expanded per-issuer limitation (stock acquired earlier keeps the prior more-than-five-years rule). Both reward investing in small C corporations and are frequent distractors against the general capital-gain rules.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 2 measured the deferred taxes that temporary book-tax differences create; REG shows the return side — the M-1 reconciliation, the 21% rate, the DRD, and the E&P that determines whether a distribution to MBG's owner is a dividend, a return of capital, or a capital gain. The entity choice itself (C corp double tax vs passthrough) is next week's decision.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply §351: tax-free if property is exchanged for stock and transferors control ≥80%; boot triggers gain up to the lesser of boot or realized gain.
  2. Tax corporate income at a flat 21%; apply the DRD (50/65/100%) and the 2026 corporate charitable floor/cap (deduct only amounts above 1% of taxable income, capped at 10%).
  3. Remember corporate capital losses offset only capital gains (back 3/forward 5) and post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely at an 80% limit.
  4. Order distributions: dividend to the extent of E&P, then return of capital, then capital gain.

Recap: a C corporation is a separate 21% taxpayer with double taxation; §351 defers gain on a controlled-corporation formation (Reed's $40,000-basis equipment for 100% stock = no gain, $40,000 carryover bases); the DRD is 50/65/100% by ownership; corporate capital losses offset only capital gains; and a distribution is a dividend only to the extent of E&P, then a return of capital and finally capital gain — while §1244 can turn a small-corporation stock loss ordinary.

Under PL 119-21 §70426, deductible only for contributions exceeding a 1%-of-taxable-income floor and capped at 10%; amounts over the 10% ceiling carry forward 5 years.
Offset only capital gains (never ordinary income); carry back 3 years, forward 5, as short-term.
No carryback; carried forward indefinitely; limited to 80% of taxable income.
Dividend to the extent of E&P, then return of capital (reduces basis), then capital gain.

weeks.title: REG U2·W2 — S Corporations & Partnerships (Passthroughs) (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — one layer of tax, not two

Last week's C corporation paid its own 21% tax and taxed shareholders again on dividends. Passthrough entities — S corporations and partnerships — avoid that second layer: income and loss flow through to the owners and are taxed once on their personal returns, whether or not cash is distributed. This is why a contractor like MBG is far more likely to operate as an S corp or partnership than a C corp. This week covers eligibility, basis, the all-important loss limits, and distributions.

S corporation eligibility and election

An S corporation is a domestic corporation that elects passthrough status, and the eligibility rules are strict and heavily tested. It may have no more than 100 shareholders; shareholders must be individuals, estates, or certain trusts — no nonresident-alien, corporate, or partnership shareholders; and it may have only one class of stock (differences in voting rights are allowed). The election is made on Form 2553 with the consent of all shareholders. Violating any requirement terminates the election.

S corporation income, basis, and loss limits

S corp income and loss pass through pro rata per share, per day, reported on each shareholder's Schedule K-1, with separately stated items (capital gains, §1231, charitable contributions) keeping their character. A shareholder's stock basis rises with income and contributions and falls with distributions and losses. Losses are deductible only up to basis — and critically, S shareholders get basis only for their direct loans to the corporation, not for entity-level debt. Worked example: a shareholder with $30,000 of stock basis and a $10,000 direct loan ($40,000 total basis) who is allocated a $50,000 loss deducts $40,000 and suspends $10,000 until basis is restored.

S corporation distributions

For an S corp with no C-corp history, a distribution is tax-free to the extent of stock basis (tracked through the accumulated adjustments account, AAA) and reduces basis; any excess is capital gain. If the S corp has accumulated C-corp E&P (from prior years as a C corp), distributions above AAA can be dividends. A few entity-level taxes survive the passthrough — the built-in gains tax and the excess net passive income tax — both legacies of a prior C-corp life.

Partnership formation and outside basis

§721 mirrors §351 for partnerships: no gain or loss is recognized when a partner contributes property in exchange for a partnership interest (with no control requirement). The partner's outside basis equals the carryover basis of contributed property plus the partner's share of partnership liabilities. That liability-sharing rule is the single biggest difference from an S corp: partners do get basis for their share of entity debt, which lets them deduct more losses. Contributing services for an interest, by contrast, is taxable compensation.

Partnership operations

A partnership is a pure conduit: partners are taxed on their distributive share of income under §704 whether or not it is distributed, reported on Schedule K-1 with separately stated items. A guaranteed payment — a fixed payment to a partner for services or capital, set without regard to profits — is deductible by the partnership and ordinary income to the partner (and subject to self-employment tax). Allocations must have substantial economic effect to be respected; otherwise income is reallocated by the partners' interests.

Partnership distributions and basis

A nonliquidating distribution is tax-free to the extent of the partner's outside basis, which it reduces; cash distributed in excess of basis triggers capital gain, and distributed property generally takes a carryover basis limited to the remaining outside basis. A decrease in a partner's share of liabilities is treated as a deemed cash distribution that can trigger gain. A liquidating distribution winds up the interest, with the partner's basis allocated to the property received. Throughout, the partner's outside basis is the running ledger that governs taxability.

Loss limits and choosing the form

Passthrough losses run a three-gate gauntlet in order: basis first, then the at-risk rules (limiting losses to amounts the owner could actually lose), then the passive activity loss rules (passive losses deductible only against passive income, unless the owner materially participates). Because partners get basis for entity debt and S shareholders do not, the partnership form often allows larger current loss deductions — a key planning point when MBG's owner weighs S corp versus LLC/partnership treatment against the S corp's self-employment-tax advantage (only wages, not the full profit, bear payroll tax).

Self-employment tax, reasonable compensation, and S termination

The passthrough forms differ on payroll tax, which often decides the choice. A general partner's distributive share of trade-or-business income is self-employment income, while a limited partner's share generally is not. An S corporation offers a planning edge: a shareholder-employee must take reasonable W-2 compensation (which bears payroll tax), but the remaining profit passes through free of self-employment tax. The IRS polices abusively low salaries, so the wage must be defensible — yet for a profitable contractor this can save meaningfully versus a partnership, where the full distributive share is exposed to SE tax. Worked outside basis: a partner who contributes land with a $50,000 basis and is allocated a 25% share of $80,000 of partnership debt has an outside basis of $50,000 + $20,000 = $70,000 — $20,000 more loss-absorbing capacity than an otherwise-identical S-corp shareholder, who gets no basis for entity debt.

Terminating an S election happens three ways: a voluntary revocation by shareholders holding more than 50% of shares; ceasing to qualify (admitting an ineligible shareholder or creating a second class of stock); or, for a former C corporation, having excess passive investment income for three consecutive years while holding accumulated C-corp E&P. After a termination the corporation generally must wait five years to re-elect S status. These mechanics, with the basis and loss rules above, complete the passthrough toolkit.

CMA bridge

The §199A QBI deduction from REG Unit 1 applies to the passthrough income computed here, and the entity choice (C corp vs S corp vs partnership) is exactly the kind of after-tax decision CMA month 9 framed — REG supplies the basis, loss-limit, and self-employment-tax mechanics that determine which structure leaves MBG's owner with more after-tax cash.

Practice and recap

  1. Know S corp eligibility (≤100 shareholders, eligible owners only, one class of stock, Form 2553) and that passthrough income is taxed whether or not distributed.
  2. Limit passthrough losses to basis, then at-risk, then passive; S shareholders get basis only for direct loans, partners for their share of entity debt.
  3. Apply §721 (no gain on contributing property) and compute outside basis including the liability share.
  4. Treat guaranteed payments as deductible to the partnership and ordinary income to the partner.

Recap: passthroughs are taxed once at the owner level; S corps cap losses at stock basis plus direct loans (so a $40,000-basis shareholder suspends $10,000 of a $50,000 loss), while partners add their share of partnership liabilities to outside basis under §721 — the difference that often makes the partnership form more loss-friendly, balanced against the S corp's payroll-tax savings — a general partner's full distributive share bears self-employment tax, while an S shareholder-employee owes payroll tax only on reasonable W-2 wages — the central entity-choice tradeoff for a profitable contractor.

weeks.title: REG U2·W3 — Business Law I: Contracts & UCC Sales (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — a construction company runs on contracts

MBG signs contracts every day — purchase orders for lumber and steel (a sale of goods), and subcontracts for framing and electrical work (a service). REG's business-law half tests which body of law governs each, when a binding contract exists, what defenses defeat it, and what remedies follow a breach. The split between the common law and the UCC is the organizing idea of the whole topic.

The three elements of a contract

A contract requires offer, acceptance, and consideration, plus capacity and a legal purpose. An offer is a manifestation of present intent to contract on definite terms, communicated to the offeree. Acceptance is assent to those terms. Consideration is a bargained-for exchange of legal value. Without all three, there is at most an unenforceable promise.

Common law versus UCC Article 2

The UCC Article 2 governs contracts for the sale of goods (movable, tangible property), while the common law governs services and real estate. A mixed contract is classified by its predominant purpose — a subcontract that is mostly labor with some materials is a service contract. The UCC is more flexible: it fills gaps (a missing price becomes a reasonable price), enforces deals despite open terms if the parties intended to contract, and imposes a duty of good faith. Merchants (those who deal in the goods) face additional rules.

Offer and acceptance mechanics

An offer can be terminated by revocation (effective when received, any time before acceptance), rejection or counteroffer, lapse of time, or the offeror's death. Two devices keep an offer open: a common-law option (supported by consideration) and the UCC merchant's firm offer — a signed writing by a merchant promising to hold the offer open, irrevocable without consideration for up to three months. On acceptance, the common law applies the mirror-image rule (acceptance must match the offer exactly; any change is a counteroffer), but UCC §2-207 rejects it: an acceptance with additional terms still forms a contract, and between merchants those terms become part of the deal unless they materially alter it, the offer limited acceptance, or they are objected to. The mailbox rule makes acceptance effective when dispatched.

Consideration and its substitutes

Consideration must be bargained for and have legal value; past consideration and a mere moral obligation do not count. The preexisting duty rule says a promise to do what one is already legally bound to do is not consideration — though the UCC allows a good-faith modification of a goods contract without new consideration. Where consideration is missing, promissory estoppel can still enforce a promise the promisee reasonably and detrimentally relied on.

Defenses and the statute of frauds

Even a formed contract may be unenforceable. Defenses include lack of capacity (a minor may disaffirm), illegality, duress, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation, mutual mistake, and unconscionability. The statute of frauds requires a signed writing for certain contracts — remembered as MY LEGS: Marriage, contracts not performable within one Year, Land, an Executor's promise to pay estate debts personally, Goods priced at $500 or more, and Suretyship (a promise to answer for another's debt). The writing need only show the essential terms and the signature of the party to be charged.

Performance, breach, and remedies

A material breach excuses the non-breaching party and triggers remedies; a minor breach entitles the injured party only to damages. The usual remedy is expectation damages — the benefit of the bargain — plus foreseeable consequential damages, reduced by the duty to mitigate. Liquidated damages are enforceable if they were a reasonable estimate and not a penalty. Specific performance is available for unique goods or real estate but not personal-service contracts. The UCC gives sellers and buyers tailored remedies — a buyer may cover (buy substitute goods and recover the difference), and either party may sue for the contract-market differential. Anticipatory repudiation lets the innocent party sue at once when the other clearly will not perform.

Third-party rights and discharge

Contract rights can be assigned and duties delegated (unless personal or barred by the contract); an intended third-party beneficiary can enforce a contract made for its benefit, while an incidental beneficiary cannot. A contract is discharged by full performance, by impossibility or impracticability (the subject is destroyed or performance becomes objectively impossible), by accord and satisfaction (agreeing to and rendering a substituted performance), or by novation (substituting a new party by agreement). Together these rules let MBG know exactly when a purchase order or subcontract binds it, when it can walk away, and what it owes if it breaches.

UCC warranties, risk of loss, and the parol evidence rule

The UCC adds protections to goods contracts. Warranties come in three kinds: an express warranty from an affirmation of fact or a sample; the implied warranty of merchantability (goods fit for their ordinary purpose), given automatically by a merchant seller; and the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose, when the seller knows the buyer is relying on the seller's skill to select goods for a stated use. Merchantability is disclaimed only by mentioning merchantability (or selling the goods as is); fitness is disclaimed by a conspicuous writing. Risk of loss turns on the shipping terms: in a shipment contract (FOB origin) risk passes to the buyer when the goods are delivered to the carrier; in a destination contract (FOB destination) it passes on tender at the destination; absent terms, a merchant seller bears risk until the buyer receives the goods. The parol evidence rule then bars prior or contemporaneous oral agreements offered to contradict a writing the parties intended as final — though such evidence may explain an ambiguity or prove fraud.

The UCC also imposes the perfect tender rule: a buyer may reject goods that fail to conform in any respect, though the seller generally has a right to cure within the contract time. These rules let MBG reject a nonconforming steel delivery while still giving the supplier a chance to fix it before breach.

CMA bridge

CMA treated MBG's purchase orders and subcontracts as cost commitments; REG explains when those commitments are legally binding — UCC Article 2 for materials, common law for subcontracted labor — and what damages a breach exposes the company to, the legal backbone under the financial obligations the management accountant tracks.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify the contract: UCC Article 2 for goods, common law for services/real estate (mixed by predominant purpose).
  2. Form the contract — offer, acceptance, consideration; know the merchant firm offer (3 months) and §2-207 vs the mirror-image rule.
  3. Apply defenses and the statute of frauds (MY LEGS; goods ≥ $500).
  4. Measure remedies — expectation damages, mitigation, liquidated (not penalty), specific performance for unique items, UCC cover.

Recap: the UCC governs goods and the common law governs services; a merchant's signed firm offer holds for up to three months without consideration and §2-207 forms a contract despite additional terms; the statute of frauds (MY LEGS) requires a writing for goods of $500 or more, land, suretyship, and the others; and the default remedy is expectation damages, with specific performance reserved for unique goods and real estate.

Expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages plus foreseeable consequential damages, reduced by mitigation; liquidated damages if reasonable (not a penalty).
Available for unique goods and real estate; not for personal-service contracts.

weeks.title: REG U2·W4 — Business Law II: Agency, Secured Transactions, Bankruptcy & Entities (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — who is bound, who gets paid, which entity

Contracts answered whether a deal binds; this week answers three more business-law questions REG loves. Agency: when does an employee or manager bind MBG? Secured transactions: when MBG borrows against its equipment, who gets paid first? Bankruptcy: what happens when a debtor cannot pay? And the entity choice that determines the owner's personal exposure. These rules complete the REG business-law core.

Agency — the three kinds of authority

An agent binds a principal to the extent of the agent's authority. Actual express authority is what the principal explicitly grants; actual implied authority is what is reasonably necessary to carry out the express task; and apparent authority arises from the principal's manifestations to a third party that lead the third party reasonably to believe the agent is authorized — even if the agent secretly is not. A principal can also ratify an unauthorized act after the fact, adopting the whole transaction. Agents owe fiduciary duties of loyalty, obedience, and care; principals owe compensation and indemnification.

Principal liability in contract and tort

In contract, the principal is bound when the agent acted with authority (actual or apparent). In tort, respondeat superior makes a principal liable for an employee's torts committed within the scope of employment — but generally not for the torts of an independent contractor (a key distinction for a builder that uses many subcontractors). Whether the principal is disclosed, partially disclosed, or undisclosed affects whether the agent is also personally liable on the contract.

Secured transactions — attachment and perfection

UCC Article 9 governs security interests in personal property. A security interest attaches (becomes enforceable against the debtor) when three things coincide: value is given, the debtor has rights in the collateral, and there is an authenticated security agreement (or the creditor has possession/control). Perfection gives the creditor priority over third parties and is usually achieved by filing a financing statement; some collateral is perfected by possession or control, and a purchase-money security interest (PMSI) in consumer goods is perfected automatically. Perfection is the step that protects the lender against other creditors of MBG.

Priority and the PMSI superpriority

Among competing secured creditors, the general rule is first to file or perfect wins, and any perfected interest beats an unperfected one. The major exception is the PMSI superpriority: a properly perfected PMSI beats an earlier-filed general security interest in the same collateral. For equipment, the PMSI holder must perfect within 20 days of the debtor receiving the collateral; for inventory, the PMSI holder must file and give authenticated notice to existing secured parties before the debtor receives the inventory. A buyer in the ordinary course of business takes free of a security interest created by the seller.

Suretyship

A surety (or guarantor) promises to answer for another's debt — the bonding relationship from CMA's risk unit, here from the legal side. The surety who pays has rights of reimbursement from the principal debtor, subrogation to the creditor's position, exoneration (forcing the debtor to pay before the surety must), and contribution from co-sureties. The surety can assert the debtor's defenses on the underlying contract (but not the debtor's personal defenses such as incapacity), and is discharged to the extent the creditor releases collateral or materially modifies the obligation without consent.

Bankruptcy

Federal bankruptcy offers Chapter 7 (liquidation — a trustee sells nonexempt assets and distributes proceeds), Chapter 11 (reorganization — the business continues under a court-approved plan), and Chapter 13 (an individual's repayment plan from future income). Filing triggers an automatic stay that halts collection actions. Claims are paid by priority — secured creditors first from their collateral, then statutory priority unsecured claims (administrative expenses, certain wages, taxes), then general unsecured creditors. A trustee can recover preferential transfers (to a creditor within 90 days, or one year for insiders) and fraudulent transfers. Most debts are discharged, but some are nondischargeable — most taxes, debts from fraud, alimony/child support, and most student loans.

Choosing the entity and the liability shield

The entity decision trades off liability and tax. A sole proprietorship and a general partnership expose owners to unlimited personal liability; a limited partnership shields the limited partners (but not the general partner); an LLP and an LLC give all owners a liability shield with passthrough taxation; and a corporation shields shareholders but adds the C-corp double tax unless an S election is made. The shield is not absolute: a court may pierce the corporate (or LLC) veil when owners commingle funds, undercapitalize, ignore formalities, or use the entity to commit fraud. For MBG's owner, the LLC/S-corp combination from last week pairs the shield with passthrough taxation — the structure most contractors choose.

Federal securities and employment regulation

Two federal regimes round out business law. The Securities Act of 1933 regulates the initial issuance of securities, requiring registration and a prospectus unless an exemption applies — the most tested being the Regulation D private placements (limited offerings to accredited investors and a capped number of non-accredited investors). The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulates secondary trading and ongoing reporting by public companies, and its Rule 10b-5 is the broad antifraud provision that also reaches insider trading. Liability under §11 of the 1933 Act for a materially false registration statement can reach the issuer, its officers, and the CPA who certified the financial statements — a direct professional-liability exposure tying REG to the AUD material. On the employment side, an employer withholds and pays FICA (Social Security and Medicare) and pays FUTA unemployment tax on employees, but not on independent contractors — so worker classification is at once a tax question and the agency question from earlier in this lesson. Misclassifying employees as contractors to dodge payroll tax is a frequent enforcement target, with back taxes and penalties the cost of getting it wrong.

CMA bridge

CMA month 10 treated surety bonds and the certificate-of-insurance program as risk transfers; REG gives the legal mechanics — the surety's reimbursement and subrogation rights, the Article 9 priority that decides whether MBG's lender or a supplier is paid first, and the entity shield that protects the owner's personal assets behind the construction risk.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish actual, implied, and apparent authority; apply respondeat superior to employees (not independent contractors) within scope.
  2. Attach (value + debtor rights + security agreement) then perfect (usually by filing); know automatic PMSI-in-consumer-goods perfection.
  3. Apply priority — first to file or perfect, with the PMSI superpriority (20 days for equipment; file + notice before delivery for inventory).
  4. Know the bankruptcy chapters, the automatic stay, claim priority, preference recovery, and nondischargeable debts; match the entity to the liability/tax goal.

Recap: apparent authority flows from the principal's conduct toward third parties and respondeat superior reaches employees within scope; a security interest attaches with value, debtor rights, and an agreement, perfects (usually) by filing, and ranks first-to-file-or-perfect with a PMSI superpriority; bankruptcy's automatic stay and priority scheme order the payouts; and the LLC/S-corp shield protects the owner unless a court pierces the veil for commingling or undercapitalization; and federal securities law (the 1933 and 1934 Acts) and the employee-versus-contractor payroll rules round out the business-law core.

units.title: REG Unit 3 — Estates & Trusts, Gift & Estate Tax, and Tax-Exempt Organizations

weeks.title: REG U3·W1 — Income Taxation of Estates & Trusts (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — a taxpayer that is also a conduit

When Jordan Reed dies or sets up a trust for the family, a new fiduciary taxpayer appears: the estate or trust files Form 1041 and pays tax on income it keeps, but income it distributes is taxed instead to the beneficiaries. The entity is part taxpayer, part conduit, and the device that splits the income between the two is distributable net income. This week builds the fiduciary return and that split.

The fiduciary return and who is taxed

An estate or trust computes income much like an individual — gross income less deductions — but with a crucial twist: it claims a distribution deduction for amounts paid or required to be paid to beneficiaries, shifting that income off the entity's return and onto the beneficiary's via a Schedule K-1. Income the entity retains is taxed to the entity; income it distributes is taxed to the beneficiary. This conduit principle prevents a second layer of tax on the same dollars.

Distributable net income (DNI)

DNI is the linchpin. It is the ceiling on both the entity's distribution deduction and the amount taxable to beneficiaries, and it preserves the character of the income (interest stays interest, tax-exempt stays tax-exempt) as it flows through. DNI is roughly taxable income plus the entity's personal exemption and tax-exempt interest, and generally minus capital gains allocated to corpus (principal) — because such gains are taxed to the entity, not distributed. The practical effect: a beneficiary is taxed only up to DNI, no matter how much cash is actually distributed.

The distribution deduction and character flow-through

The distribution deduction equals the lesser of DNI (reduced by tax-exempt income) or the amount actually distributed. The beneficiary then reports that amount, split into its components on the K-1 — so a distribution carrying out $30,000 of DNI that was 80% taxable interest and 20% tax-exempt interest is taxed to the beneficiary in those same proportions. Worked example: a simple trust with $30,000 of taxable interest that is required to distribute all income deducts $30,000, the beneficiary reports $30,000 of interest, and the trust's taxable income nets to roughly zero after its exemption.

Simple versus complex trusts

A simple trust (1) is required to distribute all income currently, (2) makes no charitable contributions, and (3) distributes no corpus. Anything else is a complex trust, which may accumulate income, distribute principal, and give to charity. The personal exemption tracks this: $600 for an estate, $300 for a simple trust, and $100 for a complex trust. Estates also enjoy more flexibility — they may elect a fiscal year and are exempt from estimated taxes for their first two years.

Grantor trusts

If the person who funds a trust keeps too much control, the trust is a grantor trust and is ignored for income-tax purposes — all its income is taxed directly to the grantor, as if the trust did not exist. Retained powers that trigger grantor status include a reversionary interest over 5%, the power to revoke, the power to control beneficial enjoyment, or the right to the trust's income. A revocable living trust — common in estate planning — is the classic grantor trust: fully taxed to the grantor during life.

Compressed brackets, IRD, and the 65-day rule

Trusts and estates face highly compressed brackets, reaching the top marginal rate and the 3.8% net investment income tax at a very low income level — a strong incentive to distribute income to beneficiaries in lower brackets. The 65-day rule helps: a complex trust or estate may elect to treat distributions made within 65 days after year-end as if made on the last day of the prior year. Income in respect of a decedent (IRD) — income the decedent earned but had not received (a final paycheck, an IRA) — is taxed to whoever receives it and does not get the date-of-death basis step-up that other inherited property enjoys.

Putting it together on the family trust

Suppose Reed's family trust earns $50,000 of dividends and $10,000 of tax-exempt municipal interest, allocates a $5,000 capital gain to corpus, and distributes $40,000 to a child. DNI is about $60,000 (the $50,000 dividends plus $10,000 tax-exempt, with the corpus capital gain excluded). The distribution deduction is the lesser of DNI net of tax-exempt ($50,000) or the $40,000 distributed — so $40,000 is deducted by the trust and taxed to the child, carrying the dividend and tax-exempt character proportionally, while the trust pays tax on the retained income and the corpus gain. The conduit has done its job: each dollar is taxed once, to whoever ends up with it.

The tiered distribution system and the separate-share rule

When a complex trust distributes more than its required income, the regulations sort beneficiaries into tiers. First-tier distributions — income the trust is required to distribute — carry out DNI first; second-tier distributions — discretionary amounts and corpus — carry out any remaining DNI, pro rata if they exceed it. This ordering decides exactly how much DNI, and which character of income, lands on each beneficiary's K-1 when there are several. The separate-share rule further requires that, when a single trust or estate has economically distinct shares for different beneficiaries, DNI be computed separately for each share, so one beneficiary is not taxed on income that economically belongs to another.

A charitable wrinkle rounds out the fiduciary deduction picture: unlike an individual's percentage-limited charitable deduction, an estate or complex trust gets an unlimited charitable deduction for amounts paid to charity from gross income pursuant to the governing instrument. Estates also carry unique privileges: an estate may elect a fiscal year (a trust generally must use a calendar year), is exempt from estimated tax payments for its first two taxable years, and can hold income to smooth it across the administration period. These flexibilities, with the tiered rules, make the executor's timing of distributions a genuine lever over who pays the tax and when.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 2 distinguished an entity's income from its owners'; fiduciary income tax is the same idea for an estate or trust — DNI is the bridge that decides whether the dividend on MBG stock held in Reed's family trust is taxed to the trust or to the child who receives the distribution, with character preserved either way.

Practice and recap

  1. File Form 1041; tax retained income to the entity and distributed income to beneficiaries.
  2. Compute DNI as the ceiling on the distribution deduction and beneficiary income; it preserves character and generally excludes capital gains allocated to corpus.
  3. Classify simple (distribute all income, no charity, no corpus) vs complex trusts; know the $600/$300/$100 exemptions.
  4. Tax grantor-trust income to the grantor; use the 65-day rule and watch IRD (no basis step-up).

Recap: an estate or trust is a conduit — it deducts distributions and shifts that income to beneficiaries, capped at DNI, with character preserved; simple trusts distribute all income (a $300 exemption) while complex trusts may accumulate ($100); a grantor trust's income is taxed to the grantor; and the compressed brackets push fiduciaries to distribute, aided by the 65-day rule.

weeks.title: REG U3·W2 — The Federal Gift Tax (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — taxing the transfer, not the income

The income tax reaches what you earn; the transfer taxes reach what you give. When Jordan Reed gifts shares of MBG to the children to move value out of a taxable estate, the gift tax applies — paid by the donor, not the recipient. The gift tax is unified with the estate tax (one lifetime exemption covers both), so this week's rules feed directly into next week's estate tax.

What is a taxable gift

A gift is a completed, gratuitous transfer in which the donor gives up dominion and control for less than full consideration. Both the giver's donative intent and delivery matter; an incomplete transfer (one the donor can revoke) is not yet a gift. The donor files Form 709 and, importantly, uses the lifetime exemption before any tax is actually due — most gifts reduce the exemption rather than generate a check.

The annual exclusion

Each donor may give up to the annual exclusion — $19,000 per donee for 2025 (indexed annually for inflation) — to any number of recipients every year, free of gift tax and without using any exemption. The catch: the exclusion applies only to a present interest — a gift the donee can enjoy immediately. A future interest (the right to receive property only later, as in many trusts) does not qualify for the annual exclusion.

Gift splitting and the unlimited deductions

A married couple may elect gift splitting, treating a gift by one spouse as made one-half by each — effectively doubling the annual exclusion to $38,000 per donee. Two transfers are entirely exempt: the unlimited marital deduction (gifts to a U.S.-citizen spouse) and the unlimited charitable deduction. Separately, direct payments of tuition or medical expenses — paid straight to the school or provider — are excluded without limit and do not even use the annual exclusion.

Computing taxable gifts and the unified exemption

Taxable gifts = total gifts − annual exclusions − marital and charitable deductions. Tax is computed on cumulative lifetime taxable gifts, but the unified credit shelters gifts up to the basic exclusion amount — about $15 million per individual for 2026, made permanent and increased by Public Law 119-21 and indexed thereafter. Worked example: in 2025 Reed gives $50,000 to each of three children. After the $19,000 annual exclusion, taxable gifts are ($50,000 − $19,000) × 3 = $93,000, which simply reduces the lifetime exemption — no tax is due until cumulative taxable gifts exceed the exemption. With gift splitting, the $38,000 combined exclusion drops the taxable gifts to $12,000 × 3 = $36,000.

Present versus future interests and Crummey powers

Because the annual exclusion needs a present interest, gifts into trust normally fail to qualify — the beneficiary cannot touch the property now. Estate planners solve this with a Crummey power: the trust gives the beneficiary a brief window to withdraw the contribution, which converts it into a present interest that does qualify for the annual exclusion, even though the beneficiary is expected not to withdraw. This is a heavily tested wrinkle linking the gift tax to trust planning.

Valuation and family-business discounts

Gifts are valued at fair market value on the date of the gift. When Reed gifts a minority block of MBG stock, the value may be reduced by a minority-interest discount (the block cannot control the company) and a lack-of-marketability discount (closely held shares are hard to sell) — legitimate reductions that move more value to the next generation per dollar of exemption used. Aggressive discounts invite IRS scrutiny and a qualified appraisal, but the technique is central to transferring a family construction business.

Carryover basis and the income-tax aftermath of a gift

A gift carries an income-tax consequence the donee inherits with the property: gifted property keeps the donor's carryover basis (the dual-basis rule from Unit 1 for losses), so the appreciation is not erased — it shifts to the donee, who pays income tax on the built-in gain when the property is later sold. This is the key contrast with property held until death, which receives a basis step-up. Gifting therefore trades a potential estate-tax saving (moving future appreciation out of the estate) against the loss of the step-up, and the planner must weigh the two: gift assets expected to appreciate (to remove future growth from the transfer-tax base) but consider holding highly appreciated assets until death (to capture the step-up). For a family construction business expected to grow, gifting minority interests early can move substantial future value out of the estate.

Indirect gifts and special situations

The gift tax reaches more than outright transfers. A below-market loan to a family member is treated as a gift of the forgone interest; forgiving a debt, paying another's expense (other than direct tuition or medical), or selling property for inadequate consideration are all gifts. A net gift — where the donee agrees to pay the gift tax — reduces the taxable gift by the tax assumed, and can even generate income to the donor to the extent that tax exceeds basis. A qualified disclaimer lets a beneficiary refuse a gift or bequest (in writing, within nine months, before accepting any benefit) so the property passes to the next taker as if the disclaimant had predeceased — a tool to redirect transfers and use exemptions efficiently. And a gift to a minor through a §2503(c) trust or a custodial account qualifies for the annual exclusion even though the child cannot yet manage the property.

Gift versus bequest — a worked comparison

The recurring planning question is whether to gift an asset now or let it pass at death. Consider MBG stock with a $100,000 basis and a $400,000 value. Gift it today: the donee takes the $100,000 carryover basis, the value (less the annual exclusion) uses lifetime exemption, and all future appreciation grows in the child's hands — but the child faces income tax on the $300,000 built-in gain whenever the stock is sold. Hold it until death: the stock is in the gross estate at its date-of-death value, yet the heir takes a stepped-up basis equal to that value, erasing the built-in gain for income-tax purposes. The answer turns on the spread between transfer-tax and income-tax rates, how much more the asset is expected to appreciate, and whether the estate will even be taxable given the large exemption. For most families under the roughly $15 million exemption the step-up often wins for highly appreciated assets, while gifting wins for assets expected to appreciate sharply that the family wants out of a potentially taxable estate.

CMA bridge

CMA valued MBG as a going concern; the gift tax values fractional interests in it, with minority and marketability discounts — the same enterprise, now measured for a generational transfer. The exemption Reed uses gifting shares this year is the same unified exemption that will shelter the estate next week.

Practice and recap

  1. Recognize a completed gift (donative intent + delivery + relinquished control); the donor pays and files Form 709.
  2. Apply the annual exclusion ($19,000 for 2025, indexed) to present-interest gifts to unlimited donees; future interests do not qualify.
  3. Use gift splitting ($38,000), the unlimited marital/charitable deductions, and the direct tuition/medical exclusion.
  4. Shelter cumulative taxable gifts with the ~$15 million (2026, PL 119-21) unified exemption; use Crummey powers and valuation discounts in planning.

Recap: the donor-paid gift tax allows a $19,000 (2025) annual exclusion per donee for present-interest gifts, unlimited marital and charitable deductions, and a direct tuition/medical exclusion; taxable gifts reduce a unified lifetime exemption of about $15 million per person for 2026 under Public Law 119-21; and Crummey powers plus minority/marketability discounts move a family business out of the estate efficiently.

Unlimited marital and charitable deductions; direct payments of tuition or medical expenses are excluded without limit.
About $15 million per individual, made permanent and increased by Public Law 119-21 (indexed); shared by gift and estate tax.
A short withdrawal right that converts a gift in trust into a present interest qualifying for the annual exclusion.
Minority-interest and lack-of-marketability discounts reduce the value of gifted closely held business interests.

weeks.title: REG U3·W3 — The Federal Estate & Generation-Skipping Tax (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the second half of the unified system

Last week's gift tax taxed lifetime transfers; the estate tax taxes the transfer at death, using the same unified exemption. When Jordan Reed dies, the executor files Form 706, totals everything Reed owned or controlled, subtracts deductions, and applies the unified credit. Because the exemption is so large, most estates owe nothing — but the computation, the inclusion surprises, and portability are squarely tested.

The gross estate

The gross estate is everything the decedent owned or controlled at death, valued at fair market value on the date of death (or the alternate valuation date six months later, if electing it lowers both the estate and the tax). It includes probate property, cash and securities (the MBG shares), real estate, and business interests — but the inclusion rules reach further than probate.

Inclusion rules that surprise

Several items pulled into the gross estate trip up candidates. Life insurance is included if the decedent owned the policy or held any incidents of ownership, or if proceeds are payable to the estate. Retained interests are caught: property the decedent transferred but kept a life estate (§2036) or the power to alter or revoke (§2038) is fully included. Gifts made within three years of death are generally not pulled back — except the gift tax paid on them (the gross-up rule) and transfers of life insurance. Jointly held property, general powers of appointment, and certain annuities are also included.

Deductions from the gross estate

From the gross estate the executor subtracts: funeral and administration expenses, the decedent's debts and unpaid taxes, casualty losses during administration, the unlimited marital deduction (property passing to a surviving U.S.-citizen spouse), the unlimited charitable deduction, and state death taxes. The marital deduction is the great deferral device — it pushes tax on the first spouse's estate to the death of the second.

From taxable estate to tax

The taxable estate is the gross estate minus deductions. To it the computation adds back post-1976 adjusted taxable gifts (so the brackets account for lifetime giving), produces a tentative tax at rates topping out near 40%, then subtracts gift taxes already paid and the unified credit. The credit shelters the basic exclusion amount — about $15 million per individual for 2026, made permanent and increased by Public Law 119-21 and indexed thereafter. Only estates above that exemption (net of lifetime gifts) actually owe tax.

Portability of the exemption

A spouse who dies without using the full exemption can pass the unused amount — the deceased spousal unused exclusion (DSUE) — to the surviving spouse, who adds it to their own. Portability is not automatic: the executor must elect it on a timely filed Form 706, even for an estate too small to owe tax. With portability a married couple can shelter roughly twice the individual exemption without complex trust planning.

The generation-skipping transfer tax and the basis step-up

The generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax is a separate, flat tax at the top rate layered on transfers that skip a generation — for example, a gift or bequest straight to a grandchild — to stop families from avoiding a layer of transfer tax. It has its own exemption (tracking the unified amount). Finally, the estate tax pairs with an income-tax benefit: property included in the gross estate gets a basis step-up to date-of-death fair market value, so heirs who later sell recognize gain only on post-death appreciation — the reason holding appreciated MBG stock until death can beat gifting it during life.

Putting it together on the family estate

Suppose Reed dies in 2026 with a $10 million gross estate, $1 million of debts and expenses, and $2 million passing to a spouse. The taxable estate is $10M − $1M − $2M (marital) = $7 million. Because that is well under the roughly $15 million exemption, the unified credit eliminates the tax entirely — and the executor may still file Form 706 to elect portability of the unused exemption to the surviving spouse, and the heirs take the assets with a stepped-up basis. The estate-and-gift system has taxed the transfer once, at a generous threshold, with the income tax forgiving the built-in gain.

Marital-deduction planning and estate liquidity
