The unlimited marital deduction defers tax but does not erase it, so planning shapes how property passes to a spouse. A QTIP (qualified terminable interest property) trust lets the first spouse to die give the survivor a lifetime income interest while controlling who ultimately receives the property — and the estate elects to treat it as qualifying for the marital deduction, deferring tax to the survivor's death. A credit-shelter (bypass) trust instead uses the first spouse's exemption at the first death, keeping that amount and its future growth out of the survivor's estate; with portability now permanent many couples rely on the DSUE election, though a bypass trust still shelters post-death appreciation that portability does not.

Large estates also face a liquidity problem: estate tax is generally due nine months after death, yet much of a construction family's wealth may be illiquid business interests and real estate. §6166 lets an estate in which a closely held business exceeds 35% of the adjusted gross estate pay the tax in installments over up to fourteen years at a reduced interest rate — relief built precisely for a family business like MBG, so heirs need not fire-sale the company to pay the tax. The executor weighs this against the alternate valuation date and the deductions to settle the estate without dismantling it.

Filing, payment, and the alternate valuation election

The estate-tax return, Form 706, is generally due nine months after death (a six-month extension is available) and must be filed when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds the exemption — or, for smaller estates, to elect portability. The executor may elect the alternate valuation date (six months after death) only if doing so decreases both the gross estate and the estate tax, which stops taxpayers from cherry-picking a higher basis without a tax cost; property sold or distributed during the six months is valued at that transaction date. These mechanics, with §6166 installments and the portability election, give the executor a toolkit to settle even an illiquid estate on time without dismantling the family business to raise cash.

CMA bridge

The gift tax (last week) and the estate tax (this week) draw on one unified exemption; together they decide how much of MBG's value Reed can move to the next generation tax-free. The date-of-death basis step-up ties back to FAR/REG property rules — the heir's basis in the inherited MBG stock is its FMV at death, not Reed's original cost.

Practice and recap

  1. Build the gross estate at date-of-death FMV (or alternate valuation); include life insurance with incidents of ownership, retained-interest transfers, and the gift tax on within-3-years gifts.
  2. Subtract debts/expenses and the unlimited marital and charitable deductions to reach the taxable estate.
  3. Add back adjusted taxable gifts, apply the ~40% rates, and shelter with the ~$15 million (2026, PL 119-21) unified credit.
  4. Elect portability of the DSUE on a timely Form 706; know the separate GST tax and the date-of-death basis step-up.

Recap: the estate tax totals everything the decedent owned or controlled (including life insurance with incidents of ownership and retained-interest transfers), subtracts the unlimited marital and charitable deductions, and shelters about $15 million per person for 2026 under Public Law 119-21; portability passes a spouse's unused exemption via a timely Form 706; the GST tax adds a flat top-rate layer on generation-skipping transfers; and inherited property takes a date-of-death basis step-up.

flashcards.back: Everything the decedent owned or controlled, at date-of-death FMV (or the alternate valuation date 6 months later, if it lowers estate and tax).

flashcards.front: Life insurance in the gross estate
flashcards.back: Included if the decedent held any incidents of ownership or the proceeds are payable to the estate.
Generally NOT pulled back into the gross estate — except the gift tax paid (gross-up) and transfers of life insurance.
Funeral/administration expenses, debts, casualty losses, and the UNLIMITED marital and charitable deductions (plus state death taxes).
About $15 million per individual, made permanent and increased by Public Law 119-21; top estate-tax rate near 40%.
A surviving spouse may use the deceased spouse's unused exemption, but only if elected on a timely filed Form 706.
A separate flat tax at the top rate on transfers that skip a generation; has its own exemption.
Property in the gross estate takes a basis equal to date-of-death FMV, so heirs are taxed only on post-death appreciation.

questions.q: Life insurance proceeds are included in the decedent's gross estate when the decedent:
choices: Held incidents of ownership in the policy
Bought the policy more than 3 years ago
questions.explain: Incidents of ownership (or proceeds payable to the estate) cause inclusion in the gross estate.

questions.q: The estate tax marital deduction for property passing to a surviving U.S.-citizen spouse is:
questions.explain: The marital deduction is unlimited, deferring tax until the surviving spouse's death.

questions.q: For 2026, the unified estate-and-gift exemption is approximately:
questions.explain: Public Law 119-21 set the basic exclusion at roughly $15 million per individual for 2026, indexed thereafter.

questions.q: Portability of a deceased spouse's unused exemption (DSUE):
choices: Requires a timely filed Form 706 election
Doubles the surviving spouse's income tax
questions.explain: Portability must be elected on a timely filed estate-tax return, even if no tax is due.

questions.q: Property included in the gross estate generally takes a basis equal to:
questions.explain: Inherited property is stepped to date-of-death FMV, so heirs are taxed only on later appreciation.

questions.q: The generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax applies to:
choices: Transfers that skip a generation (e.g., to a grandchild)
questions.explain: The GST tax is a separate flat top-rate tax on transfers skipping a generation.

questions.q: Gifts made within three years of death are generally:
choices: Not pulled back into the gross estate, except gift tax paid and life insurance
questions.explain: The three-year rule pulls back the gift tax paid (gross-up) and life-insurance transfers, but not most gifts themselves.

weeks.title: REG U3·W4 — Tax-Exempt Organizations (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — when an entity pays no income tax

If Jordan Reed endows a family foundation or MBG supports a local charity, a different creature appears: a tax-exempt organization that pays no federal income tax on income furthering its exempt purpose. Exemption is a privilege with strings — strict organizational rules, prohibited activities, special taxes on private foundations, and a tax on business income unrelated to the mission. This closes REG Unit 3.

Qualifying under §501(c)(3)

The best-known exemption, §501(c)(3), covers organizations organized and operated exclusively for charitable, religious, educational, scientific, or literary purposes. Two tests must both be met: the organizational test (the governing documents limit the entity to exempt purposes and dedicate assets to charity on dissolution) and the operational test (it actually operates that way). A §501(c)(3) is uniquely valuable because contributions to it are tax-deductible to donors.

The prohibited activities

Exemption is lost or penalized for three things. Private inurement — letting the organization's earnings benefit insiders (excess compensation, sweetheart deals) — is strictly forbidden, and excess benefit transactions trigger intermediate-sanction excise taxes on the insiders. Lobbying must be insubstantial (or within a measured election). And political campaign activity — supporting or opposing a candidate — is an absolute prohibition for a §501(c)(3); even a single endorsement can cost the exemption.

Applying for recognition

An organization seeks recognition of exemption by filing Form 1023 (a streamlined 1023-EZ exists for small organizations). The IRS issues a determination letter. While churches and very small organizations have relief from applying, recognition is what assures donors their gifts are deductible and the entity is exempt — so most file. Recognition is prospective discipline, not a one-time pass: the entity must keep meeting the operational test.

Public charity versus private foundation

Every §501(c)(3) is presumed a private foundation unless it qualifies as a public charity — typically by passing a public support test (drawing a broad base of public donations) or by being an inherently public institution like a church, school, or hospital. The distinction matters greatly: private foundations (such as Reed's family foundation, funded by one family) face a battery of excise taxes and tighter rules that public charities escape.

Private foundation excise taxes

Private foundations bear special excise taxes designed to force charitable use and prevent abuse: a tax on net investment income; a penalty for failing to make the required minimum distributions (roughly 5% of investment assets) for charitable purposes each year; prohibitions on self-dealing between the foundation and its insiders; limits on excess business holdings (owning too much of a business); and taxes on jeopardizing investments and improper taxable expenditures (such as lobbying). These rules are why a family foundation is more tightly regulated than a community public charity.

Unrelated business income tax (UBIT)

Even an exempt organization pays regular corporate tax — UBIT, reported on Form 990-T — on income from a trade or business that is regularly carried on and not substantially related to its exempt purpose. The classic example: a charity that runs a commercial business unrelated to its mission. Debt-financed income is also taxed. But key exceptions remove income produced by substantially all volunteer labor, the sale of donated goods, or activities run for the convenience of members (a hospital cafeteria) — and passive dividends, interest, and rents are generally excluded. UBIT keeps tax-exempt entities from competing untaxed with ordinary businesses.

Annual compliance and other exempt types

Most exempt organizations file an annual information return — Form 990 (with 990-EZ and the postcard 990-N for smaller groups; private foundations file 990-PF). Failing to file for three consecutive years automatically revokes exemption. Beyond §501(c)(3), other categories exist — §501(c)(4) social-welfare organizations (which may lobby and do limited political work, but gifts are not deductible) and §501(c)(6) trade associations and chambers of commerce, the kind a construction industry group would use. Each is exempt, but only the §501(c)(3) offers donors a deduction.

Intermediate sanctions and donor substantiation

Two compliance points round out §501(c)(3) practice. Rather than revoking exemption for every insider abuse, the IRS can impose intermediate sanctions — excise taxes on a disqualified person who receives an excess benefit (and on managers who knowingly approve it) — a more proportionate remedy than killing the charity. And to claim a deduction, donors must meet substantiation rules: a contemporaneous written acknowledgment for any gift of $250 or more, additional appraisal requirements for larger noncash gifts, and disclosure on the receipt of the value of any goods or services the donor received in return (the quid pro quo rule). A charity that fails to provide these disclosures can itself be penalized — tying the exempt entity's compliance directly to its donors' deductions.

Choosing among the exempt categories

Not every mission fits §501(c)(3). A §501(c)(4) social-welfare organization may engage in substantial lobbying and some political activity that a charity cannot, but contributions to it are not deductible — a trade-off advocacy groups accept. A §501(c)(6) business league, trade association, or chamber of commerce serves a common business interest (a construction-contractors association, say); member dues may be deductible as a business expense, though the portion used for lobbying is not. §501(c)(7) social clubs round out the common list. The throughline of REG Unit 3 is that the tax law follows the purpose of a transfer or an entity — income earned, value transferred at gift or death, or income devoted to charity — taxing each once under its own regime, leaving the planner to route value through the regime that serves the family and the mission at the least tax.

State registration and the compliance calendar

Exempt status is federal, but an organization must also register and report under state charity and solicitation laws and maintain the governance records the §990 makes public — board minutes, a conflict-of-interest policy, and documented compensation approvals. The §990 has itself become a transparency document: it discloses program-versus-overhead spending, the highest-paid people, and related-party transactions, so the form a charity files is in practice its public accountability statement. For a family foundation like Reed's the calendar is unforgiving — the annual 990-PF, the excise-tax computation on net investment income, and the yearly 5% minimum distribution must all be met, and a lapse converts the privilege of exemption into penalties. Exemption, in short, is earned every year, not granted once.

CMA bridge

CMA's ethics and governance themes reappear here as the law of the nonprofit sector: the private-inurement bar and self-dealing rules are the legal backbone of the tone-at-the-top controls a foundation's board must keep — and the §990 information return is the public's window into how an exempt organization actually spends its money.

Practice and recap

  1. Qualify under §501(c)(3) by meeting the organizational and operational tests; contributions are deductible only to (c)(3) organizations.
  2. Avoid private inurement, keep lobbying insubstantial, and never engage in political campaign activity.
  3. Distinguish public charities (public support test) from private foundations, which bear net-investment-income, minimum-distribution, self-dealing, and excess-business-holdings excise taxes.
  4. Pay UBIT (Form 990-T) on regularly carried-on unrelated business income and debt-financed income; file the annual Form 990 (three missed years revokes exemption).

Recap: a §501(c)(3) must be organized and operated exclusively for exempt purposes, avoid private inurement and political activity, and offers donors a deduction; private foundations face extra excise taxes (net investment income, 5% minimum distribution, self-dealing, excess business holdings) that public charities escape; UBIT taxes unrelated, regularly carried-on business income; and the annual Form 990 is the compliance backbone — three missed filings revoke the exemption.

flashcards.back: Organized AND operated exclusively for charitable/religious/educational/scientific purposes; meets the organizational and operational tests. Contributions are tax-deductible.
Private inurement (insider benefit), more-than-insubstantial lobbying, and ANY political campaign activity (absolute bar).
File Form 1023 (or 1023-EZ for small orgs); the IRS issues a determination letter.
Every (c)(3) is a private foundation unless it passes a public support test or is an inherently public institution (church/school/hospital).
Net investment income tax, ~5% minimum-distribution requirement, self-dealing, excess business holdings, jeopardizing investments, and taxable expenditures.
Regular tax (Form 990-T) on a trade/business regularly carried on and not substantially related to the exempt purpose; debt-financed income too.
Volunteer labor, sale of donated goods, member-convenience activities, and passive dividends/interest/rents are generally excluded.
Form 990 series (990/990-EZ/990-N; 990-PF for foundations); failing to file for 3 consecutive years revokes exemption.

questions.q: Contributions are tax-deductible to the donor when made to which organization?
questions.explain: Only §501(c)(3) organizations offer donors a charitable contribution deduction.

questions.q: Which activity is ABSOLUTELY prohibited for a §501(c)(3)?
choices: Political campaign activity for or against a candidate
questions.explain: Campaign intervention is an absolute bar; lobbying need only be insubstantial.

questions.q: Every §501(c)(3) is presumed to be a private foundation unless it:
choices: Qualifies as a public charity (e.g., passes a public support test)
questions.explain: A (c)(3) is a private foundation unless it qualifies as a public charity via the public support test or its institutional type.

questions.q: Private foundations must generally distribute for charitable purposes at least about:
questions.explain: Foundations face a minimum-distribution requirement of roughly 5% of net investment assets each year.

questions.q: The unrelated business income tax (UBIT) applies to income from a trade or business that is:
choices: Regularly carried on and not substantially related to the exempt purpose
questions.explain: UBIT taxes regularly carried-on business income not substantially related to the exempt purpose (and debt-financed income).

questions.q: Which is excepted from UBIT?
choices: Income from a member-convenience activity such as a hospital cafeteria
A commercial business unrelated to the mission
questions.explain: Volunteer labor, donated-goods sales, and member-convenience activities are excepted from UBIT.

questions.q: An exempt organization that fails to file its annual return for three consecutive years:
choices: Owes a small late fee only
Is converted to a private foundation
questions.explain: Three consecutive years of non-filing automatically revokes tax-exempt status.

units.title: BAR Unit 1 — Financial Analysis, Forecasting, Business Combinations & Financial Instruments

weeks.title: BAR U1·W1 — Ratio & Financial-Statement Analysis (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — reading the company through its ratios

The CPA BAR discipline (Business Analysis & Reporting) is where the analysis skills from the CMA program become an exam section. It reuses the most construction content of any discipline — WIP, working capital, and ratios — so MBG is the perfect lens. This week turns the financial statements into ratios that reveal liquidity, efficiency, solvency, and profitability, and decomposes return with the DuPont model.

Liquidity ratios

Liquidity measures the ability to pay short-term obligations. The current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities (a contractor wants comfortably above 1.0, often 1.2–1.5 for bonding). The quick (acid-test) ratio = (current assets − inventory − prepaids) ÷ current liabilities, a sterner test that strips slow assets. The cash ratio uses only cash and equivalents. Working capital (current assets − current liabilities) is the absolute-dollar cushion sureties scrutinize before bonding a job.

Activity ratios and the cash cycle

Activity ratios gauge how efficiently assets are used. Receivables turnover = net credit sales ÷ average receivables, converted to days sales outstanding (DSO) = 365 ÷ turnover. Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ average inventory, converted to days inventory. Payables turnover gives days payable. Combine them into the operating cycle (DSO + days inventory) and the cash conversion cycle (operating cycle − days payable) — the number of days cash is tied up before a job's costs are recovered, a central liquidity driver for a builder financing work in progress.

Solvency and leverage

Solvency measures long-run ability to meet obligations. Debt-to-equity = total liabilities ÷ total equity and debt-to-assets = total liabilities ÷ total assets gauge leverage. Times interest earned = EBIT ÷ interest expense shows how comfortably operating earnings cover interest, and the debt-service-coverage ratio extends that to principal-plus-interest. Sureties and lenders cap a contractor's leverage because a thinly capitalized builder cannot absorb a problem job.

Profitability

Profitability ratios scale earnings to sales or capital. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue, operating margin = operating income ÷ revenue, and net margin = net income ÷ revenue. Return on assets (ROA) = net income ÷ average assets, return on equity (ROE) = net income ÷ average equity, and return on invested capital (ROIC) measures after-tax operating return on debt-plus-equity capital. For a contractor, gross margin by job type is the most actionable — it isolates estimating and field execution.

The DuPont decomposition

The DuPont model breaks ROE into three levers: ROE = net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier (profitability × efficiency × leverage). Worked example: if MBG earns a 5% net margin, turns assets 2.0 times, and carries an equity multiplier (assets ÷ equity) of 2.5, then ROE = 5% × 2.0 × 2.5 = 25%. The power of the decomposition is diagnostic: a high ROE driven by leverage rather than margin is riskier, and DuPont tells you which lever is doing the work.

Construction-specific analysis

A contractor's statements carry accounts general analysis ignores. Costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings (underbillings) is an asset signaling work performed but not yet billed; billings in excess of costs (overbillings) is a liability signaling the job is billed ahead of cost — generally the healthier financing position. The backlog (signed but unperformed work) predicts future revenue, and the ratio of working capital and equity to backlog is exactly what a surety tests to set bonding capacity. Underbillings that grow faster than revenue can warn of estimating problems or unapproved change orders — a red flag the analyst learns to chase.

Horizontal, vertical, and common-size analysis

Ratios gain meaning in context. Horizontal (trend) analysis compares line items across periods to spot direction; vertical analysis expresses each line as a percentage of a base (sales for the income statement, total assets for the balance sheet); and common-size statements let you compare MBG to a larger competitor despite different scale. The analyst always asks for a benchmark — prior periods, industry medians, or covenant thresholds — because a ratio alone is just a number until it is compared. The standard caveats apply: ratios rely on historical cost, can be distorted by accounting choices, and must be read together, never in isolation.

Market and valuation ratios

Investors layer market ratios on top of the operating ratios. Earnings per share (EPS) drives the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio (market price ÷ EPS), the headline valuation multiple. The dividend yield (dividend per share ÷ price) and the dividend payout ratio (dividends ÷ net income) describe distribution policy, while the retention ratio (1 − payout) feeds sustainable growth. Book value per share and the price-to-book ratio compare market and accounting value, and enterprise-value multiples such as EV/EBITDA value the whole capital structure rather than just equity. A privately held contractor has no market price, so analysts apply these multiples from comparable public companies (with discounts) to estimate value — the same comparable-company logic used to value MBG for a sale or an owner buy-in.

Quality of earnings and the limits of ratios

Ratios are only as good as the earnings beneath them, so the analyst probes quality of earnings. Net income built on aggressive accruals — recognizing revenue early, under-reserving, capitalizing costs that should be expensed — diverges from cash flow, so a persistent gap between net income and operating cash flow is a warning sign. One-time gains, changes in accounting estimates, and off-balance-sheet arrangements can flatter a ratio without improving the business. The disciplined analyst reconciles earnings to cash, strips out nonrecurring items, reads the notes and segment data, and benchmarks against peers — because a single ratio, divorced from cash quality and context, can mislead as easily as inform. For a contractor, the classic distortion is an optimistic estimated cost to complete that inflates percentage-of-completion profit; the analyst tests it against physical progress and change-order history.

Cash-flow-based metrics

Because earnings can be managed, analysts lean on cash. Free cash flow (operating cash flow − capital expenditures) measures the cash a business actually generates after sustaining itself, and operating-cash-flow ratios (operating cash flow ÷ current liabilities, or ÷ total debt) test solvency without accrual noise. The cash-flow-to-net-income ratio gauges earnings quality directly. For a contractor whose reported profit depends on percentage-of-completion estimates, these cash-based measures are an essential cross-check on the accrual story.

CMA bridge

CMA month 7 introduced these same ratios and the DuPont model for internal performance; BAR tests them at exam depth and adds the construction-specific WIP and bonding analysis. The under/overbilling accounts trace straight back to the CMA cost-management and FAR revenue-recognition units — here they become analytical signals.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute liquidity (current, quick, cash, working capital) and read them against bonding thresholds.
  2. Build the operating and cash conversion cycles from DSO, days inventory, and days payable.
  3. Assess leverage (debt-to-equity, times interest earned) and profitability (margins, ROA, ROE, ROIC).
  4. Decompose ROE with DuPont (margin × turnover × leverage) and layer in construction WIP/backlog analysis.

Recap: ratios convert the statements into signals — liquidity and the cash conversion cycle for short-term health, leverage and coverage for solvency, margins and returns for profitability — and DuPont splits a 25% ROE into margin (5%), turnover (2.0), and leverage (2.5) so you can see which lever drives it; for a contractor, underbillings, overbillings, and backlog add the bonding lens a general analysis would miss, while cash-based measures like free cash flow guard against earnings flattered by optimistic percentage-of-completion estimates.

flashcards.back: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; quick ratio strips inventory and prepaids (a sterner liquidity test).
Operating cycle (DSO + days inventory) − days payable; days cash is tied up before costs are recovered.
EBIT ÷ interest expense; how comfortably operating earnings cover interest.
ROE = net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier (profitability × efficiency × leverage).
5% margin × 2.0 turnover × 2.5 equity multiplier = 25% ROE.
Underbillings (costs/earnings in excess of billings) = asset (work done, not billed); overbillings (billings in excess of costs) = liability (billed ahead of cost).
Backlog = signed but unperformed work; sureties test working capital and equity against backlog to set bonding capacity.
Vertical = each line as a % of a base (sales or total assets); horizontal = trend across periods; common-size enables cross-company comparison.

questions.q: The quick (acid-test) ratio differs from the current ratio by:
choices: Excluding inventory and prepaids from current assets
questions.explain: The quick ratio removes inventory and prepaids — the least liquid current assets.

questions.q: The cash conversion cycle equals:
choices: Days sales outstanding + days inventory − days payable
questions.explain: CCC = operating cycle (DSO + days inventory) minus days payable.

questions.q: In the DuPont model, ROE equals:
choices: Net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier
questions.explain: DuPont decomposes ROE into profitability, efficiency, and leverage.

questions.q: Net margin 5%, asset turnover 2.0, equity multiplier 2.5. ROE is:
For a contractor, 'billings in excess of costs' (overbillings) is reported as:
questions.explain: Overbillings are a liability — the job is billed ahead of cost incurred.

questions.q: Times interest earned is calculated as:
questions.explain: Times interest earned = EBIT ÷ interest expense, a coverage measure.

questions.q: Vertical (common-size) analysis expresses each line item as:
choices: A percentage of a base such as sales or total assets
A change from the prior year
questions.explain: Vertical analysis states each line as a percentage of a base, enabling cross-company comparison.

weeks.title: BAR U1·W2 — Forecasting, Projection & Variance Analysis (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — from history to expectation

Last week analyzed what happened; BAR also tests what will happen and why results differed from plan. This week covers prospective financial information, the cost-estimation and pro-forma tools behind a forecast, and the variance analysis that explains the gap between MBG's budget and its actual job results — the analytical core of the BAR Business Analysis area.

Forecasts versus projections

The profession draws a sharp line between two kinds of prospective financial information. A financial forecast presents expected results given conditions management believes will occur — appropriate for general use. A financial projection presents results under one or more hypothetical ("what-if") assumptions — "what if we win the new stadium contract?" — and is limited to users who understand the hypothesis. Both require disclosure of significant assumptions; the difference is whether the assumptions are expected or hypothetical.

Building pro forma statements

A forecast is assembled into pro forma financial statements. The usual chain starts with a sales/revenue forecast (driven by backlog and bid pipeline for a contractor), flows through cost relationships to a projected income statement, then to a pro forma balance sheet and a cash budget. The percent-of-sales method scales variable items to revenue; capital items and financing are layered in separately. The cash budget — the 13-week tool from CMA — is the most consequential output, because a profitable forecast that runs out of cash mid-job is still a failure.

Estimating cost behavior

Forecasting requires separating fixed from variable costs. The high-low method estimates the variable rate as (cost at high activity − cost at low activity) ÷ (high units − low units), then backs into fixed cost — quick but sensitive to outliers. Regression analysis fits a cost line to all the data (cost = fixed + variable × activity), and its R-squared measures how much of the cost variation the activity driver explains. A high R-squared gives confidence that the driver (labor hours, square footage) genuinely predicts the cost.

Flexible budgets and variance analysis

Comparing actual results to a static budget conflates volume and efficiency, so analysts use a flexible budget — the budget recomputed at the actual activity level. The total variance then splits cleanly. For an input cost, the price (rate) variance = (actual price − standard price) × actual quantity, and the quantity (efficiency) variance = (actual quantity − standard quantity) × standard price. Worked example: a framing crew has a standard of 2 hours per unit at $30; it actually works 2,100 hours for 1,000 units (standard 2,000 hours) at $32. The rate variance = ($32 − $30) × 2,100 = $4,200 unfavorable; the efficiency variance = (2,100 − 2,000) × $30 = $3,000 unfavorable.

Overhead and revenue variances

Overhead splits further. The variable-overhead variances mirror labor (spending and efficiency), while fixed-overhead analysis adds a volume variance — the under- or over-application of fixed cost caused by operating above or below the planned activity used to set the rate. On the top line, a sales-price variance isolates pricing and a sales-volume variance isolates quantity. The discipline is always the same: hold one factor at standard to isolate the other, so management knows whether a missed margin came from prices, usage, or volume.

Sensitivity, scenario, and simulation

Because forecasts rest on assumptions, analysts stress them. Sensitivity analysis changes one variable at a time to see how the outcome moves (how does net income respond to a 5% cost overrun?). Scenario analysis bundles consistent assumptions into best/expected/worst cases. Monte Carlo simulation runs thousands of trials drawing variables from probability distributions to produce a range of outcomes and the likelihood of each. These techniques convert a single-point forecast into an honest picture of risk — directly relevant to bidding a fixed-price construction job.

Non-financial measures and the balanced scorecard

Financial results are lagging indicators, so BAR tests non-financial KPIs and the balanced scorecard, which complements the financial perspective with customer, internal-process, and learning-and-growth perspectives. For a contractor, leading measures like safety incident rates, schedule variance, rework percentage, and bid hit-rate predict the financial results before they appear in the statements. A good scorecard ties each non-financial driver to the strategy and to an eventual financial outcome, so the analyst sees trouble while it can still be fixed.

Capital budgeting in the projection

A multiyear projection often hinges on a capital decision, so BAR tests the time-value tools. Net present value (NPV) discounts a project's cash flows at the required rate and accepts the project if NPV is positive; the internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate that sets NPV to zero, compared against the hurdle rate. The profitability index (PV of inflows ÷ initial outflow) ranks projects under capital rationing, and payback measures how fast the outlay is recovered (ignoring the time value of money and later cash flows). NPV is the theoretically preferred rule because it measures value added in dollars; IRR can mislead with non-conventional cash flows or when ranking mutually exclusive projects. For MBG, deciding whether to buy a tower crane rather than rent it is exactly this analysis. Worked NPV: a $300,000 crane generating $90,000 of annual net cash inflow for five years, discounted at 10% (five-year annuity factor 3.7908), has a present value of inflows of about $341,000 and a positive NPV near $41,000 — so buying adds value, and the IRR that equates the inflows to the $300,000 outlay comfortably exceeds the 10% hurdle.

Relevant costs and special decisions

Short-run decisions turn on relevant costs — the future cash flows that differ between alternatives — while sunk costs and unavoidable allocated overhead are ignored. This framing drives the classic analyses: make-or-buy a component, accept-or-reject a special order priced above incremental cost, keep-or-drop a segment, and sell-or-process-further. Opportunity cost — the contribution forgone from the next-best use of a constrained resource — belongs in every such analysis. A contractor weighing whether to self-perform or subcontract a scope is running a make-or-buy decision on relevant cost, and the projection should reflect only the cash flows that actually change.

CMA bridge

CMA month 2 built the budget and the 13-week cash forecast and month 3 covered variances and the balanced scorecard; BAR tests the same toolkit with the AICPA forecast-versus-projection distinction and at exam depth. The variance mechanics here are the analytical complement to the cost-management accounting MBG already practices.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish a forecast (expected) from a projection (hypothetical what-if); both disclose significant assumptions.
  2. Build pro forma statements and a cash budget; separate fixed/variable cost with high-low or regression (watch R-squared).
  3. Use a flexible budget to split variances into price/rate and quantity/efficiency (and the fixed-overhead volume variance).
  4. Stress assumptions with sensitivity, scenario, and Monte Carlo analysis; track leading non-financial KPIs via the balanced scorecard.

Recap: a forecast shows expected results and a projection shows hypothetical ones; the flexible budget isolates a price/rate variance (actual vs standard price × actual quantity) from a quantity/efficiency variance — so the framing crew's overrun splits into $4,200 of rate and $3,000 of efficiency variance — and sensitivity, scenario, and simulation analysis plus balanced-scorecard KPIs turn a single forecast into a risk-aware view of the future. Capital-budgeting rules — a positive NPV and an IRR above the hurdle rate — and relevant-cost analysis then decide which investments and special orders genuinely add value, so the projection rests on decisions that create value rather than merely cash that moves.

flashcards.back: Forecast = expected results given expected conditions (general use); projection = results under hypothetical what-if assumptions (limited use). Both disclose assumptions.
Variable rate = (high cost − low cost) ÷ (high units − low units), then solve for fixed cost. Quick but outlier-sensitive.
The fraction of cost variation explained by the activity driver; higher means the driver predicts cost well.
(Actual price − standard price) × actual quantity.
(Actual quantity − standard quantity) × standard price.
Under/over-application of fixed cost from operating above or below the planned activity used to set the rate.

flashcards.front: Sensitivity vs scenario vs Monte Carlo
flashcards.back: Sensitivity = change one variable; scenario = bundled best/expected/worst cases; Monte Carlo = many trials from probability distributions.
Financial, customer, internal process, and learning & growth — linking leading non-financial KPIs to strategy and financial outcomes.

questions.q: A financial projection differs from a financial forecast because it:
choices: Is based on one or more hypothetical assumptions
Presents expected results for general use
questions.explain: A projection uses hypothetical what-if assumptions and is limited-use; a forecast presents expected results.

questions.q: The price (rate) variance for an input is:
questions.explain: The price/rate variance holds quantity at actual and measures the price difference.

questions.q: Standard 2 hours/unit at $30; actual 2,100 hours for 1,000 units at $32. The labor RATE variance is:
Using the same data, the labor EFFICIENCY variance is:
A flexible budget is:
choices: The budget recomputed at the actual activity level
questions.explain: A flexible budget restates the budget at actual activity, separating volume from efficiency effects.

questions.q: Monte Carlo simulation produces:
choices: A range of outcomes and their likelihoods from many trials
questions.explain: Monte Carlo draws variables from distributions across many trials to produce a probability-weighted range.

questions.q: Which is a leading (non-financial) indicator on a balanced scorecard?
questions.explain: Non-financial leading measures like safety rates predict financial results before they appear.

weeks.title: BAR U1·W3 — Business Combinations & Consolidated Financial Statements (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — when one company controls another

BAR's technical-accounting area tests the hard consolidations the core sections only introduce. When MBG acquires a specialty subcontractor to bring electrical work in-house, accounting must combine two companies into one set of statements under the acquisition method, recognize goodwill, carve out the noncontrolling interest, and eliminate everything the two entities did with each other. This week builds that consolidation.

The acquisition method (ASC 805)

Every business combination uses the acquisition method. The acquirer (1) identifies itself and the acquisition date, (2) recognizes the acquiree's identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value — even ones the target never booked, like internally developed intangibles — and (3) recognizes goodwill or a bargain-purchase gain. Acquisition-related costs (legal, advisory) are expensed as incurred, not capitalized — a favorite exam point. Contingent consideration (an earnout) is recorded at fair value on the acquisition date.

Goodwill and the bargain purchase

Goodwill is the residual: consideration transferred + the fair value of any noncontrolling interest + the fair value of any previously held equity interest, minus the fair value of the net identifiable assets acquired. Worked example: MBG pays $800,000 for 80% of the sub, the 20% NCI fair value is $200,000, and the target's net identifiable assets have a fair value of $900,000. Goodwill = ($800,000 + $200,000) − $900,000 = $100,000. If instead the fair value of net assets exceeded the total consideration, the acquirer would recognize a bargain-purchase gain in earnings after rechecking its measurements.

The noncontrolling interest

When the parent buys less than 100%, the noncontrolling interest (NCI) — the outside owners' share — is reported within consolidated equity, not as a liability, and is measured at fair value at acquisition (the full-goodwill approach US GAAP uses). On the consolidated income statement, net income is shown in total and then allocated between the controlling interest and the NCI. The NCI rises with its share of subsidiary income and falls with its share of dividends — the same mechanics as the equity method, but presented inside the consolidated equity section.

The consolidation process

Consolidation combines the parent and subsidiary line by line and then eliminates the double-counting. The core eliminations: remove the parent's investment-in-subsidiary account against the subsidiary's equity (replacing it with the fair-valued assets and goodwill); eliminate intercompany receivables and payables; eliminate intercompany dividends; and eliminate intercompany sales and the related cost of sales. Without these, the consolidated statements would overstate assets, revenue, and equity by counting internal transactions as if they were with outsiders.

Eliminating intercompany profit

The subtle elimination is unrealized intercompany profit. If the acquired electrical sub sells materials to MBG at a markup and MBG has not yet used them on a job, the profit on that inventory is not yet earned from the group's perspective and must be deferred until the goods are sold outside the group. The same applies to intercompany sales of equipment (deferring the gain and adjusting depreciation). For downstream sales (parent to sub) the deferral reduces the controlling interest; for upstream sales (sub to parent) it is shared between the controlling interest and the NCI in proportion to ownership.

Goodwill impairment and VIEs

Goodwill is not amortized by public companies; it is tested for impairment at least annually at the reporting-unit level, writing it down when the unit's carrying amount exceeds its fair value (a private company may elect to amortize goodwill instead). Consolidation is also required when control exists without majority ownership: a variable interest entity (VIE) is consolidated by its primary beneficiary — the party with the power to direct the activities that most affect the VIE's performance and the obligation to absorb its losses or right to receive its benefits. The VIE model exists precisely to stop off-balance-sheet structuring of controlled entities.

Reading the consolidated result

The payoff of all this machinery is a single set of statements that presents the parent and its controlled subsidiaries as one economic entity, with outside owners shown as NCI and internal transactions erased. For an analyst applying last week's ratios, this matters enormously: a consolidated balance sheet shows the group's true leverage and the goodwill that a string of acquisitions has piled up, while the intercompany eliminations ensure the revenue and margins reflect only real, outside business. Combinations done well build capacity; combinations that generate mostly goodwill and intercompany churn are a warning the ratios will eventually expose.

The measurement period and step acquisitions

Two timing rules round out the acquisition method. The measurement period gives the acquirer up to one year to finalize provisional fair values as new information about acquisition-date facts emerges, with adjustments applied retrospectively to goodwill rather than to current earnings. A step acquisition — gaining control over a previously held equity interest — requires remeasuring that prior interest to fair value at the acquisition date, with the resulting gain or loss in earnings, before computing goodwill. This is why the goodwill formula includes the fair value of any previously held interest: control is treated as a fresh start that re-bases the whole investment.

Intra-entity debt and the consolidation worksheet

When one member of the group holds the other's bonds, consolidation treats the debt as retired from the group's perspective: the intercompany payable and receivable are eliminated, and any difference between the carrying amounts (a constructive gain or loss on extinguishment) is recognized in the consolidated statements. More broadly, the consolidation worksheet is where it all comes together — the parent and subsidiary trial balances are combined, the elimination entries are posted in worksheet columns (never on either company's books), and the consolidated totals fall out. Mastering which entries are worksheet-only versus recorded on the legal entities is exactly what the BAR consolidation simulations test, and the eliminations repeat every period the intercompany relationship persists, because the worksheet starts fresh from the legal-entity books each time.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 1 distinguished significant influence (equity method) from control (consolidation); BAR completes the picture with the full acquisition method, NCI at fair value, and the intercompany eliminations. The intercompany-elimination logic is the same discipline as the CMA construction-group consolidations across MBG's related entities.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply the acquisition method: identifiable assets/liabilities at fair value; expense acquisition costs.
  2. Compute goodwill = consideration + NCI fair value + prior interest − fair value of net identifiable assets; recognize a bargain-purchase gain if negative.
  3. Present NCI at fair value within consolidated equity; allocate consolidated net income to controlling and noncontrolling interests.
  4. Eliminate intercompany balances, sales, dividends, and unrealized profit; test goodwill for impairment; consolidate VIEs by their primary beneficiary.

Recap: the acquisition method fair-values the acquiree and books goodwill as the residual (MBG's purchase yields $100,000 of goodwill), NCI sits in consolidated equity at fair value, and consolidation eliminates intercompany balances, sales, dividends, and unrealized profit; goodwill is impairment-tested (not amortized) for public companies, and a VIE is consolidated by the primary beneficiary that controls it; the measurement period allows up to a year to finalize fair values, a step acquisition remeasures any prior interest to fair value before goodwill, and intra-entity bonds are treated as retired on consolidation — all of it posted on the consolidation worksheet, not the legal-entity books, and repeated each period the relationship persists.

flashcards.back: Recognize the acquiree's identifiable assets/liabilities at fair value; EXPENSE acquisition-related costs; record contingent consideration at fair value.
Consideration transferred + NCI fair value + fair value of any prior interest − fair value of net identifiable assets acquired.
($800,000 + $200,000 NCI) − $900,000 net identifiable assets = $100,000 goodwill.
When fair value of net assets exceeds total consideration; recognize a gain in earnings after rechecking measurements.
Outside owners' share, measured at fair value at acquisition and reported within consolidated equity (not a liability).
Eliminate investment-in-sub against sub equity, intercompany receivables/payables, intercompany dividends, and intercompany sales/COGS.
Defer profit on intercompany sales until the goods/assets leave the group; upstream deferrals are shared with the NCI.
Public-company goodwill is tested for impairment, not amortized; a VIE is consolidated by its primary beneficiary (control + absorbs losses/benefits).

questions.q: Under the acquisition method, acquisition-related costs (legal, advisory) are:
questions.explain: ASC 805 requires acquisition-related costs to be expensed, not capitalized.

questions.q: Goodwill in a business combination equals:
choices: Consideration + NCI fair value + prior interest − fair value of net identifiable assets
Purchase price − book value of net assets
questions.explain: Goodwill is the residual after fair-valuing net identifiable assets and including NCI and any prior interest.

questions.q: MBG pays $800,000 for 80%, NCI fair value is $200,000, and net identifiable assets are $900,000. Goodwill is:
The noncontrolling interest is reported:
choices: Within consolidated equity at fair value
questions.explain: US GAAP presents NCI within consolidated equity, measured at fair value at acquisition.

questions.q: Unrealized profit on an intercompany sale of inventory still held by the buyer is:
choices: Deferred until the goods are sold outside the group
questions.explain: Intercompany profit is not earned by the group until the goods leave it, so it is deferred.

questions.q: For public companies, goodwill is:
questions.explain: Public-company goodwill is impairment-tested at least annually; private companies may elect to amortize.

questions.q: A variable interest entity (VIE) is consolidated by:
questions.explain: The primary beneficiary — the party that controls the VIE and absorbs its losses/benefits — consolidates it.

weeks.title: BAR U1·W4 — Derivatives, Hedging & Foreign Currency (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — accounting for managed risk

CMA month 10 managed MBG's exposure to interest rates, material prices, and currency; BAR tests how that risk management is accounted for. Derivatives sit on the balance sheet at fair value, and where their gains and losses land depends on the hedge designation. Add the rules for foreign-currency transactions and the translation of a foreign subsidiary, and you have the BAR financial-instruments area.

Derivatives carried at fair value

A derivative derives its value from an underlying (a rate, price, or index), requires little or no net initial investment, and settles in the future. Under ASC 815, all derivatives are recognized on the balance sheet at fair value, with changes flowing to net income unless the instrument is designated and qualifies as a hedge. That default — fair value through earnings — is what makes hedge accounting an election that must be documented at inception.

The four instruments

The toolkit: a forward (a customized OTC agreement to transact at a set price later, carrying counterparty risk), a futures (its exchange-traded, daily-settled cousin), an option (the right but not the obligation to transact, bought for a premium), and a swap (an exchange of cash-flow streams, most often fixed-for-floating interest — essentially a series of forwards). Matching the instrument to the exposure is the skill: a swap to convert floating debt to fixed, a forward to lock a foreign-currency payment, an option when the firm wants downside protection while keeping upside.

Hedge accounting designations

ASC 815 recognizes three hedges, and the destination of the gain or loss differs. A fair value hedge (hedging the change in fair value of a recognized asset/liability or firm commitment) records the derivative's gain/loss and the hedged item's offsetting change in net income. A cash flow hedge (hedging variability in future cash flows — a forecasted purchase or floating-rate interest) records the effective portion in other comprehensive income, reclassified to earnings when the hedged transaction affects income. A net investment hedge (hedging the currency exposure of a foreign operation) records the effective portion in OCI within the cumulative translation adjustment.

Cash flow hedge mechanics

The recurring exam trap is the cash-flow-hedge destination: the effective portion parks in OCI first, not income. An interest-rate swap converting floating-rate debt to fixed is the classic cash flow hedge — its value runs through OCI until the interest affects earnings. Note that under ASU 2017-12, hedge ineffectiveness is no longer separately measured and immediately recognized for a qualifying hedge; the older rule that an “ineffective portion” hit income each period no longer applies, though an entity may still exclude components such as time value from the assessment.

Foreign-currency transactions

A transaction denominated in a foreign currency — buying equipment from a European manufacturer on account — is recorded at the spot rate on the transaction date, then remeasured at each balance-sheet date and at settlement, with the transaction gain or loss recognized in net income. Worked example: MBG owes €100,000 when the rate is $1.08 per euro (a $108,000 payable). If the euro strengthens to $1.12, the payable now costs $112,000 — a $4,000 transaction loss, because it takes more dollars to settle the same euro obligation. A forward contract to lock the rate would hedge exactly this exposure.

Translating a foreign subsidiary

Consolidating a foreign operation first requires identifying its functional currency — the currency of its primary economic environment. If the foreign currency is functional, the statements are translated using the current-rate method: assets and liabilities at the current rate, equity at historical rates, and income at the average rate, with the balancing translation adjustment reported in OCI (the cumulative translation adjustment). If instead the reporting currency is functional (or the economy is highly inflationary), the statements are remeasured using the temporal method: monetary items at the current rate, nonmonetary items at historical rates, with the remeasurement gain or loss in net income.

Where the adjustment lands — the unifying idea

The thread tying the week together is where a gain or loss is recognized. A naked derivative and a fair value hedge hit net income; a cash flow hedge and a net investment hedge wait in OCI; a foreign-currency transaction hits net income; translation under the current-rate method goes to OCI while remeasurement under the temporal method goes to net income. The exam rewards candidates who can place each item on that map instantly — income now, or comprehensive income until later — because that single distinction drives the reported earnings of any company that hedges or operates abroad.

Embedded derivatives, the fair-value hierarchy, and disclosures

Three further topics complete the financial-instruments picture. An embedded derivative — a derivative-like feature inside a host contract, such as a conversion option in a bond or a price-adjustment clause tied to an index — must be bifurcated and accounted for separately at fair value when its economics are not clearly and closely related to the host and the whole instrument is not already at fair value through income. Fair value itself follows the three-level hierarchy from FAR: Level 1 quoted prices in active markets, Level 2 observable inputs other than quoted prices, and Level 3 unobservable, model-based inputs (the least reliable, requiring the most disclosure). ASC 815 also demands extensive disclosures: the objectives and strategies for holding derivatives, their fair values by type, the income-statement and OCI effects, and any credit risk and collateral or master-netting arrangements that reduce it.

Put together, the financial-instruments area rewards a single habit of mind: identify the instrument, decide whether it is a stand-alone derivative or a designated hedge, place its gains and losses in net income or OCI, and disclose enough that a user understands the risk. The same discipline that lets MBG hedge a euro equipment purchase or a floating-rate construction loan is what the BAR exam tests — the accounting that turns a risk decision into a faithful number.

CMA bridge

CMA month 10 chose the hedging instruments; FAR month 7 introduced fair value; BAR puts them together with the ASC 815 designations and the foreign-currency translation rules. The cash-flow-hedge-to-OCI distinction and the FX remeasurement-to-income rule are the accounting counterpart to the risk decisions MBG already makes.

Practice and recap

  1. Carry all derivatives at fair value; changes hit net income unless designated as a qualifying hedge.
  2. Place hedge gains/losses: fair value hedge → net income; cash flow hedge effective portion → OCI; net investment hedge → OCI/CTA.
  3. Recognize foreign-currency transaction gains/losses in net income (remeasure at each date and settlement).
  4. Translate (current-rate, adjustment to OCI) when the foreign currency is functional; remeasure (temporal, gain/loss to net income) when the reporting currency is functional.

Recap: derivatives are at fair value with changes in income unless hedged; a fair value hedge runs through income while a cash flow hedge's effective portion waits in OCI; a foreign-currency payable produces a transaction gain/loss in net income (MBG's €100,000 payable costs $4,000 more when the euro rises to $1.12); and a foreign subsidiary is translated to OCI under the current-rate method or remeasured to income under the temporal method depending on its functional currency.

flashcards.back: Recognized at fair value; changes flow to net income unless designated and qualifying as a hedge (ASC 815).
Gain/loss on the derivative AND the hedged item are recognized in net income.
Effective portion goes to OCI, reclassified to net income when the hedged transaction affects earnings (e.g., a floating-to-fixed interest-rate swap).
Effective portion goes to OCI within the cumulative translation adjustment.
Hedge ineffectiveness is no longer separately measured and immediately recognized for a qualifying hedge.
Remeasure the foreign-denominated balance each date and at settlement; the gain/loss goes to NET INCOME.
Foreign currency is functional: assets/liabilities at current rate, equity at historical, income at average; adjustment to OCI (CTA).
Reporting currency is functional (or highly inflationary): monetary at current, nonmonetary at historical; gain/loss to NET INCOME.

questions.q: Absent hedge designation, changes in a derivative's fair value are reported in:
questions.explain: By default a derivative is at fair value with changes in net income; hedge accounting is an election.

questions.q: The effective portion of a CASH FLOW hedge is recorded in:
choices: Other comprehensive income, later reclassified to income
questions.explain: The effective portion parks in OCI and is reclassified when the hedged transaction affects earnings.

questions.q: A gain or loss on a FAIR VALUE hedge and its hedged item is recognized in:
questions.explain: Both the derivative and the hedged item's offsetting change run through net income.

questions.q: MBG owes €100,000; the rate moves from $1.08 to $1.12 per euro. The result is a:
questions.explain: The payable rises from $108,000 to $112,000 — a $4,000 loss, since more dollars are needed to settle the euro obligation.

questions.q: When the foreign currency is the functional currency, financial statements are:
choices: Translated using the current-rate method, with the adjustment in OCI
Remeasured using the temporal method, with the gain/loss in net income
questions.explain: Functional = foreign currency → current-rate translation, adjustment to OCI (CTA).

questions.q: Under the temporal (remeasurement) method, the remeasurement gain or loss is reported in:
questions.explain: Temporal-method remeasurement gains/losses go to net income (used when the reporting currency is functional).

questions.q: An interest-rate swap converting floating-rate debt to fixed is typically a:
questions.explain: It hedges variability in future interest cash flows — a cash flow hedge (effective portion to OCI).

units.title: BAR Unit 2 — Cost Accounting, Public/SEC Reporting, Governmental II & Economics/Valuation

weeks.title: BAR U2·W1 — Cost Accounting & Managerial Analysis (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — what a job actually costs

BAR's business-analysis area tests the cost accounting that drives MBG's bids and margins. Before you can analyze a contractor's profitability you must know how costs are classified, accumulated into jobs, and behaved as volume changes. This week builds the costing systems, cost-volume-profit analysis, and standard-cost variances that turn raw spending into decision-useful numbers.

Classifying costs

Costs are sorted several ways. Product costs (direct materials, direct labor, manufacturing overhead) attach to the output and sit in inventory until sold; period costs (selling, general, and administrative) are expensed as incurred. Costs are also direct (traceable to a cost object) or indirect (allocated), and by behavior — variable (changes with volume), fixed (constant in total within the relevant range), or mixed. For decisions, the only costs that matter are relevant — future costs that differ between alternatives; sunk costs are ignored.

Job-order versus process costing

The accumulation system fits the production. Job-order costing traces costs to distinct jobs — perfect for a contractor, where each project (the cost object) accumulates its own materials, labor, and applied overhead. Process costing averages costs over homogeneous mass-produced units, computing equivalent units of production (partially complete units expressed as whole units) under the weighted-average or FIFO method. Overhead is applied using a predetermined rate (budgeted overhead ÷ budgeted activity), with any over- or under-applied overhead closed to cost of goods sold at period end.

Activity-based costing

Activity-based costing (ABC) improves overhead allocation by assigning costs to activities (setups, inspections, material handling) and then to products using cost drivers that cause the activity. ABC is more accurate than a single plant-wide rate when products consume overhead in different proportions than the volume base — it stops high-volume simple products from subsidizing low-volume complex ones. The trade-off is cost and complexity, so ABC is used where overhead is large and diverse.

Cost-volume-profit analysis

CVP analysis links cost, volume, and profit through the contribution margin (sales − variable costs), the amount each sale contributes to covering fixed costs and then profit. The break-even point in units = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit; in dollars = fixed costs ÷ the contribution-margin ratio. Worked example: fixed costs of $300,000 and a $50 contribution margin per unit break even at 6,000 units; to earn a $100,000 target profit requires ($300,000 + $100,000) ÷ $50 = 8,000 units. The margin of safety (actual minus break-even sales) and operating leverage (contribution margin ÷ operating income) measure how sensitive profit is to a sales change.

Absorption versus variable costing

Two costing philosophies treat fixed manufacturing overhead differently. Absorption (full) costing — required for GAAP and tax — treats fixed overhead as a product cost that stays in inventory until sold. Variable (direct) costing — for internal use — expenses fixed overhead as a period cost. The result: when production exceeds sales, absorption income is higher (fixed overhead is deferred in inventory), and the difference reverses when sales exceed production. Reconciling the two is a classic exam computation.

Standard costs and variances

A standard cost system sets expected prices and quantities and analyzes the variances from actual (the foundation laid in BAR Unit 1). Direct cost variances split into price/rate and quantity/efficiency; overhead is analyzed more finely. The four-variance overhead method computes a variable-overhead spending and efficiency variance and a fixed-overhead budget (spending) and volume variance. The volume variance — fixed overhead applied versus budgeted — measures capacity utilization and has no cash effect; it simply reflects producing above or below the level used to set the rate.

Joint products, by-products, and spoilage

When a single process yields multiple outputs, joint costs incurred before the split-off point are allocated among joint products — usually by relative sales value at split-off (or net realizable value), sometimes by physical units. A minor by-product is often credited against the main product's cost. Spoilage is split into normal (inherent in the process — a product cost spread over good units) and abnormal (avoidable — a period loss recognized separately). Each rule keeps inventory and cost of goods sold faithful when production is messy.

Service-department allocation and decision analysis

Overhead from service departments (maintenance, IT) is allocated to operating departments by the direct, step-down, or reciprocal method — the reciprocal method being the most accurate because it recognizes services the departments provide to each other. Cost data also feeds short-run decision analysis: a special order is accepted if its price exceeds the incremental (relevant) cost, even below full cost, when capacity is idle; a make-or-buy decision compares the avoidable cost of making to the purchase price plus the opportunity cost of the freed capacity; and a keep-or-drop decision turns on whether a segment's contribution margin covers its avoidable fixed costs. The unifying rule is that only future costs that differ between alternatives are relevant — allocated common costs and sunk costs are ignored.

Quality and constraint costs

Modern cost management tracks the cost of quality in four buckets — prevention and appraisal (conformance costs spent to avoid defects) versus internal and external failure (nonconformance costs of defects caught before or after delivery) — the insight being that spending on prevention usually lowers total quality cost. The theory of constraints focuses improvement on the bottleneck resource, maximizing throughput (sales minus direct materials) per unit of the constraint. For a contractor, the scarce resource is often skilled crews or key equipment, so scheduling around that constraint drives profitability more than shaving unit costs elsewhere.

A worked equivalent-units calculation

Process costing's signature computation is equivalent units. Suppose a department finishes 17,000 units and leaves 3,000 units 60% complete in ending work in process. Under the weighted-average method, equivalent units = units completed (17,000) + ending WIP × completion (3,000 × 60% = 1,800) = 18,800 equivalent units, and the cost per equivalent unit = total costs (beginning WIP + costs added) ÷ 18,800. The FIFO method instead isolates the work done this period — the effort to finish beginning WIP, plus units started and completed, plus ending WIP's progress. Either way, the equivalent-unit cost is applied to units transferred out and to ending inventory — the mechanism that values partially complete production.

CMA bridge

CMA months 3 and 4 built this cost-management toolkit for MBG; BAR tests it at exam depth and ties it to the financial-analysis ratios from BAR Unit 1. Job-order costing is exactly how MBG accumulates construction costs into the WIP that FAR's percentage-of-completion then recognizes — cost accounting is where the construction numbers begin.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify costs: product vs period, direct vs indirect, variable/fixed/mixed, relevant vs sunk.
  2. Use job-order costing for distinct projects and process costing (equivalent units) for mass production; apply overhead with a predetermined rate and close over/under-applied to COGS.
  3. Compute CVP: break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin; reconcile absorption vs variable costing.
  4. Analyze four-variance overhead (variable spending/efficiency; fixed budget/volume); allocate joint costs by relative sales value and split normal vs abnormal spoilage.

Recap: cost accounting classifies and accumulates costs — job-order for a contractor, process costing with equivalent units for mass output, and ABC when overhead is diverse; CVP finds the break-even (fixed costs ÷ contribution margin, so $300,000 ÷ $50 = 6,000 units); absorption costing defers fixed overhead in inventory while variable costing expenses it; and four-variance analysis plus joint-cost allocation and spoilage rules complete the managerial toolkit.

flashcards.back: Product costs (DM, DL, MOH) inventory until sold; period costs (SG&A) are expensed as incurred.
Job-order traces costs to distinct jobs (e.g., a construction project); process averages costs over homogeneous units via equivalent units (FIFO or weighted average).
Assigns overhead to activities, then to products via cost drivers; more accurate when products consume overhead in different proportions than volume.
Units = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit; dollars = fixed costs ÷ contribution-margin ratio. Target profit adds desired profit to fixed costs.
$300,000 fixed ÷ $50 CM = 6,000 units; +$100,000 target profit → 8,000 units.
Absorption (GAAP/tax) makes fixed overhead a product cost (deferred in inventory); variable costing expenses it as a period cost. Production > sales → absorption income higher.
Fixed overhead applied vs budgeted; measures capacity utilization, no cash effect.
Allocate pre-split-off joint costs by relative sales value (or NRV) at split-off; by-products often credited against main product cost.

questions.q: A construction contractor accumulating costs by project uses:
questions.explain: Distinct projects are cost objects under job-order costing; process costing suits homogeneous mass production.

questions.q: The break-even point in units equals:
choices: Fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit
questions.explain: Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit.

questions.q: Fixed costs $300,000, contribution margin $50/unit. Units to earn a $100,000 target profit:
Activity-based costing improves accuracy by:
choices: Assigning overhead to activities via cost drivers
questions.explain: ABC traces overhead to activities and then to products through cost drivers.

questions.q: When production exceeds sales, absorption-costing net income compared with variable costing is:
questions.explain: Absorption defers fixed overhead in ending inventory, raising income relative to variable costing.

questions.q: Joint costs incurred before the split-off point are most commonly allocated by:
questions.explain: Relative sales value (or NRV) at split-off is the usual joint-cost allocation base.

questions.q: Normal spoilage is treated as:
choices: A product cost spread over good units
questions.explain: Normal spoilage is inherent and absorbed into the cost of good units; abnormal spoilage is a separate period loss.

weeks.title: BAR U2·W2 — Public-Company & SEC Reporting (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — reporting to the public markets

A company that sells securities to the public enters the SEC's reporting regime, and BAR tests its mechanics: the required filings, the diluted EPS the market watches, segment and interim disclosures, and the controls regime under Sarbanes-Oxley. MBG is privately held, but understanding public reporting is squarely on the BAR blueprint and rounds out the technical-reporting area.

The SEC filing framework

Public companies file on prescribed forms. The 10-K is the audited annual report (financial statements, MD&A, risk factors, controls); the 10-Q is the quarterly report (reviewed, not audited); and the 8-K reports material events between periodic reports (an acquisition, a change of auditor, a bankruptcy) within four business days. A proxy statement supports shareholder votes, an S-1 registers a new securities offering, and insiders file Forms 3, 4, and 5 for their holdings and trades. Filing deadlines vary by filer status (large accelerated, accelerated, non-accelerated).

MD&A and the annual report

Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) is the narrative bridge between the numbers and the business — management's explanation of results, liquidity and capital resources, known trends and uncertainties, and critical accounting estimates. It is required but unaudited (the auditor reads it for material inconsistency, as in AUD Unit 2). Together with the audited statements, the risk factors, and the controls report, MD&A makes the 10-K the central document a public-company analyst reads.

Diluted earnings per share

The public-company metric is EPS. Basic EPS = (net income − preferred dividends) ÷ weighted-average common shares. Diluted EPS adds the dilutive effect of options/warrants (the treasury-stock method) and convertibles (the if-converted method). Worked example: net income available to common of $900,000 over 300,000 weighted shares is $3.00 basic; if 30,000 options with a $20 exercise price exist while the average market price is $25, the treasury-stock method adds 6,000 net shares ($600,000 of proceeds buys back 24,000 shares), so diluted EPS = $900,000 ÷ 306,000 = $2.94. Only dilutive securities are included; antidilutive ones are ignored, so diluted EPS is always less than or equal to basic.

Segment and interim reporting

Public companies disclose operating segments under the management approach (ASC 280) — any segment meeting a 10% test of revenue, profit/loss, or assets is reportable, with reported segments covering at least 75% of external revenue, plus entity-wide disclosures (products, geography, major customers). Interim reports (ASC 270) treat each period as an integral part of the year — income taxes use the estimated annual effective rate — while recognizing some items discretely (a permanent inventory write-down). Both give investors visibility the annual aggregate hides.

Related parties, subsequent events, and uncertainties

Three disclosure areas protect investors. Related-party transactions must be disclosed (the nature of the relationship, the amounts, and terms) because arm's-length cannot be presumed. Subsequent events are recognized (Type I) or disclosed (Type II) per the FAR rules, through the date the statements are issued. Risks and uncertainties — significant estimates, concentrations (a major customer or supplier), and vulnerabilities — are disclosed so users can assess what could change. These narrative disclosures are as exam-relevant as the numbers.

Non-GAAP measures and XBRL

Companies often present non-GAAP measures (adjusted EBITDA, free cash flow) to tell their story, but Regulation G requires the most comparable GAAP measure with a reconciliation, and the non-GAAP figure may not be more prominent or misleading. Filings are tagged in XBRL (eXtensible Business Reporting Language), machine-readable tags that let regulators and analysts extract and compare data automatically. Both reflect the SEC's push for transparency and comparability in how results are communicated.

Sarbanes-Oxley and internal control

Sarbanes-Oxley reshaped public-company reporting. §302 requires the CEO and CFO to certify the financial statements and disclosure controls; §404 requires management to assess internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) and, for accelerated and large accelerated filers, the external auditor to attest to it (the integrated audit and CAMs from AUD Unit 2). SOX also created the PCAOB to oversee auditors, mandated audit-committee independence, and restricted auditor non-audit services. The controls regime is the structural backbone behind the reliability the SEC filings promise.

Registration, exemptions, and comprehensive income

Going public starts with registration under the Securities Act of 1933 (the S-1 and prospectus), unless an exemption applies — the most common being Regulation D private placements to accredited investors. Ongoing reporting then follows under the 1934 Act. Public statements also present comprehensive income — net income plus other comprehensive income (OCI) — in a single statement or two consecutive statements; OCI collects the AFS, hedge, pension, and foreign-currency items routed around net income in earlier FAR units, with a reclassification adjustment when they are realized. Reporting discontinued operations (a disposed component representing a strategic shift) separately, net of tax, and presenting earnings per share for income from continuing operations and for net income, complete the income-statement presentation the SEC expects.

Filer status, deadlines, and the audit committee

A company's filer status — large accelerated, accelerated, or non-accelerated — sets its filing deadlines and whether the §404(b) auditor ICFR attestation applies (only accelerated and large accelerated filers). The audit committee, composed of independent directors, hires and oversees the external auditor, pre-approves services, and handles whistleblower complaints — a Sarbanes-Oxley governance requirement. These structural rules, with the certification and ICFR requirements, are why public reporting carries a credibility a private company's statements achieve only through a voluntary audit.

Required statements and the going-concern note

A complete set of public financial statements includes the balance sheet, income statement (with continuing operations, discontinued operations, and EPS), statement of comprehensive income, statement of cash flows, statement of changes in stockholders' equity, and the notes. Management must also evaluate and, where substantial doubt exists, disclose going-concern uncertainty, on which the auditor reports (AUD Unit 2). The summary of significant accounting policies opens the notes, followed by the detail behind line items, commitments and contingencies, fair-value disclosures, and subsequent events. Quarterly statements are condensed but must still disclose material changes since the annual report. Together these give the market a complete, comparable picture — the disclosure depth that distinguishes public reporting from a private company's leaner statements.

CMA bridge

This week ties FAR's EPS and segment rules, AUD's integrated-audit and CAM reporting, and REG's 1933/1934 Acts into the single public-reporting picture. For a closely held contractor like MBG the SOX and SEC requirements are not mandatory, but the same control discipline and the same EPS/segment mechanics are exactly what the exam tests across sections.

Practice and recap

  1. Match SEC forms to purpose: 10-K (annual/audited), 10-Q (quarterly/reviewed), 8-K (material events), S-1 (registration), Forms 3/4/5 (insiders).
  2. Compute diluted EPS with the treasury-stock and if-converted methods; include only dilutive securities.
  3. Apply segment (10% tests, 75% coverage, management approach) and interim (integral, estimated annual effective tax rate) reporting; disclose related parties, subsequent events, and risks.
  4. Reconcile non-GAAP measures (Reg G), tag in XBRL, and apply SOX §302/§404 certification and ICFR requirements.

Recap: public companies file the 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K with MD&A and risk factors; diluted EPS adds dilutive options (treasury-stock method) and convertibles (if-converted) — $900,000 over 306,000 shares is $2.94; segment and interim rules plus related-party, subsequent-event, and risk disclosures inform investors; non-GAAP measures need a Reg G reconciliation; and Sarbanes-Oxley §302/§404 certification, ICFR, and the PCAOB underpin the reliability of it all.
