weeks.title: BAR U2·W3 — Governmental Accounting II: Funds, Entries & Reconciliation (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the two-perspective government

FAR Unit 3 introduced fund accounting; BAR drills the mechanics — the budgetary and encumbrance entries, the modified-accrual recognition rules, and the conversion that bridges the fund statements to the government-wide statements. A government keeps its books two ways at once, and the BAR exam tests whether you can move cleanly between them.

Budgetary accounting

Unlike a business, a government records its legally adopted budget in the accounts. The opening entry debits Estimated revenues, credits Appropriations (the spending authority), and books the difference to budgetary fund balance. Worked entry: with estimated revenues of $1,000,000 and appropriations of $950,000, the government debits Estimated Revenues $1,000,000, credits Appropriations $950,000, and credits Budgetary Fund Balance $50,000. These budgetary accounts are memorandum control accounts, closed at year-end, separate from the actual revenue and expenditure accounts.

The encumbrance cycle

To prevent overspending, governments encumber appropriations when a commitment is made. Issuing a purchase order debits Encumbrances and credits Budgetary fund balance reserved for encumbrances, reserving the appropriation. When the goods arrive, the entry is reversed and the actual expenditure and a liability (vouchers payable) are recorded. Encumbrances are not expenditures and not GAAP-basis expenses — they are a budgetary control — and any outstanding at year-end are reported as a commitment.

Governmental-fund recognition

Governmental funds use the modified-accrual basis and the current-financial-resources focus. Revenue is recognized when measurable and available (collectible within the period or soon enough after — commonly 60 days — to pay current liabilities); property taxes are recognized in the period for which levied. Expenditures are recognized when the related liability is incurred, with two exceptions: capital outlay is an expenditure in full (no capitalization or depreciation in the fund), and debt service (principal and interest) is an expenditure only when due and payable, not as it accrues.

Capital projects and debt service funds

Two governmental funds handle infrastructure. A capital projects fund accounts for resources to build major assets (a road or school); bond proceeds are an other financing source (the fund records no long-term liability), and payments to contractors are expenditures as incurred. A debt service fund accumulates resources and records principal and interest as expenditures when due. The capital asset and the bond payable both appear only in the government-wide statements, not the funds — the gap the reconciliation must close.

Government-wide conversion and reconciliation

The government-wide statements use full accrual and the economic-resources focus, so a reconciliation converts the governmental funds' change in fund balance to the change in net position. The major adjustments: add capital outlay and subtract depreciation (funds expensed the whole asset; government-wide capitalizes and depreciates it); subtract bond proceeds and add debt principal repayments (funds treated them as financing source/expenditure; government-wide treats them as a liability change); and adjust for accrued interest and other revenues earned but not yet available. Mastering this bridge is the single most tested BAR governmental skill.

Proprietary and fiduciary funds

Proprietary funds — enterprise (services to the public for a fee, like a water utility) and internal service (services to other government departments) — already use full accrual and the economic-resources focus, so they look like a business, with a statement of net position, a statement of revenues/expenses/changes in net position, and a four-category statement of cash flows. Fiduciary funds — custodial and trust — hold resources for others and are excluded from the government-wide statements because they are not the government's to use.

Interfund activity and the reporting package

Resources moving between funds carry specific labels: interfund transfers are other financing sources/uses (not revenues/expenditures); interfund loans create a due-to/due-from. The full annual report — the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) — wraps the government-wide and fund statements with Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A), the notes, and required supplementary information (RSI) such as the budgetary comparison schedule and pension/OPEB schedules. The ACFR is the government's full accountability document, the public-sector parallel to a corporation's 10-K.

Specific governmental transactions and GASB measurement

Several transactions have their own GASB rules. Special assessments — charges to property owners for improvements that benefit them — are accounted for in a capital projects or debt service fund depending on the government's obligation. Grants follow the nonexchange rules: recognized when eligibility requirements are met (and, on modified accrual, when available). Under GASB 87, most government leases create a right-to-use lease asset and a corresponding liability in the government-wide statements, paralleling ASC 842. Pensions (GASB 68) and OPEB (GASB 75) put the net pension/OPEB liability — the total liability minus plan fiduciary net position — on the government-wide statement of net position, with deferred inflows and outflows smoothing the changes.

Net position, fund balance, and budgetary reporting

Governments classify their residual equity two ways. In the government-wide statements, net position divides into net investment in capital assets, restricted, and unrestricted. In the governmental funds, GASB 54 sorts fund balance into nonspendable, restricted, committed, assigned, and unassigned — a hierarchy of spending constraints. The budgetary comparison schedule (original budget, final budget, and actual) is required supplementary information that holds the government accountable to its adopted budget — the public-sector analogue to a company explaining results against its guidance.

The reporting entity and the statistical section

Defining the financial reporting entity matters in government: the primary government combines with its component units — legally separate organizations for which it is financially accountable — either blended (reported as if part of the primary government) or discretely presented (in a separate column). Beyond the basic statements and RSI, a full ACFR contains an introductory section (the transmittal letter), the audited financial section, and a statistical section with roughly ten years of economic, demographic, and debt-trend data. This breadth lets bondholders and citizens assess the government's long-run fiscal health — the accountability purpose that distinguishes governmental from for-profit reporting.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 3 summarized governmental accounting; BAR supplies the entries and the fund-to-government-wide reconciliation the exam tests in simulations. The budgetary and encumbrance discipline mirrors the appropriation control a construction client's public-sector owner uses on the very projects MBG bids — government accounting is where the owner's side of a public job is recorded.

Practice and recap

  1. Record the budgetary entry (Estimated revenues / Appropriations / budgetary fund balance) and the encumbrance cycle (PO → reverse + expenditure on receipt).
  2. Recognize modified-accrual revenue when measurable and available; expenditure when the liability is incurred; capital outlay in full; debt service when due.
  3. Reconcile fund balance to net position: add capital outlay, subtract depreciation, subtract bond proceeds, add principal repayments, adjust accrued interest.
  4. Treat proprietary funds on full accrual; exclude fiduciary funds from government-wide statements; label interfund transfers as other financing sources/uses; assemble the ACFR (MD&A + RSI).

Recap: governments record budgets and encumbrances as control accounts, recognize governmental-fund revenue when measurable and available and expenditures when the liability is incurred (capital outlay in full, debt service when due), and then reconcile the fund change in balance to the government-wide change in net position by adding capital outlay, subtracting depreciation, subtracting bond proceeds, and adding principal repayments — with proprietary funds on full accrual, fiduciary funds excluded, and the ACFR wrapping it all in MD&A and RSI.

Recorded as an OTHER FINANCING SOURCE (no long-term liability in the fund); the bond payable appears only government-wide.
Proprietary (enterprise/internal service) use full accrual and appear government-wide; fiduciary funds are EXCLUDED from government-wide statements.
MD&A, government-wide + fund financial statements, notes, and required supplementary information (budgetary comparison, pension/OPEB schedules).

weeks.title: BAR U2·W4 — Economics, Financial Risk & Business Valuation (CPA Discipline)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the analyst's wider lens

BAR's business-analysis area reaches beyond the statements to the economic environment, the risks a business faces, and how it is valued. To advise on MBG — or analyze any company — you need the economic concepts that move demand and rates, the risk-management toolkit, and the valuation methods that turn forecasts into a number. This week closes the discipline.

Microeconomics

Supply and demand set price where they intersect; shifts in either move the equilibrium. Price elasticity of demand measures how quantity responds to price — elastic (greater than 1, total revenue falls when price rises) versus inelastic (less than 1, revenue rises with price). Market structures range from perfect competition (many price-takers, no pricing power) through monopolistic competition and oligopoly to monopoly (one price-maker). Construction is closer to competitive bidding, so MBG is largely a price-taker constrained by the market.

Macroeconomics

The economy moves through the business cycle — expansion, peak, contraction, trough. GDP measures output; inflation erodes purchasing power; and unemployment tracks slack. Governments respond with fiscal policy (taxes and spending) and central banks with monetary policy (the money supply and interest rates). For a capital-intensive contractor, the cycle and interest rates drive demand for new construction and the cost of financing equipment — the macro backdrop to every bid.

Interest rates and the cost of capital

A firm's cost of capital is the blended return its investors require — the weighted-average cost of capital (WACC). WACC = (E/V) × cost of equity + (D/V) × after-tax cost of debt, where the debt cost is reduced by the tax shield. Worked example: 60% equity at a 12% cost and 40% debt at a 6% pre-tax cost with a 21% tax rate gives WACC = (0.60 × 12%) + (0.40 × 6% × (1 − 0.21)) = 7.2% + 1.9% = 9.1%. WACC is the discount rate for valuing the whole firm and the hurdle rate for its investments.

Business valuation — discounted cash flow

The discounted-cash-flow (DCF) method values a business as the present value of its expected free cash flows discounted at the WACC, plus a terminal value capturing cash flows beyond the forecast horizon (often a growing perpetuity: terminal value = next-year FCF ÷ (WACC − growth)). DCF is theoretically the soundest method because it rests on the cash a business actually produces, but it is sensitive to the assumptions — small changes in the discount rate or growth rate swing the value materially, which is why analysts test the inputs.

Business valuation — market and asset approaches

Two other approaches complement DCF. The market (comparable) approach applies multiples from similar public companies or transactions — P/E, EV/EBITDA, price-to-book — to the subject's metrics, with discounts for a private company's lack of marketability and any minority interest. The asset (cost) approach values the business at the fair value of its net assets, a floor most relevant for asset-heavy or liquidating entities. A contractor like MBG is typically valued with a blend — DCF on its backlog-driven cash flows, sanity-checked against construction-industry multiples.

Financial risk management

A business faces several financial risks: interest-rate, credit (a customer or counterparty defaulting), market/price, liquidity, and foreign-exchange risk. Value at risk (VaR) estimates the maximum loss over a period at a given confidence level. Firms mitigate with the derivatives and hedges from BAR Unit 1 (swaps, forwards, options), with diversification, and with operational measures (credit limits, matching foreign revenues to foreign costs). The goal is not zero risk but the right residual risk at a justified cost — the risk-appetite discipline from the CMA program.

Enterprise risk management and working capital

The COSO ERM framework embeds risk management in strategy and governance: identifying risks across the enterprise, assessing likelihood and impact, and responding within the board's risk appetite. On the operational side, working-capital management optimizes the cash tied up in receivables, inventory, and payables — shortening the cash conversion cycle from BAR Unit 1, managing the cash budget, and balancing the cost of holding liquidity against the risk of running short. For a contractor financing work in progress, working-capital discipline is often the difference between a profitable job and a cash crisis.

Capital structure and dividend policy

How a firm finances itself shapes its risk and value. Capital-structure theory weighs the tax benefit of debt (interest is deductible, lowering WACC) against the rising costs of financial distress as leverage grows — the trade-off that produces an optimal mix. Operating leverage (fixed operating costs) and financial leverage (fixed financing costs) both magnify how a change in sales flows to earnings, raising return and risk together. Dividend policy balances returning cash to shareholders against retaining it for growth; the residual theory pays dividends only from cash left after positive-NPV projects, while a stable-dividend policy signals confidence. For a contractor financing equipment and work in progress, the leverage decision interacts directly with the bonding capacity from BAR Unit 1.

Working-capital financing and short-term decisions

Beyond managing the cash conversion cycle, a firm chooses how to finance current assets. A conservative strategy funds even temporary needs with long-term capital (lower risk, higher cost); an aggressive strategy funds some permanent needs with short-term debt (lower cost, higher refinancing risk). Tools include a line of credit, commercial paper for large firms, and factoring or pledging receivables for quick cash. Evaluating a cash discount (whether to pay early to capture a 2/10, net 30 offer) and setting credit policy round out the short-term decisions that, for a working-capital-intensive contractor, often matter more to survival than the long-run valuation.

Inflation, exchange rates, and globalization

Two macro forces close the analysis. Inflation raises nominal interest rates (the Fisher effect: the nominal rate roughly equals the real rate plus expected inflation) and erodes the value of fixed cash flows, so a valuation must discount at a rate consistent with its inflation assumption. Exchange rates move with relative interest rates, inflation, and trade balances, affecting any firm that buys or sells across borders — the FX exposure hedged in BAR Unit 1. For a domestic contractor these are mostly a backdrop, but the BAR exam expects awareness of how the macro environment feeds the discount rate and the cash flows a valuation rests on.

CMA bridge

This week unifies the CMA finance threads — cost of capital and capital budgeting (month 8/11), risk management (month 10), and the analysis ratios (month 7) — into the BAR business-analysis area. WACC, DCF, and the risk framework are exactly the tools used to value MBG and decide its investments, the analytical capstone of the whole discipline.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply micro concepts (supply/demand, elasticity, market structures) and macro concepts (business cycle, fiscal/monetary policy).
  2. Compute WACC as the tax-adjusted blend of equity and debt costs; use it as the discount and hurdle rate.
  3. Value a business by DCF (free cash flows + terminal value), market multiples, or the asset approach.
  4. Identify and mitigate financial risks (interest, credit, market, liquidity, FX), apply VaR and COSO ERM, and manage working capital.

Recap: economic concepts set the demand and rate environment; WACC blends the after-tax cost of debt and the cost of equity (here 9.1%) to serve as the discount and hurdle rate; business value comes from DCF (free cash flows plus a terminal value), market multiples, or net assets; and financial-risk management — risk types, VaR, hedging, COSO ERM, and working-capital discipline — protects the value the analysis identifies.

Income (DCF), market (comparable multiples like EV/EBITDA, P/E), and asset (net asset value) approaches; private companies take marketability/minority discounts.
The maximum expected loss over a period at a given confidence level.
Interest-rate, credit, market/price, liquidity, and foreign-exchange risk — mitigated by hedging, diversification, and operational controls within risk appetite (COSO ERM).
